cause.where: FFI-2, p16-ffi.md 33-42: the safe-to-call fact. Three spellings assert it for a call: `safe fn` (FFI-10), an overlay function entry (FFI-2 36-38; GRM-35 277-281: 'a function entry, which asserts the function safe to call') and `@ffi(safe)` on a function-pointer typedef (FFI-56, 596-598). The fact has no limit on raw pointers. The only limit is FFI-10's sentence at 82-84, and it covers one spelling and one position: a raw-pointer parameter or result of a hand declaration. A contract (FFI-1, 26-32) counts only pointer-typed parameters and results; contract words attach only to those slots (FFI-11, 284-286), and an overlay never changes a type's fields (FFI-30a, 210-212). So a raw pointer in a struct field, in an array or span element, in a C++ method's object, or returned by a callback the call gives C, is in no contract and under no limit.
cause.why_there: ODR-073's reason (p26-appx-h.md 361; OWNER-QUEUE.md 3672-3673: 'a safe caller may pass a null, dangling or forged pointer; the contract cannot establish validity') is a property of what any assertion of safety can cover. It is not specific to hand declarations or to parameter slots. Safe code makes such a pointer: `null[P]()`, `ref_to_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr()` (p04-types.md 340-348, p07-ownership.md 837-838), a pointer-cast constant (FFI-6a, p16 150-151). It can then put that pointer in a struct field or a span element. So the limit belongs where the fact is defined, and every spelling that asserts the fact shares it. FFI-11 and FFI-30a are right as written: they explain why a field pointer can never be contracted, which is why no assertion may cover it. FFI-10's and FFI-56's lists accept 'a `@layout(c)` value type' only because no limit sat above them, so each list gets a cite, not a rule of its own. A fourth assertion, `@ffi(std_function)` (p21-annex-c.md 67), has no limit at all, not even on a raw-pointer parameter, and its way out needs a spelling the language lacks. It is decision 4, for the owner, and its text is left as it is.

existing_rule.rule: FFI-10 (with ODR-073's reason), applied through FFI-2's definition of the safe-to-call fact
existing_rule.words: FFI-2: "The safe-to-call fact is never derived ...: it is asserted by `safe fn` in an extern block (`[FFI-10]`), or by an overlay entry for the function, which asserts that a call within its contract cannot break memory safety". FFI-10: "A raw `*T` can be declared for an unsafe call, but complete facts do not make a raw-pointer parameter or result safe to expose; `safe fn` with one is `E5002`." ODR-073 (OWNER-QUEUE.md 3672-3673, 3682-3684): "a safe caller may pass a null, dangling or forged pointer; the contract cannot establish validity". IV.5: "Creating one from a reference is safe (ODR-075) ... `null[P]()` (ODR-076) is safe". SPN-8: "`as_ptr()` and `as_mut_ptr()` return raw pointers; extracting one is safe". FFI-6a: a pointer-cast macro "is a `const` of that pointer type holding the address as an integer".

  depth, of what an argument passes, by value or behind a contracted pointer, as its Ember type
  declares it, a method's object included; or what an Ember function given to the call, as an
  argument or in one, returns, itself or in its result. Safe code can make a raw pointer that is null
  (`null[P]()`), that outlives what it points at or points at fewer elements than a length beside it
  counts (`ref_to_ptr`, `as_ptr()`, §IV.5, `[SPN-8]`), or that holds a constant address (`[FFI-6a]`),
  and nothing checks one. So a declaration or entry whose calls the other rules make safe, and whose
  calls would carry such a pointer, is `E5002` where it is written. Its message names where the
  pointer is held (`buf.data`) and gives the lines that leave the calls unsafe: `@safety("…")` above
  the declaration or entry written `unsafe fn` (a hand declaration with its C ABI parameters,
  `[FFI-10]`), or the typedef's entry without `@ffi(safe)`; and each call outside unsafe code in an
  `unsafe:` block with a `# SAFETY:` note (`[DIA-25]`). For an entry in another package's overlay, it
  gives that entry as an `override` in the importing package's own overlay (`[FFI-30c]`). A raw pointer
  that foreign code hands Ember (a result, an `out` value, a callback's parameter) is outside this

edits.why_general: It is one property of the safe-to-call fact: a raw pointer the caller supplied never reaches foreign code under an assertion of safety. Its reason is ODR-073's. It names no type and no construct, and it reaches every type that carries a pointer (a struct, a union, a fixed array, a span's elements, a nested struct) and every route by which the caller's arguments reach C (by value, behind `one`, `count(n)`, `exclusive` or `owns`, a C++ method's object, a callback's result). The reach is judged by the value's Ember type, so opaque classes, `extern type`s and bridge types, which declare no fields, are not reached. The trigger, 'whose calls the other rules make safe', is a property of what a declaration says, so an entry whose own words already leave its calls unsafe (an unknown fact, an uncontracted raw-pointer slot, `retained` on a plain pointer) keeps today's unsafe calls. The direction sentence states scope only. The message is given for each spelling, and each message line compiles (DIA-25).
edits.why_here: This is where the safe-to-call fact is defined, and the spellings that assert it refer to it. A limit placed here applies to all of them at once. FFI-10's sentence at 82-84 stays true as the hand-declaration case of the same property.

readability.verdict: The ordinary program that calls a binding gets no longer and no harder. A binding of a C API whose structs carry pointers writes one wrapper for each such function, which is the price Rust binding authors pay too. That price is heaviest for Vulkan, where every create-info has `pNext`. Hand bindings now refused also write their raw form (the pointer and the length by hand), because an unsafe hand declaration keeps its C ABI parameters; the fix for that is listed for the owner. Field contracts would let such structs become safe types, but that is a whole feature, which FFI-30a rules out today; it is listed for the owner.

impact.cost: Nothing runs: the limit is checked when compiling. A wrapper fills the struct from the span's pointer and length, as C code fills it, and makes the same single direct C call (FFI-9: one `call` instruction). To measure: the wrapper `clear` against a direct C call with the same pointer and length. The expectation is identical instructions after inlining, as in C. Report both times and both code sizes.

answers.question: J8-08
answers.program:
@layout(c)
struct PixelBuf:
    data: *mut u8      # C writes `len` bytes here
    len: usize

unsafe extern "C":
    @ffi(no_callbacks)
    safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)

fn main():
    x: u8 = 7
    clear_pixels(PixelBuf(data=ref_to_ptr(ref mut x), len=4096))   # every line is safe code
    println(x)
answers.today: Compiles. `PixelBuf` is 'a `@layout(c)` value type', so FFI-10's list (p16 59-61) accepts `safe fn clear_pixels`. The raw-pointer refusal (82-84) covers only a raw-pointer parameter itself. At run time C writes 4,096 bytes from the address of the one-byte `x` (C++: a buffer overflow through a pointer-and-length struct, from code the compiler calls safe).
answers.after: E5002 at line 8 (`safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)`), naming `buf.data`. FFI-10's list makes the calls safe, so the declaration is one 'whose calls the other rules make safe', and its call carries a raw pointer in a field of what the argument passes. The message gives `@safety("…")` above `unsafe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)`, and line 12 in an `unsafe:` block with a `# SAFETY:` note; with both, the program compiles (DIA-25). The intended program is that declaration plus a wrapper `fn clear(ref mut bytes: MutSpan[u8])` that builds the struct from the checked span inside `unsafe:`. The program calls `clear(ref mut frame)`, and for a 4-byte frame it prints `0 0 4` (test 2).
answers.decides: FFI-2 as added (p16 after 42): "No assertion of the fact — `safe fn`, ... — covers a raw pointer (`*T`, `*mut T`) that the caller's arguments carry to foreign code: ... a field or an element, at any depth, of what an argument passes, by value or behind a contracted pointer, as its Ember type declares it ... So a declaration or entry whose calls the other rules make safe, and whose calls would carry such a pointer, is `E5002` where it is written."

decisions.title: What happens to a safe C declaration whose argument's struct holds a raw pointer
decisions.problem: A safe C function may not take a raw pointer, because safe code can make one that is null, dangling or short. The same pointer inside a struct argument passes the safe-call list, and nothing can state its count or lifetime: contract words attach only to parameters, and overlays may not change fields. Safe code fills the struct with any address and length, and C writes through it.

options.outcome: `safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)` is E5002, naming `buf.data`. The wrapper compiles, safe callers can clear only bytes they own, and the program prints `0 0 4`.
Compiles (today). C writes 4,095 bytes past `x`: memory corruption in safe code. `ember tcb` lists the assertion.

Writing a raw pointer into a struct needs `unsafe:`, Ember's own structs included. The hole stays: the length beside the pointer is a plain integer that safe code changes, and C writes 4,096 bytes into a 4-byte list.

Not in the specification. FFI-30a forbids an overlay to change a type's fields, so packages with different overlays could no longer exchange `PixelBuf` values. It would be a whole feature with its own cases, listed for the owner.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: A keeps one direct C call, closes the hole, and gives callers a shorter line. B gives up safety. C gives up readability, since every line that puts a pointer into a struct needs `unsafe:`, and it still leaves the hole. D is not in the language. 2. Safety, never given up: only A is safe. Under B, safe code corrupts memory. Under C, `buf.len = 4096` is safe code and C writes past the buffer. 3. Compile time first: A is decided when compiling, and nothing runs. 4. A written word only for meaning: A's `unsafe fn` and `@safety` say who vouches and for what (verdicts 120, 133). 5. The ordinary program no longer or harder: callers write `clear(ref mut frame)`, which is shorter than building the struct by hand; a binding author writes one wrapper. 6. Consistency with the nearest rule and the verdicts: FFI-10's 'complete facts do not make a raw-pointer parameter ... safe to expose' and ODR-073's reason hold exactly for a pointer in a field; verdicts 130, 133 and 136 give the spelling.

owner_short.one_line: A C function declared safe takes `struct { uint8_t* data; size_t len; }` by value, and safe code can fill it with any address and length: may the safe declaration stand?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | binding author | declares `clear_pixels(PixelBuf)` safe | refused: the struct carries a raw pointer
2 | binding author | declares it unsafe, with what callers must make true, and writes `clear(ref mut bytes: MutSpan[u8])` | compiles
3 | program | calls `clear(ref mut frame)` | only bytes it owns reach C
4 | program runs | one direct C call | the same cost as C
owner_short.today: The safe declaration compiles, and safe code can hand C a pointer to one byte with a length of 4,096; C writes past it.
options: A: refuse a safe C declaration that hands C a raw pointer inside a struct; a wrapper builds the struct from a checked view
B: keep today: the declarer's word covers the struct's pointers too (memory corruption from safe code)
C: make writing a raw pointer into a struct unsafe instead (still a hole: the length beside it is a plain number safe code changes)
D: let overlays give struct fields contracts (not in the language: overlays may not change a type's fields)
owner_short.recommendation: A: the only choice that closes the hole when compiling, with no cost while running, and callers get a shorter line.

decisions.title: Which ways a raw pointer the caller supplied can reach C are covered
decisions.problem: Once a raw pointer inside a struct argument is refused, the same pointer can still reach C by other routes: in a C++ method's object, in a span's elements, or as the result of an Ember function the call gives C (an allocator or buffer callback). Pointers that C hands back to Ember flow the other way.

options.outcome: Only struct arguments are covered. `stream_read` compiles, and C writes 4,096 bytes into a dead stack slot.

Every raw pointer the caller's arguments carry to C is covered: in an argument at any depth, in a method's object, in what a function given to the call returns, and in the items of a two-call enumeration, which C may read. `stream_read` is E5002 naming `get_buf`'s result. `camera_latest_frame` compiles and prints `3 2`, and reading through `f.pixels` needs `unsafe:`. Exports, export tables and C++ overrides, which C calls with no call handing it anything, stay as they are; they are listed for the owner.

ii, plus what C hands back. `camera_latest_frame`, `SDL_GetCurrentDisplayMode`'s `out` mode and `returns_owned` image loaders are refused, and no safety is gained: reading through a raw pointer is unsafe already (IV.5).

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: ii keeps every correct program that only reads what C hands back, and costs nothing while running. 2. Safety: i leaves a callback's dangling pointer reaching C from safe code; ii and iii close it. 3. Compile time first: all three are decided when compiling. 4. A written word only for meaning: none adds a word. 5. The ordinary program: iii refuses programs that only read C's struct (a camera frame, a display mode, an image loader); ii refuses none of them. 6. Consistency: ii follows the direction the value flows, as FFI-21a does for raw pointers given back to C, and leaves to IV.5 what IV.5 already fences.

owner_short.one_line: Besides struct arguments, which other ways can a call hand C a pointer the caller made, e.g. an allocator callback `uint8_t* (*get_buf)(size_t)` returning the address of a dead local?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | binding author | declares `stream_read(want, get_buf)` safe; C writes `want` bytes at what `get_buf` returns | refused: the callback's result is a raw pointer
2 | binding author | declares `camera_latest_frame() -> FrameInfo`, holding C's pixel pointer | compiles: C hands it to Ember
3 | program | reads `f.width` | allowed
4 | program | reads through `f.pixels` | only in unsafe code, as today
owner_short.today: A callback that returns a raw pointer passes, and so does any struct C returns.
options: i: only struct arguments (a callback returning a dangling pointer still reaches C from safe code)
ii: every pointer the call's arguments carry to C: fields, elements, a C++ object, what a callback given to the call returns
iii: ii plus what C hands back (refuses programs that only read C's struct, with no safety gained)
owner_short.recommendation: ii: covers every pointer a call hands C, and nothing C hands back, which is already unsafe to read through.

decisions.title: What a plain overlay line, or an @ffi(safe) typedef, that would hand C such a pointer becomes
decisions.problem: An overlay line such as `fn cp_load(opts: borrowed one)` reads as complete, but the header's struct holds a `const char*` that the line cannot contract. The line could be refused, or its calls could become unsafe, the way an unknown fact makes them.

options.outcome: Refused at the overlay line, naming `opts.path`, with the lines to write. In another package's overlay, the message gives the same entry as an `override` in the importing package's own overlay. An entry whose own words already leave its calls unsafe (a TODO word, an uncontracted raw-pointer slot, `retained` on a plain pointer) is not reached.

The line is accepted, but its calls are unsafe because of a header field that the line does not show. Each call outside unsafe code is refused, and inside `unsafe:` L3015 sends the writer back to the overlay.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: both are safe and free at run time; a reads better, with one error at the line to change. 2. Safety: both refuse a safe call. 3. Compile time first: both. 4. A written word only for meaning: under b, a plain overlay line, which says 'safe to call' (GRM-35), would have unsafe calls because of a header field the overlay's reader never sees (verdict 132's lesson). 5. The ordinary program: a gives one error at the overlay line with the lines to write; b gives an error at every call, then L3015. Under a, a dependant that never calls the entry also fails until it writes the override or the dependency is fixed, as with a drifted entry today (FFI-55). 6. Consistency: a matches FFI-10's E5002 for `safe fn` and verdict 136 (no line silently means unsafe). The trigger is what the entry itself says ('whose calls the other rules make safe'), so FFI-11's `retained` row and FFI-11c's TODO words keep deciding their entries.

owner_short.one_line: An overlay line `fn cp_load(opts: borrowed one)` looks complete, but the header's struct holds a `const char*`: refuse the line, or quietly make its calls unsafe?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | overlay writer | writes `fn cp_load(opts: borrowed one)` | refused at this line, naming `opts.path`
2 | overlay writer | writes it unsafe, with what callers must make true | compiles
3 | program | calls `cp_load` in unsafe code with a note | compiles
4 | another package using this overlay | builds before the fix | refused, told the line to write in its own overlay
owner_short.today: The line declares the call safe and is accepted.
options: a: refuse the line, with the unsafe line to write
b: accept it, and make its calls unsafe, as for a fact not yet written
owner_short.recommendation: a: a line means what it says; a plain overlay line means safe to call, so one that cannot be made safe is refused where it is written.

decisions.title: Whether a C++ std::function imported as a callable is limited the same way
decisions.problem: `@ffi(std_function)` turns a C++ `std::function<R(A…)>` into an Ember callable that is safe to call, with no limit on its parameters. Safe code can call it with a raw pointer, or with a struct holding one, and C++ writes through it. Refusing the entry would leave no Ember line that calls the value, because the language has no spelling for an unsafe callable import. A fix also changes what every existing `@ffi(std_function)` entry means.

options.outcome: Calls of a `std::function` value go in `unsafe:` unless its entry says `safe` (`@ffi(std_function, safe)`), and that word is refused when a call would carry a raw pointer, as `@ffi(safe)` is for a C function pointer. Every existing `@ffi(std_function)` entry's calls become unsafe until its entry says `safe`.

options.code:
# the same overlay, as today
fn main():
    fill = f.px.make_filler()
    x: u8 = 7
    fill(f.px.Buf(data=ref_to_ptr(ref mut x), len=4096))   # safe code
options.outcome: Compiles. C++ writes 4,096 bytes from the address of `x`: memory corruption from safe code, for a struct or for a plain `std::function<void(int*)>`.
Refused. The message can only say to remove `@ffi(std_function)`, which leaves `Fill` an opaque object that Ember cannot call at all, so no line it gives makes the program compile (DIA-25).

decisions.chosen: none applied: recommendation a, for the owner
decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: a keeps the callable usable from Ember at C++'s cost and closes the hole; b gives up safety; c refuses correct programs with no Ember way to call them. 2. Safety: a and c are safe; under b, safe code hands C++ a dangling pointer. 3. Compile time first: all three. 4. A written word only for meaning: a's `safe` says who vouches, as `@ffi(safe)` does for a C function pointer. 5. The ordinary program: under a, calls of a `std::function` go in `unsafe:` unless its entry vouches; under c there is no call at all. 6. Consistency: a is FFI-56's rule for C function pointers and the owner's 'C++ too, same rule' (verdict 125). The parameters pick a, but a changes the meaning of a delegated ruling (ODR-199) and of every existing `@ffi(std_function)` program, and it adds the word `safe` to a `std_function` entry. So it goes to the owner, and this change leaves FFI-17a as it is.
decisions.departs_from_verdict: a would change ODR-199 (delegated: `@ffi(std_function)` makes an owned callable value, safe to call); not applied

owner_short.one_line: A C++ `std::function<void(Buf)>`, where `Buf` holds a `uint8_t*`, imported as a callable: safe code can call it with any address. Should calling it be unsafe, as calling a C function pointer is?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | overlay writer | maps `std::function<void(Buf)>` to a callable | today: safe to call
2 | program | calls it with a one-byte address and a length of 4,096 | today: C++ writes past the byte
3 | under a | the call goes in unsafe code with a note, unless the overlay vouches (it cannot vouch here: the struct holds a raw pointer) | the caller vouches
4 | under c | the overlay line is refused | Ember cannot call it at all
owner_short.today: A mapped `std::function` is safe to call whatever its parameters hold.
options: a: unsafe to call unless the overlay says it is safe, which it cannot say for raw pointers (the C function pointer's rule)
b: keep today (C++ can be handed a dangling pointer from safe code)
c: refuse such an overlay line (Ember can then never call it)
owner_short.recommendation: a: the same rule as a C function pointer: unsafe to call unless someone vouches, and never vouched for raw pointers.

responses.objection: S1-7 (the E5002 row's reach disagrees with FFI-2 on FFI-6b's `PAIR_FIRST`)
responses.how: The row now repeats the limit's reach and its trigger: 'a `safe fn`, overlay function entry or `@ffi(safe)` typedef whose calls would otherwise be safe and would carry foreign code a raw pointer from the caller's arguments (one an argument is or holds at any depth, or one an Ember function given to the call returns)', with `[FFI-56]` added to the rule column. `PAIR_FIRST(p: *Pair)`'s calls are unsafe by its own words (an uncontracted raw-pointer slot, FFI-2 p16 33-34), so neither the row nor FFI-2 reaches it. Test 9 keeps `25 4.5 7 7 true false` and its L3015.

responses.objection: E1-1 (the message pushes hand bindings to the raw form, and the line it gives may not compile)
responses.how: Fixed in part: the message now gives a line that compiles under today's rules. For a hand declaration that is the raw form FFI-10 decides ('A raw `*T` can be declared for an unsafe call', p16 82; 'An unsafe raw-pointer declaration keeps its written C ABI parameters', 91-92). For writev it is `@ffi(no_callbacks)` and `@safety("…")` above `unsafe fn writev(fd: c_int, iov: *IoVec, iovcnt: c_int) -> isize`, with the `param(iov, …)` words of the slot written raw dropped, so no type/contract question arises (p16 84). The call line becomes `writev(1, parts.as_span().as_ptr(), parts.len() as c_int)`, in `unsafe:` with a `# SAFETY:` note (DIA-25, p17 474-476). Kept: the hand form and the overlay form of one unsafe function still differ, and the wrapper author writes the pointer and the length conversion by hand. That difference exists today for every unsafe hand declaration (FFI-10 91-92 and 109-110 against FFI-11's count row, p16 291), and E1-1's own program is undecided without this change (nothing says an `unsafe fn` may write `Span[IoVec]`). E1-1's property (contract words decide the Ember signature of `safe fn` and `unsafe fn` alike) is the consistent one (verdict 133: 'as in overlays'). But it rewrites ODR-074's sentence and decides how witnesses, nullable carriers, `out` and `status` behave on unsafe declarations, so it is listed for the owner with that recommendation. Impact: each newly refused hand binding writes `as_ptr()` and a length cast in its wrapper; overlay bindings keep the mapped form.

responses.objection: E1-2 (`@ffi(std_function)` is a fourth assertion; the universal claim is not kept; the FFI-31b cite misleads; the sentence is too long)
responses.how: Rewritten as E1-2 asks, using its fallback. The limit is now its own sentences at the end of FFI-2: the property, the reason, the refusal and its message, the direction. The first sentence names exactly the assertions it decides ('No assertion of the fact — `safe fn`, an overlay function entry not written `unsafe fn`, or `@ffi(safe)` on a function-pointer typedef — covers ...'), so it claims nothing about `@ffi(std_function)`. That spelling (p21 67) has no raw-pointer limit at all, not even for `std::function<void(int*)>`, and its way out needs a spelling the language lacks. It is decision 4, for the owner, with the recommendation to treat it as a C function pointer is treated (FFI-56): unsafe to call, with `safe` asserting within the same limits, using FN-6's `unsafe fn(…) -> R` type (p05 179-183). The `[FFI-31b]` cite is gone, and the reach is defined once in FFI-2's own words. FFI-31b's `char` reach is left as written: it is a separate rule.

responses.objection: E1-3 (the 'reading through it is unsafe already' reason undercuts FFI-10's result refusal)
responses.how: The direction is now scope only: 'A raw pointer that foreign code hands Ember (a result, an `out` value, a callback's parameter) is outside this limit; `[FFI-10]` decides a hand declaration's raw-pointer result.' No reason is given that disagrees with FFI-10 82-84. Listed for the owner: ODR-073's result half (a delegated ruling, p26 361) can only be about the API's shape, since a struct result such as `camera_latest_frame() -> FrameInfo` already brings C's raw pointer into safe code. The owner can keep it as a shape rule or drop it.

responses.objection: E1-4 (read literally, every method of an opaque C++ class with a pointer member is refused)
responses.how: The reach is anchored to the value 'as its Ember type declares it'. An opaque class (FFI-44, p21 43; FFI-32, 76-77), an `extern type` (FFI-8, p16 183) and the bridge types `CppVector[T]` and `CppString` (FFI-17e, p21 69-71) declare no fields in Ember. So nothing in `vertex_count`'s object is reached, and the program prints `3` (test 11).

responses.objection: E1-5 (the impact report undercounts fields holding pointers to opaque types and handle typedefs)
responses.how: The Unchanged row now reads 'an opaque type behind a contracted parameter'. A new programs_changed row lists structs holding a pointer to an opaque type or a pointer typedef (`app_cfg.window`, a field of type `FT_Face`, `VkDescriptorBufferInfo.buffer`) as refused. K46's question, whether `@ffi(handle)` or `@ffi(newtype)` makes such a field something other than a raw pointer, is named for every handle field. `app_start` is test 12 (E5002 naming `cfg.window`) and is in to_verify.

responses.objection: E1-6 (the ordinary call is shown longer than it is; XVI.4 shows no safe layer)
responses.how: Every program now uses `clear(ref mut frame)` (SPN-1, p07 812-814: an `Array[T]` converts to `MutSpan[T]` for a `ref mut` parameter), and test 2 still prints `0 0 4`. One sentence follows XVI.4's example, with no second example: '`vkCreateBuffer` is an `unsafe fn` entry because the structs its call hands Vulkan hold raw pointers (...); a wrapper in an `extend` block of the overlay (`[FFI-13]`) gives safe callers a create call, building those structs from checked views.'

responses.objection: E1-8 (another package's overlay breaks dependants that never call the entry, and the message points at a file they cannot change)
responses.how: For an entry in another package's overlay, the message gives the line the importing package can write: the entry as an `override` in its own overlay, applied after the dependency's (FFI-30c, p16 216-222; ODR-149: 'override before an item'). The build-break scope is in the impact report: once this lands, every build that applies such an overlay fails at the entry, as a build applying an overlay that drifted from its header already does (FFI-55, p16 345-351). That lasts until the dependency writes `unsafe fn` or the dependant writes the override.

responses.objection: I1-1 (X: FFI-11's `retained` row accepts `fn net_keep(cfg: retained one)` with unsafe calls; FFI-2 refused it)
responses.how: The trigger is now a property of what the declaration says: 'a declaration or entry whose calls the other rules make safe, and whose calls would carry such a pointer, is `E5002`'. The other rules leave `net_keep`'s calls unsafe (FFI-11's ownership row, p16 290: 'the call stays `unsafe`, with a raw pointer'), so FFI-2 does not reach it and FFI-11 decides it alone: it compiles and prints `net` (test 10). The same holds for TODO words (FFI-11c, 318-321), for uncontracted raw-pointer slots (FFI-6b's `PAIR_FIRST`), and for any later word that leaves calls unsafe. The two rules no longer decide one entry differently.

responses.objection: I1-2 (the items of an `inout_count` enumeration are filled by C, like an `out` value, and should not be reached)
responses.how: C may read what an enumeration's items hold, so the items are something the call hands C. FFI-11b (p16 313-317) defines the idiom only as 'call once for the count, again to fill'. It does not say that C never reads the items, and no contract word can say so (FFI-30a, 210-212). Vulkan's `vkGetPhysicalDeviceQueueFamilyProperties2(physicalDevice, pQueueFamilyPropertyCount, pQueueFamilyProperties)` is exactly that idiom, and its items `VkQueueFamilyProperties2` hold `pNext`, which the driver reads to find the chained structures it fills. With the items reached, a `pNext` that safe code set to a dead local is refused; with them excluded, the driver writes through it (C++: writing through a dangling pointer). An `out` value is different: Ember passes C no value of its own there. So `font_names` is E5002 naming the elements of `names` (test 13). Its binding writes `unsafe fn` and a wrapper, and the impact report lists two-call enumerations whose items are or hold raw pointers.

responses.objection: I1-3 (the words leave `@ffi(std_function)` undecided; the claim that it is unchanged is unsupported)
responses.how: The words now name only the assertions they cover (`safe fn`, an overlay function entry, `@ffi(safe)` on a typedef), so `@ffi(std_function)` is decided as unchanged by this text, and the impact report and decision 4 say so. I1-3's suggested consequence ('remove `@ffi(std_function)`') would not give a line that compiles in its program (DIA-25, p17 474-475). Without the attribute, `fill` is an opaque object (p21 67), and `fill(…)` has no meaning. The route, with or without a struct, is decision 4 for the owner. The recommended answer applies FFI-56's rule for a C function pointer to C++'s callable: unsafe to call unless the entry says `safe`, within the same limits.

responses.objection: I1-4 (the recommendation claims every route is covered; exports, export tables and overrides are not)
responses.how: The claim is narrowed, in the decision, its owner_short and the impact report, to 'every raw pointer the caller's arguments carry to C', which is what the words reach. Routes where C calls Ember without any call of the program handing it anything stay as they are and are listed for the owner: an `@unsafe(export(...))` function, an `@export_table` field and an override of a C++ class (FFI-52, p16 451-458), whose raw-pointer results C trusts. FFI-26's note vouches only for the name (633-634). These belong to the exports question (K08) and are not caused here (rule E).

responses.objection: I1-5 (`ember bind --init` output and the C++ routes are missing from the impact report; FFI-11 is not unchanged in outcome)
responses.how: CLI-5 (p17 115-116) now says that a declaration the limit keeps from being safe is written `unsafe fn`. So `ember bind --init pixels.h` writes `unsafe fn clear_pixels(buf)`, and its promise 'compiles unchanged' holds; the change is in programs_changed. The C++ routes are listed: a `T&` parameter (FFI-40, p21 161-163), `std::span<S>`, `std::unique_ptr<S>` and `std::optional<S>` (FFI-17a, 58, 63, 64), and a method of a by-value class (FFI-32, 74-80). rules_changed now says that FFI-11's text is unchanged, that its `retained` row keeps its outcome (I1-1), and that two-call enumerations whose items hold raw pointers are newly refused (I1-2).

responses.objection: I1-6 (placement, the general claim, per-spelling messages, FFI-10's naming clause, 'forged', the codes row)
responses.how: (1) The limit is now separate sentences after the DIA-18 sentence, so 'nothing of the kind' stays next to what it refers to. (2) FFI-2's second sentence reads 'makes the call safe, within the limit on raw pointers below'. (3) The message is given for each spelling: the `unsafe fn` line for a declaration or function entry, the typedef's entry without `@ffi(safe)`, and each call outside unsafe code in `unsafe:`. (4) FFI-10's clause reads 'naming the fact that is missing or, under that limit, where the raw pointer is held'. (5) Forging is cited as the spec allows it: a pointer-cast constant (FFI-6a, p16 150-151), beside null, dangling and short pointers (IV.5, SPN-8). (6) The codes row names the reach and cites `[FFI-56]`.

responses.objection: (test2 hole 1, 4) An owned foreign struct holding a pointer (`blob`, `SDL_Surface`, `image_load -> returns_owned(...)`) is refused, and safe code writing `asset.data` before its destructor brings back the invalid free.
responses.how: The words reach only what the caller's arguments carry to C. They do not reach results, `returns_owned` results or `destroys(f)`, so `blob_new`, `image_load` and an `owns SDL_Surface` compile as today. A destructor freeing a field that safe code wrote goes wrong the same way with and without this change, so under rule E it is a gap that already exists; it is listed in notes.

responses.objection: (test2 hole 3) A game loop taking a `ref mut` view of a C struct with pointer fields (ImGui's IO block, `engine_input() -> borrowed one exclusive from(static)`) is refused.
responses.how: A result view is something foreign code hands Ember, which is outside the limit, so `engine_input()` and `engine_begin_frame()` compile as today. The danger the breaker named, safe code writing `input.ini_path`, is the same existing field-write gap, listed for later.

responses.objection: (anticipated) User-data cookies C never dereferences (`SDL_UserEvent.data1`, `VkAllocationCallbacks.pUserData`, `uv_handle_t.data`) are refused although harmless to C.
responses.how: C is unchecked code. The compiler cannot tell a cookie that C hands back from a buffer that C writes, and principle 6 allows no exception where the general rule is not untrue. The cost is one wrapper in the binding. A field word saying 'C never reads through it' belongs to the field-contract feature, which FFI-30a rules out today; it is listed for the owner.

responses.objection: (anticipated) Vulkan cost: every `vkCreate*` create-info has `pNext`, so every create call needs `unsafe fn` and a wrapper.
responses.how: Vulkan walks `pNext` and reads `sType` at each link, so a forged chain from safe code is memory corruption. The safe route is an `extend` wrapper in the overlay (FFI-13), a renderer's checked builder (what vulkano does over ash), or the field-contract feature. The cost falls on the binding, not on code that calls it. It is stated in the readability verdict and in notes.

responses.objection: (anticipated) A wrapper taking the public struct only moves the hole into the wrapper.
responses.how: A sound wrapper builds the struct from checked views (decision 1, option A) or keeps the foreign struct in a private field (MOD-2, p05 19-22; MOD-7, 34-37), so no safe code outside its module can write the pointer. A wrapper that vouches for a struct anyone may fill makes a false `# SAFETY:` claim in unsafe code. That is the unsafe author's error, as in Rust, and `ember tcb` lists it.

final.notes:
The change is rewritten as a whole. The cause stays in FFI-2, where the safe-to-call fact is defined.

The limit is now its own sentences at the end of FFI-2:
- The property: no `safe fn`, overlay function entry or `@ffi(safe)` typedef covers a raw pointer that the caller's arguments carry to foreign code. That means an argument itself, a field or element at any depth of what an argument passes (as its Ember type declares it, a method's object included), or what an Ember function given to the call returns.
- The reason: safe code can make null, dangling, short and constant-address pointers.
- The refusal: E5002 where the declaration or entry is written, but only when the other rules make its calls safe. The message is given for each spelling, with an `override` line for another package's overlay.
- The direction: pointers foreign code hands Ember are outside the limit.

FFI-10 and FFI-56 cite the limit, and FFI-10's E5002 clause names what the message says. The other edits: XVI.4's `vkCreateBuffer` becomes `@safety` plus `unsafe fn`, with one sentence on `extend` wrappers under the example. The E5002 row repeats the limit's reach and adds `[FFI-56]`. CLI-5 writes such declarations `unsafe fn`.

Every open objection is answered: 12 fixed, 1 rebutted (I1-2, which Vulkan's `*2` queries settle), and 1 trade-off kept with a fix (E1-1). The one blocking objection (I1-1, X) is fixed by the trigger 'whose calls the other rules make safe'.

Decisions:
- Decisions 1 to 3 were made by the owner's parameters, with no departure from a verdict: refuse the safe declaration; reach every pointer the caller's arguments carry to C; refuse the overlay line rather than quietly making its calls unsafe.
- Decision 4 (`@ffi(std_function)`) is the owner's. No change is applied and FFI-17a is left as it is. The recommendation is FFI-56's rule for C function pointers: unsafe to call unless the entry says `safe`, within the same limits.

For the owner, besides decision 4:
1. E1-1's property: contract words decide a hand declaration's Ember signature whether it is `safe fn` or `unsafe fn`, as an overlay entry's words already do. It rewrites ODR-074's sentence (FFI-10 91-92, 109-110). Recommended.
2. ODR-073's result half rests on API shape, not safety, since struct results already bring C's raw pointers into safe code (E1-3). Keep it as a shape rule or drop it.
3. Routes where C calls Ember with no call handing it anything: exports, export tables and C++ overrides returning raw pointers (I1-4). These belong to the exports question, K08.
4. Field contracts in overlays, so that create-info and cookie structs could become safe types. This is a whole feature, which FFI-30a forbids today. Undecided cases: Vulkan's `pNext` chains, count fields shared by two pointers, and user-data cookies C never reads through.

Dependencies:
- K46 (J8-14) rewrites the same `vkCreateBuffer` entry and decides whether handle fields count as raw pointers.
- K51 (J2-11) sets the spelling of `ref_to_ptr(ref mut x)`.

Gaps that already exist and are not caused here (rule E):
- Safe code writing pointer or length fields of foreign memory: ImGui-style result views, and `owns` foreign structs whose destructor frees a field.
- A plain overlay entry whose own slot is an uncontracted raw pointer, such as FFI-6b's `PAIR_FIRST`, means unsafe without saying so.
- What an `out` slot holds when C reads it before filling it (Vulkan's `VkPhysicalDeviceFeatures2` reads `sType` and `pNext`).

Read-only work:
- The rules file, the input file, OWNER-DIRECTION.md and JOB.md (verdicts 121, 130-137).
- The part files p16-ffi.md, p04-types.md, p05-declarations.md, p07-ownership.md, p17-toolchain.md, p17a-codes.md and p21-annex-c.md, and p26-appx-h.md for the ODRs.
- compiler-0.9.15/decisions.md and tests/conformance/FFI-6b.

FFI-2, p16 35-38: "The safe-to-call fact is never derived ...: it is asserted by `safe fn` ..., or by an overlay entry for the function". closed.closed_why: The rebuttal is right. Here the items are `const char*`, which is `*c_char` (FFI-8, p16 180). FFI-2 as added (p16 38) reaches "a raw pointer (`*T`, `*mut T`) that a call hands C inside what an argument ... passes, by value or behind a pointer, at any depth (a field, an element)". The call hands C the span, and its elements are raw pointers. The only exclusion is "a raw pointer C hands Ember (a result, an `out` value, a callback's parameter)", and an `inout_count` item is none of these. So the entry is E5002 at overlays/fonts.em line 4, naming the elements of `names`. Yet by the asserted idiom ('again to fill'), C only writes these elements, exactly as it writes an `out` value, which the words exclude. The pointers safe code put there never reach C as pointers.
closed.impact: Every two-call enumeration whose items are or hold raw pointers is refused, and the binding needs a wrapper for each, with no safety gained. Examples: `SDL_Vulkan_GetInstanceExtensions(window, &count, names)`. If K46 keeps dispatchable handles as raw pointers, also `vkEnumeratePhysicalDevices` and `vkGetSwapchainImagesKHR`. Two 'C fills' words get opposite treatment (`out` excluded, `inout_count` items reached). The impact report lists FFI-11 and its rows as unchanged.
closed.suggestion: State the direction by what the slot's contract says C does with it, not by the contract word. The limit reaches only what C may read. What a slot's contract says C only fills (an `out` value, the items of an `inout_count` enumeration) is a pointer C hands Ember.

closed.closed_why: For exports and export tables (I1-4's program `scratch`), the narrowed claim is true: no call of the program hands C the function, and the routes are listed for the owner. The stated reason is untrue for overrides of an object that a call hands C++ ('C calls Ember there, so no call hands C anything'). That is raised as new objection 3.
closed.walk: Decision 2 recommends option ii with: "ii: covers every way a pointer made in safe code reaches C" (owner_short), and its outcome says 'Everything the call hands C'. FFI-52 (p16 451-458) lists the Ember functions C can run: kept callbacks, "every `@export` and `@export_table` function", "every override of an Ember class derived from a C++ class whose objects C++ may hold", borrowed callbacks and `extern "C" fn` values. The added words reach only "one that a function the call gives C returns". The `@unsafe(export(...))` note vouches only "why nothing else defines that name" (FFI-26, p16 633-634). FFI-31b (p16 647-651) refuses only owning values in an exported signature, so a raw-pointer result is allowed. FFI-21a (p16 428-434) refuses only a pointer into a parameter's copy, and `x` is a local. So `scratch` compiles before and after the change. A host that calls `game_scratch(4096)` and writes the bytes writes into a dead stack frame (C++: returning the address of a local). The same holds for an `@export_table` field and for a C++ virtual override (FFI-39).
closed.impact: The owner would read that every route is closed. Three routes stay open: exports, export tables and C++ overrides. They are not caused by this change (rule E), but the recommendation's reason is untrue as written.
closed.suggestion: Either let the result reach follow FFI-52's set of Ember functions C can call, refused where the function's export or value is written (one property, which also covers the callback route). Or narrow the claim to 'every pointer a call hands C', and list exports, export tables and overrides for the owner as routes that remain.

out.intent: Clear a caller's pixel buffer from safe code through a C function that takes a pointer-and-length struct.

cause.where: FFI-1 (p16-ffi.md 26-31). The contract covers only "each pointer-typed parameter and result". A raw pointer held inside a parameter's or result's value (a struct field, an array element, the struct a contracted pointer views) belongs to no contract, so none of its facts is ever `unknown`. FFI-2 (33-34: "a call to a foreign function whose contract contains an `unknown` fact requires `unsafe`") therefore never makes the call unsafe because of it. FFI-10's raw-pointer refusal (82-84) looks only at the parameter's own type. FFI-10's list (59-61) and FFI-56's list (596-598) then accept the struct as "a `@layout(c)` value type".
cause.why_there: FFI-1 is the one definition that every route to a safe foreign call shares: a hand-written `safe fn` (FFI-10), an overlay or import entry (FFI-2, which is the route of the spec's own XVI.4 `vkCreateBuffer`), a function-pointer typedef (FFI-56) and C++ (Annex C, verdict 125). A fix only in FFI-10's list would leave the overlay route and C++ open. FFI-30a (fields belong to the type, so packages exchange values) and FFI-11 (contract words follow a parameter's name) are right as they stand. They explain why a held pointer's facts can never be supplied, so those facts must stay `unknown`; they are not the cause.

existing_rule.rule: FFI-10 together with FFI-2 (the raw-pointer refusal and the unknown-fact fence)
existing_rule.words: FFI-10: "A raw `*T` can be declared for an unsafe call, but complete facts do not make a raw-pointer parameter or result safe to expose; `safe fn` with one is `E5002`. Missing facts or a type/contract mismatch is `E5002`, naming the slot." FFI-2: "A call to a foreign function whose contract contains an `unknown` fact requires `unsafe`." The property is this: a raw pointer's address and extent are chosen by safe code that nothing checks (`ref_to_ptr`, `null[P]()` IV.5 p04-types.md 340-348; `as_mut_ptr()` SPN-8 p07-ownership.md 837), so no promise made when the function is declared can cover every call. Today that property is applied only to the parameter's own type.

edits.before: Every foreign declaration has a **contract**: for each pointer-typed parameter and result, its ownership, mutability, nullability, count and lifetime (§XVI.4), and for the function its effects, its thread rule, whether it may call back into Ember (`[FFI-52]`) and whether it is **safe to call** at all. Facts derivable from the C declaration are derived (`[FFI-2a]`); the rest are `unknown` until a contract supplies them.
edits.after: Every foreign declaration has a **contract**: for each pointer-typed parameter and result, and for each raw pointer a call hands the foreign code or gets back from it inside another value (a field or an element of a `@layout(c)` aggregate passed by value or behind a pointer or a reference, at any depth), its ownership, mutability, nullability, count and lifetime (§XVI.4), and for the function its effects, its thread rule, whether it may call back into Ember (`[FFI-52]`) and whether it is **safe to call** at all. Facts derivable from the C declaration are derived (`[FFI-2a]`); the rest are `unknown` until a contract supplies them. No contract supplies a held raw pointer's facts, since contract words follow a parameter's name (`[FFI-11]`) and an overlay never changes a type's fields (`[FFI-30a]`), so they stay `unknown`: safe code may have put any address and length there (`ref_to_ptr` and `null[P]()` are safe, §IV.5; so is `as_mut_ptr()`, `[SPN-8]`), and nothing checks what the foreign code does through it. A call of such a function is therefore unsafe (`[FFI-2]`), and its declaration is `unsafe fn` with `@safety("…")` above it (verdicts 130, 133).
edits.why_general: It is one property: a raw pointer's facts are unknown wherever it sits in what crosses the boundary. It is stated where the contract is defined, so every route (hand declaration, overlay, import, function-pointer typedef, C++) and both directions (parameter, result) follow it with no list of cases. The reach is written exactly as the language already writes it for `char` and range types (FFI-31b p16-ffi.md 652-653 "directly or in a `@layout(c)` aggregate passed by value or behind a pointer"; RNG-10b p04-types.md 254-255).

answers.question: J8-08: May a safe C call take a struct that holds raw pointers?
answers.program:
@layout(c)
struct PixelBuf:
    data: *mut u8      # C writes `len` bytes here
    len: usize

unsafe extern "C":
    @ffi(no_callbacks)
    safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)    # accepted by the parameter list today

fn main():
    x: u8 = 7
    clear_pixels(PixelBuf(data=ref_to_ptr(ref mut x), len=4096))   # every line is safe code; C writes 4,096 bytes over one
    println(x)
answers.today: Compiles. `PixelBuf` passes FFI-10's list as "a `@layout(c)` value type" (p16-ffi.md 60), and `data` is in no contract (FFI-1 26-31 covers only pointer-typed parameters and results), so no fact is unknown. At run time C writes 4,096 bytes at a one-byte local: a stack buffer overflow from safe code. The block's missing `# SAFETY:` note gives W3012, as it does today.
answers.after: E5002 at line 8, `safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)`: "`clear_pixels` cannot be `safe fn`: its parameter `buf` holds a raw pointer, `PixelBuf.data`, and nothing can say how many bytes it points at or for how long, nor check the address a caller puts there; write `unsafe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)`, with `@safety("…")` above it saying what its callers must make true". The safe interface is a wrapper `fn clear(ref mut bytes: MutSpan[u8])` that builds the struct inside `unsafe:`.
answers.decides: FFI-1 (new words): "for each raw pointer a call hands the foreign code or gets back from it inside another value (a field or an element of a `@layout(c)` aggregate passed by value or behind a pointer or a reference, at any depth) ... they stay `unknown`". FFI-10 (new words): "and none holds a raw pointer (`[FFI-1]`), `safe` on any other function being `E5002`".

decisions.title: D1: a raw pointer held inside a struct that a safe C call is given
decisions.problem: A safe C function may not take a raw pointer, yet the same pointer inside a `@layout(c)` struct passes, and safe code can fill it with any address and length (`ref_to_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr()`, `null[P]()` are safe).

options.outcome: `safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)` is E5002, naming `PixelBuf.data`. The wrapper compiles, and safe callers can clear only bytes they hold. Applies through every route (FFI-1).
Compiles; C overwrites 4,095 bytes past `x`, memory corruption from safe code.

options.code:
fn main():
    x: u8 = 7
    # SAFETY: …
    unsafe:
        p = ref_to_ptr(ref mut x)
options.outcome: Making a raw pointer needs `unsafe`. This reverses ODR-075 and still misses `as_mut_ptr()` (SPN-8), `null[P]()` and pointers C returned earlier, which safe code can still put in the struct.

options.code:
@ffi(param(buf, field(data, borrowed, count(len), exclusive)))
safe fn clear_pixels(ref mut buf: PixelBuf)
options.outcome: A new feature: contract words for fields. Its open cases are counts taken from sibling fields, the lifetime of a struct value, the `pNext` chains, and FFI-30a's ban on changing fields. No rule decides them.

decisions.parameters_in_order: (1) Three goals: B fails memory safety; A, C and D cost nothing at run time. (2) Safety never given up: B is out; C leaves holes (`as_mut_ptr()`, C's own pointers). (3) Compile time first: A decides it now from existing rules; D needs a feature first. (4) A written word only for meaning: A adds no word (existing `unsafe fn` and `@safety`); D adds field words. (5) The ordinary program no longer or harder: A keeps callers on a safe wrapper; C puts `unsafe` around every `ref_to_ptr` and `as_mut_ptr()` in safe code. (6) Consistency: A is the refusal a bare raw pointer already gets (FFI-10 82-84), reaching inside an aggregate the way `char` and range types already do (FFI-31b, RNG-10b).
decisions.departs_from_verdict: none (C would depart from ODR-075 and was not chosen)

owner_short.one_line: A C function declared safe takes a struct by value whose `uint8_t* data` field the caller can aim anywhere: a buffer overflow from code marked safe.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | binding author | declares `safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)`, where `PixelBuf` holds `data: *mut u8` and `len` | accepted today |
| 2 | safe caller | builds `PixelBuf(data=ref_to_ptr(ref mut x), len=4096)` for a one-byte `x` | nothing checks it: making a raw pointer is safe |
| 3 | C | writes 4,096 bytes at `data` | stack overwritten past `x` |
| 4 | after the fix | the `safe fn` line is refused; the author writes `unsafe fn` with `@safety` and a wrapper over a `MutSpan[u8]` | callers can clear only bytes they hold |
owner_short.today: Compiles, and C writes 4,095 bytes past a one-byte local.
options: A: a raw pointer inside a struct counts as a raw pointer; the `safe fn` is refused and the author writes `unsafe fn` with `@safety` and a safe wrapper over a span.
B: as today; the `safe fn` also vouches for the struct's pointers; memory corruption from safe code.
C: make creating a raw pointer unsafe; reverses your ruling that `ref_to_ptr` is safe and still misses pointers from `as_mut_ptr()` and from C.
D: let a declaration give a field's length and lifetime; a new feature, for later.
owner_short.recommendation: A: no run-time cost, the same refusal a bare raw pointer already gets, and a safe wrapper keeps correct callers working.

decisions.title: D2: the result direction (a struct that C returns or fills, holding a raw pointer)
decisions.problem: Once held pointers are part of the contract, the reach can cover parameters and results (as FFI-1 already covers "pointer-typed parameter and result") or parameters only. A raw pointer in a by-value result can be read only in `unsafe`, so it opens no hole by itself.

options.outcome: `safe fn lib_name() -> NameRef` is E5002, naming `NameRef.p`; the binding writes `unsafe fn` and a wrapper. One rule in both directions.

options.code:
unsafe extern "C":
    safe fn lib_name() -> NameRef
options.outcome: Compiles; safe code holds `r.p` and can use it only in `unsafe`. A bare `-> *u8` result stays refused (FFI-10 82-84, ODR-073), so the same pointer is refused alone and accepted inside a struct.

decisions.parameters_in_order: (1) Three goals: speed and safety tie (shown: a by-value result's held pointer is used only in `unsafe`; an `out one` struct is a parameter under both, which matters because C reads its `pNext`). Ease of reading decides: R1 is one sentence for both directions, in the shape the language already uses for `char` and range types; R2 refuses a bare raw-pointer result but accepts the same pointer in a struct result, a second shape to learn. (5) R2 accepts a rare binding that R1 refuses (a by-value struct result holding a raw pointer), at the cost of one wrapper; this is listed as a trade-off. (6) R1 matches ODR-073 ("never a raw pointer") and FFI-2a ("in result position a pointer's lifetime is never derived"), and is the smaller edit: it extends FFI-1's "parameter and result" without carving results out.

owner_short.one_line: Should a C function that returns, by value, a struct holding a `char*` still be declarable safe?
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | binding author | declares `safe fn lib_name() -> NameRef`, where `NameRef` holds `p: *u8` and `n` | accepted today |
| 2 | safe caller | gets `r.p`, which it can read only inside `unsafe:` | no hole by itself |
| 3 | with R1 | the `safe fn` line is refused; the author writes `unsafe fn` and a wrapper returning a `StrView` | one rule: no raw pointer anywhere in a safe C signature |
owner_short.today: Compiles; safe code holds a raw pointer that it cannot read without `unsafe`.
options: R1: refuse it too: a safe C function's signature carries no raw pointer anywhere, as a bare raw-pointer result is already refused.
R2: refuse only what C is given: a struct result holding a raw pointer stays safe, while a bare raw-pointer result stays refused.
owner_short.recommendation: R1: one rule both ways, matching the refusal a bare pointer result already gets; the cost is one wrapper in the binding.

responses.objection: Correct programs are refused: epoll's `data.ptr`, a `void* user_data` that C only hands back, Vulkan's `pNext = NULL`. C never dereferences these.
responses.how: The declaration cannot state that fact: contract words follow a parameter's name (FFI-11 p16-ffi.md 284-286), and an overlay never changes fields (FFI-30a 210-212). Safe callers choose the value with nothing checking it (IV.5, SPN-8). A bare `void*` parameter is refused today for the same reason (FFI-10 82-84). There are zero-cost ways out: a wrapper, or hand-declaring the field as the scalar it is to C (`data: u64`). Field contracts (option D) are a feature for later.

responses.objection: Fix it where the pointer is made: make `ref_to_ptr` unsafe.
responses.how: That reverses ODR-075 (p26-appx-h.md 363) and does not close the hole: `as_mut_ptr()` is safe (SPN-8 p07-ownership.md 837), `null[P]()` is safe (IV.5 347), and a pointer C returned earlier is already in safe code. The danger is at the C call that receives an unchecked address, which is where FFI-10 82-84 already fences the bare pointer.

responses.objection: Fix only FFI-10's list, where it was reported.
responses.how: The spec's own example takes the overlay route (XVI.4 `vkCreateBuffer`, p16-ffi.md 239-241), which never reads FFI-10's list: FFI-2 (33-42) makes an overlay entry safe once its contract has no unknown fact. Only FFI-1's definition of the contract reaches hand declarations, overlays, imports, typedefs and C++ at once.

responses.objection: A struct result holding a raw pointer is harmless; refusing it is over-strict.

I read only the spec parts, JOB.md, OWNER-DIRECTION.md, the team rules and the input. I ran nothing and edited no file.

Gaps that already exist and are not caused by this change, listed for later:
(1) FFI-31b's E5015 (owning values such as `String` and `owns T`) reaches only exported signatures (p16-ffi.md 647-650). Every struct is C-layout by default (TYP-11), so a hand-declared `safe fn` taking a struct that holds a `String` is refused by no words, and C could free it. This belongs to P04's "C struct fields in general".
(2) A function pointer held in a struct field given to C (an Ember `extern "C" fn` that C may call later or from another thread) is not a raw pointer under these words. FFI-22's thread rule names only exports and trampolines.
(3) FFI-52's example declares `safe fn register_cb(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void), ud: *mut void)` (p16-ffi.md 493). FFI-10 82-84 reads as refusing the raw `ud`, unless a `user_data` parameter leaves the callable signature the way `count(n)`'s witness does, and no rule says that it does.
(4) The XVI.4 `vkCreateBuffer` entry is marked `no_callbacks` while `pAllocator` can carry allocation callbacks. Edit 5's `@safety` (\"`pAllocator` is null\") keeps the mark true. K46 rewrites the same lines.
(5) Field contracts (option D) would let some of these calls be safe. It is a whole feature: its cases are counts from sibling fields, the lifetime of a struct value, `pNext` chains, and FFI-30a. It is for the owner to ask for later.

The outcome is `decided`: FFI-10's existing raw-pointer property, together with FFI-2's unknown-fact fence, reaches the case once FFI-1 says where a raw pointer may sit. D1 and D2 are recorded and were made by the parameters. No verdict is departed from. The cost is weighed and listed for the owner: some correct bindings are refused (by-value struct results holding a raw pointer, and pointers C never dereferences), each with a way out at zero run-time cost.

out.intent: Have a C routine zero a pixel buffer the program owns, where the buffer reaches C as a pointer and a length inside a struct.

cause.where: FFI-2, p16-ffi.md 33-42: the safe-to-call fact. All three spellings assert it: `safe fn` (FFI-10), an overlay entry (FFI-2, GRM-35) and an `@ffi(safe)` typedef (FFI-56). The fact has no limit on raw pointers. The only limit is FFI-10's sentence at 82-84, and it covers one spelling and one position: a raw-pointer parameter or result of a hand declaration. An overlay's contract (FFI-1, 26-32) counts only pointer-typed parameters and results. So a raw pointer inside a struct, or one returned by a callback the call gives C, is in no contract and under no limit.
cause.why_there: ODR-073's reason (OWNER-QUEUE.md 3672-3673: 'a safe caller may pass a null, dangling or forged pointer; the contract cannot establish validity') is a property of what any assertion of safety can cover. It is not specific to hand declarations or to parameter slots: safe code makes such a pointer with `ref_to_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr()` or `null[P]()` (p04-types.md 340-348, p07-ownership.md 837-838) and can put it in a struct field. The limit therefore belongs where the fact is defined, so that all three spellings share it. FFI-11 (contract words attach to parameter and result slots) and FFI-30a (an overlay never changes a type's fields, so packages can exchange values) are right as written. They explain why a field pointer can never be contracted, and that is why no assertion may cover it. FFI-10's and FFI-56's lists only accept 'a `@layout(c)` value type' because no limit sat above them, so each list gets a cite and no rule of its own.

existing_rule.rule: FFI-10 (with ODR-073's reason, and FFI-31b's reach through aggregates)
existing_rule.words: FFI-10: "A raw `*T` can be declared for an unsafe call, but complete facts do not make a raw-pointer parameter or result safe to expose; `safe fn` with one is `E5002`." ODR-073 (p26-appx-h.md 361; OWNER-QUEUE.md 3672-3673, 3682-3684): "a safe caller may pass a null, dangling or forged pointer; the contract cannot establish validity"; "complete `@ffi` facts alone never make that raw pointer safe to pass from Safe code". FFI-31b's reach for the same kind of limit: "directly or in a `@layout(c)` aggregate passed by value or behind a pointer (`E5054`)". IV.5: "Creating one from a reference is safe (ODR-075): `ref_to_ptr(r: T) -> *T` ... `null[P]()` (ODR-076) is safe".

edits.after: safety; such an overlay is an `unsafe overlay` (`[GRM-35]`). edits.why_general: It is one property of the safe-to-call fact: a raw pointer that safe code made never reaches C under an assertion of safety. Its reason is ODR-073's. It names no type and no construct. It reaches every type that can carry a pointer into C (a struct, a union, a fixed array, a span's elements, a nested struct), every route by which a call hands C a value (an argument by value, behind `one`, `count(n)`, `exclusive` or `owns`, a C++ method's object, a callback's result), and all three spellings that assert the fact. The reach reuses FFI-31b's words for the same kind of limit. Values flowing the other way are left alone, because §IV.5 already fences reading through them. So are slots whose own words leave a fact unknown, which keep today's unsafe calls (FFI-2, FFI-11c).

readability.before: The caller writes `clear_pixels(PixelBuf(data=ref_to_ptr(ref mut x), len=4096))`. It reads as safe code and corrupts memory. The binding is one line, `safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)`.

The binding author writes `@safety("…")` above `unsafe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)` and a four-line wrapper, `fn clear(ref mut bytes: MutSpan[u8]):` with `unsafe:` building the struct from `bytes.as_mut_ptr()` and `bytes.len() as usize`.
readability.verdict: No longer and no harder for the ordinary program that calls a binding. A binding of a C API whose structs carry pointers writes one wrapper per such function, which is the price Rust binding authors pay too. It is heaviest for Vulkan, where every create-info has `pNext`. Field contracts would let such structs become safe types, but that is a whole feature that FFI-30a rules out today; it is listed in notes for the owner, not added here.

impact.cost: Nothing runs: the limit is checked when compiling. A wrapper fills the struct from the span's pointer and length, as C code fills it, and makes the same single direct C call (FFI-9: one `call` instruction). To measure: the wrapper against a direct C call with the same arguments. The expectation is identical code after inlining, as with C.

    data: *mut u8      # C writes `len` bytes here
    len: usize

unsafe extern "C":

answers.today: Compiles. `PixelBuf` is 'a `@layout(c)` value type', so FFI-10's list (p16 59-61) accepts `safe fn clear_pixels`. The raw-pointer refusal (82-84) covers only a raw-pointer parameter itself. At run time C writes 4,096 bytes from the address of the one-byte `x` (C++: a buffer overflow through a struct of pointer and length, from code the compiler calls safe).
answers.after: E5002 at line 8 (`safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)`), naming `buf.data`: a call hands C a raw pointer inside what its argument passes by value. The message gives the line to write: `unsafe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)`, with `@safety("…")` above it. The intended program is that declaration plus a wrapper `fn clear(ref mut bytes: MutSpan[u8])` that builds the struct from the checked span inside `unsafe:`, called as `clear(ref mut frame.as_mut_span())`. It prints `0 0 4` for a 4-byte frame (test 2).

So a `safe fn` ... whose call would hand C one, is `E5002`, naming where the pointer is held (`buf.data`) and the `unsafe fn` line to write".

decisions.title: What happens to a safe C declaration whose argument's struct holds a raw pointer
decisions.problem: A safe C function may not take a raw pointer, because safe code can make one that is null, dangling or forged. The same pointer inside a struct argument passes the safe-call list, and nothing can state its count or lifetime: contract words attach only to parameters, and overlays may not change fields. Safe code fills the struct with any address and length, and C writes through it.

options.outcome: `safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)` is E5002, naming `buf.data`. The wrapper compiles, safe callers can clear only bytes they own, and the program prints `0 0 4`.
Compiles (today). C writes 4,095 bytes past `x`: memory corruption in safe code. `ember tcb` lists the assertion.

Writing a raw pointer into a struct needs `unsafe:`. That applies to Ember's own structs too, since every struct is laid out as C's (TYP-11). The hole stays: the length beside the pointer is a plain integer that safe code changes, and C writes 4,096 bytes into a 4-byte list.

Not in the specification. FFI-30a forbids an overlay to change a type's fields, so packages with different overlays could no longer exchange `PixelBuf` values. This would be a whole feature with its own cases, listed for the owner later.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: A keeps one direct C call, closes the hole, and gives callers a shorter line. B gives up safety. C gives up readability, since every line putting a pointer into a struct needs `unsafe:`, Ember's own structs included, and still leaves the hole. D is not in the language. 2. Safety, never given up: only A is safe. Under B, safe code corrupts memory. Under C, `buf.len = 4096` is safe code and C writes past the buffer. 3. Compile time first: A is decided when compiling, and nothing runs. 4. A written word only for meaning: A's `unsafe fn` and `@safety` say who vouches and for what (verdicts 120, 133), and nothing else. 5. The ordinary program no longer or harder: callers write `clear(ref mut frame.as_mut_span())`, shorter than building the struct by hand; a binding author writes one wrapper. 6. Consistency with the nearest rule and the verdicts: FFI-10's 'complete facts do not make a raw-pointer parameter ... safe to expose' and ODR-073's reason ('a safe caller may pass a null, dangling or forged pointer') hold exactly for a pointer in a field. Verdicts 130, 133 and 136 give the spelling of the unsafe declaration.

owner_short.one_line: A C function declared safe takes `struct { uint8_t* data; size_t len; }` by value, and safe code can fill it with any address and length: may the safe declaration stand?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | binding author | declares `clear_pixels(PixelBuf)` safe | refused: the struct carries a raw pointer
2 | binding author | declares it `unsafe fn` with what callers must make true, and writes `clear(ref mut bytes: MutSpan[u8])` | compiles
3 | program | calls `clear(ref mut frame.as_mut_span())` | only bytes it owns reach C
4 | program runs | one direct C call | the same cost as C
owner_short.today: The safe declaration compiles, and safe code can hand C a pointer to one byte with a length of 4,096; C writes past it.
options: A: refuse a safe C declaration that hands C a raw pointer inside a struct; a wrapper builds the struct from a checked view
B: keep today: the declarer's word covers the struct's pointers too (memory corruption from safe code)
C: make writing a raw pointer into a struct unsafe instead (still unsafe: the length beside it is a plain number safe code changes)
D: let overlays give struct fields contracts (not in the language: overlays may not change a type's fields)
owner_short.recommendation: A: the only choice that closes the hole when compiling, with no cost while running, and callers get a shorter line.

decisions.title: Which ways a raw pointer made in safe code can reach C are covered
decisions.problem: Once a raw pointer inside a struct argument is refused, the same pointer can still reach C by other routes: in a C++ method's object, or as the result of an Ember function the call gives C (an allocator or buffer callback). Pointers that C hands back to Ember flow the other way.

options.outcome: Only arguments are covered. `stream_read` compiles, and C writes 4,096 bytes into a dead stack slot.

Everything the call hands C is covered: arguments, a method's object, what a function given to C returns. `stream_read` is E5002 naming `get_buf`'s result. `camera_latest_frame` compiles and prints `3 2`, and reading through `f.pixels` needs `unsafe:`.

ii, plus what C hands back. `camera_latest_frame`, `SDL_GetCurrentDisplayMode`'s `out` mode and `returns_owned` image loaders are refused, with no safety gained: reading through a raw pointer is unsafe already (IV.5).

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: ii keeps every correct program that only reads what C hands back, and costs nothing while running. 2. Safety: i leaves a callback's dangling pointer reaching C from safe code; ii and iii close it. 3. Compile time first: all three are decided when compiling. 4. A written word only for meaning: none adds a word. 5. The ordinary program: iii refuses programs that can only read C's struct (camera frame, display mode, image loader); ii refuses none of them. 6. Consistency: ii follows the direction the value flows, as FFI-21a does for raw pointers given back to C, and leaves to IV.5 what IV.5 already fences.

owner_short.one_line: Besides struct arguments, which other ways can safe code hand C a pointer it made, e.g. an allocator callback `uint8_t* (*get_buf)(size_t)` returning the address of a dead local?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | binding author | declares `stream_read(want, get_buf)` safe; C writes `want` bytes at what `get_buf` returns | refused: the callback's result is a raw pointer
2 | binding author | declares `camera_latest_frame() -> FrameInfo`, holding C's pixel pointer | compiles: C hands it to Ember
3 | program | reads `f.width` | allowed
4 | program | reads through `f.pixels` | only in `unsafe:`, as today
owner_short.today: A callback that returns a raw pointer passes, and so does any struct C returns.
options: i: only arguments (a callback returning a dangling pointer still reaches C from safe code)
ii: everything the call hands C: arguments, a method's object, what a callback it gives C returns
iii: ii plus what C hands back (refuses programs that only read C's struct, with no safety gained)
owner_short.recommendation: ii: covers every way a pointer made in safe code reaches C, and nothing C hands back, which is already unsafe to read through.

decisions.title: What a plain overlay line, or an @ffi(safe) typedef, that would hand C such a pointer becomes
decisions.problem: An overlay line such as `fn cp_load(opts: borrowed one)` reads as complete, but the header's struct holds a `const char*` that the line cannot contract. The line could be refused, or its calls could become unsafe the way an unknown fact makes them.

options.outcome: Refused at the overlay line, naming `opts.path`, with the `unsafe fn` line to write. After the rewrite, calls go in `unsafe:` with a `# SAFETY:` note.
The line is accepted, but its calls are unsafe, because of a header field that the line does not show. Each first call is refused, and in `unsafe:` L3015 sends the writer back to the overlay.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: both are safe and free at run time; a reads better, with one error at the line to change. 2. Safety: both refuse a safe call. 3. Compile time first: both. 4. A written word only for meaning: under b, a plain overlay line, which says 'safe to call' (GRM-35), would have unsafe calls because of a header field the overlay's reader never sees, so its meaning would no longer come from what is written (verdict 132's lesson). 5. The ordinary program: a gives one error at the overlay line with the line to write; b gives an error at every call site, then L3015. 6. Consistency: a matches FFI-10's E5002 for `safe fn` and verdict 136 (no line means unsafe without saying so). A line whose own words leave a fact unknown (TODO words, an uncontracted pointer slot such as FFI-6b's `p: *Pair`) keeps today's unsafe calls, because its unknown fact is written in it. The new words reach only an entry 'whose other facts are all known'.

owner_short.one_line: An overlay line `fn cp_load(opts: borrowed one)` looks complete, but the header's struct holds a `const char*`: refuse the line, or quietly make its calls unsafe?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | overlay writer | writes `fn cp_load(opts: borrowed one)` | refused at this line, naming `opts.path`
2 | overlay writer | writes `@safety("…")` above `unsafe fn cp_load(opts: borrowed one)` | compiles
3 | program | calls `cp_load` in `unsafe:` with a `# SAFETY:` note | compiles
4 | program | calls it outside `unsafe:` | refused at the call
owner_short.today: The line declares the call safe and is accepted.
options: a: refuse the line, with the `unsafe fn` line to write
b: accept it, and make its calls unsafe, as for a fact not yet written
owner_short.recommendation: a: a line means what it says; a plain overlay line means safe to call, so one that cannot be made safe is refused where it is written.

responses.objection: (test2 hole 1, 4) An owned foreign struct holding a pointer (`blob`, `SDL_Surface`, `image_load -> returns_owned(...)`) is refused, and safe code writing `asset.data` before its destructor brings back the invalid free.
responses.how: The new words reach only what a call hands C ('inside what an argument or a method's object passes'). They do not reach results, `returns_owned` results or `destroys(f)`, so `blob_new`, `image_load` and an `owns SDL_Surface` compile as today ('a raw pointer C hands Ember (a result ...) is not one'). A destructor freeing a field that safe code wrote goes wrong the same way with and without this change, so under rule E it is a gap that already exists. It is listed in notes for later (safe writes to pointer or length fields of foreign memory), not caused here.

responses.objection: (test2 hole 2) A C++ `std::function` with a raw pointer in its parameters becomes uncallable.
responses.how: `@ffi(std_function)` (Annex C, p21 67) is none of the three assertions the words name ('a `safe fn`, an `@ffi(safe)` typedef, or an overlay entry not written `unsafe fn`'), so its import is unchanged. Its own raw-pointer route is an existing gap that needs an unsafe callable form (checklist 12), listed in notes.

responses.objection: (test2 hole 3) An ordinary game loop taking a `ref mut` view of a C struct with pointer fields (ImGui's IO block, `engine_input() -> borrowed one exclusive from(static)`) is refused.
responses.how: A result view is something C hands Ember, so it is not reached. `engine_input()` and `engine_begin_frame()` (no arguments) compile as today. The danger the breaker named, safe code writing `input.ini_path`, is the same existing field-write gap as for objection 1, listed for later.

responses.objection: (test2 hole 5) FFI-6b's conformance test (`@ffi(macro_fn) fn PAIR_FIRST(p: *Pair)`) and FFI-11c's day-one path change outcome.
responses.how: A raw pointer written in an entry's own slot is not 'inside what an argument passes', and the E5002 applies only to an entry 'whose other facts are all known'. `PAIR_FIRST` keeps its unsafe call, its L3015 and its output `25 4.5 7 7 true false` (test 9). TODO entries and headers without entries keep today's unsafe calls.

responses.objection: (anticipated) User-data cookies C never dereferences (`SDL_UserEvent.data1`, `VkAllocationCallbacks.pUserData`, `uv_handle_t.data`) are refused although harmless to C.
responses.how: C is unchecked code. The compiler cannot tell a cookie C hands back from a buffer C writes, and principle 6 allows no exception where the general rule is not untrue. The cost is one wrapper in the binding. A field word saying 'C never reads through it' belongs to the field-contract feature listed for the owner, which FFI-30a rules out today.

responses.objection: (anticipated) Vulkan cost: every `vkCreate*` create-info has `pNext`, so every create call needs `unsafe fn` and a wrapper.
responses.how: Vulkan walks `pNext` and reads `sType` at each link, so a forged chain from safe code is memory corruption. The safe route is a renderer's checked builder (what vulkano does over ash) or the field-contract feature. The cost falls on the binding, not on code that calls it. It is stated in the readability verdict and in notes.

responses.objection: (anticipated) A wrapper taking the public struct only moves the hole into the wrapper.
responses.how: A sound wrapper builds the struct from checked views (decision 1, option A) or keeps the foreign struct in a private field (MOD-2, p05 19-22; MOD-7, 34-37), so no safe code outside its module can write the pointer. A wrapper that vouches for a struct anyone may fill makes a false `# SAFETY:` claim in unsafe code. That is the unsafe author's error, as in Rust, and `ember tcb` lists it.
