decisions.title: What happens to a safe C declaration whose argument's struct holds a raw pointer
decisions.problem: A safe C function may not take a raw pointer, because safe code can make one that is null, dangling or short. The same pointer inside a struct argument passes the safe-call list, and nothing can state its count or lifetime: contract words attach only to parameters, and overlays may not change fields. Safe code fills the struct with any address and length, and C writes through it.

options.outcome: `safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)` is E5002, naming `buf.data`. The wrapper compiles, safe callers can clear only bytes they own, and the program prints `0 0 4`.
Compiles (today). C writes 4,095 bytes past `x`: memory corruption in safe code. `ember tcb` lists the assertion.

Writing a raw pointer into a struct needs `unsafe:`, Ember's own structs included. The hole stays: the length beside the pointer is a plain integer that safe code changes, and C writes 4,096 bytes into a 4-byte list.

Not in the specification. FFI-30a forbids an overlay to change a type's fields, so packages with different overlays could no longer exchange `PixelBuf` values. It would be a whole feature with its own cases, listed for the owner.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: A keeps one direct C call, closes the hole, and gives callers a shorter line. B gives up safety. C gives up readability, since every line that puts a pointer into a struct needs `unsafe:`, and it still leaves the hole. D is not in the language. 2. Safety, never given up: only A is safe. Under B, safe code corrupts memory. Under C, `buf.len = 4096` is safe code and C writes past the buffer. 3. Compile time first: A is decided when compiling, and nothing runs. 4. A written word only for meaning: A's `unsafe fn` and `@safety` say who vouches and for what (verdicts 120, 133). 5. The ordinary program no longer or harder: callers write `clear(ref mut frame)`, which is shorter than building the struct by hand; a binding author writes one wrapper. 6. Consistency with the nearest rule and the verdicts: FFI-10's 'complete facts do not make a raw-pointer parameter ... safe to expose' and ODR-073's reason hold exactly for a pointer in a field; verdicts 130, 133 and 136 give the spelling.

owner_short.one_line: A C function declared safe takes `struct { uint8_t* data; size_t len; }` by value, and safe code can fill it with any address and length: may the safe declaration stand?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | binding author | declares `clear_pixels(PixelBuf)` safe | refused: the struct carries a raw pointer
2 | binding author | declares it unsafe, with what callers must make true, and writes `clear(ref mut bytes: MutSpan[u8])` | compiles
3 | program | calls `clear(ref mut frame)` | only bytes it owns reach C
4 | program runs | one direct C call | the same cost as C
owner_short.today: The safe declaration compiles, and safe code can hand C a pointer to one byte with a length of 4,096; C writes past it.
options: A: refuse a safe C declaration that hands C a raw pointer inside a struct; a wrapper builds the struct from a checked view
B: keep today: the declarer's word covers the struct's pointers too (memory corruption from safe code)
C: make writing a raw pointer into a struct unsafe instead (still a hole: the length beside it is a plain number safe code changes)
D: let overlays give struct fields contracts (not in the language: overlays may not change a type's fields)
owner_short.recommendation: A: the only choice that closes the hole when compiling, with no cost while running, and callers get a shorter line.

decisions.title: Which ways a raw pointer the caller supplied can reach C are covered
decisions.problem: Once a raw pointer inside a struct argument is refused, the same pointer can still reach C by other routes: in a C++ method's object, in a span's elements, or as the result of an Ember function the call gives C (an allocator or buffer callback). Pointers that C hands back to Ember flow the other way.

options.outcome: Only struct arguments are covered. `stream_read` compiles, and C writes 4,096 bytes into a dead stack slot.

Every raw pointer the caller's arguments carry to C is covered: in an argument at any depth, in a method's object, in what a function given to the call returns, and in the items of a two-call enumeration, which C may read. `stream_read` is E5002 naming `get_buf`'s result. `camera_latest_frame` compiles and prints `3 2`, and reading through `f.pixels` needs `unsafe:`. Exports, export tables and C++ overrides, which C calls with no call handing it anything, stay as they are; they are listed for the owner.

ii, plus what C hands back. `camera_latest_frame`, `SDL_GetCurrentDisplayMode`'s `out` mode and `returns_owned` image loaders are refused, and no safety is gained: reading through a raw pointer is unsafe already (IV.5).

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: ii keeps every correct program that only reads what C hands back, and costs nothing while running. 2. Safety: i leaves a callback's dangling pointer reaching C from safe code; ii and iii close it. 3. Compile time first: all three are decided when compiling. 4. A written word only for meaning: none adds a word. 5. The ordinary program: iii refuses programs that only read C's struct (a camera frame, a display mode, an image loader); ii refuses none of them. 6. Consistency: ii follows the direction the value flows, as FFI-21a does for raw pointers given back to C, and leaves to IV.5 what IV.5 already fences.

owner_short.one_line: Besides struct arguments, which other ways can a call hand C a pointer the caller made, e.g. an allocator callback `uint8_t* (*get_buf)(size_t)` returning the address of a dead local?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | binding author | declares `stream_read(want, get_buf)` safe; C writes `want` bytes at what `get_buf` returns | refused: the callback's result is a raw pointer
2 | binding author | declares `camera_latest_frame() -> FrameInfo`, holding C's pixel pointer | compiles: C hands it to Ember
3 | program | reads `f.width` | allowed
4 | program | reads through `f.pixels` | only in unsafe code, as today
owner_short.today: A callback that returns a raw pointer passes, and so does any struct C returns.
options: i: only struct arguments (a callback returning a dangling pointer still reaches C from safe code)
ii: every pointer the call's arguments carry to C: fields, elements, a C++ object, what a callback given to the call returns
iii: ii plus what C hands back (refuses programs that only read C's struct, with no safety gained)
owner_short.recommendation: ii: covers every pointer a call hands C, and nothing C hands back, which is already unsafe to read through.

decisions.title: What a plain overlay line, or an @ffi(safe) typedef, that would hand C such a pointer becomes
decisions.problem: An overlay line such as `fn cp_load(opts: borrowed one)` reads as complete, but the header's struct holds a `const char*` that the line cannot contract. The line could be refused, or its calls could become unsafe, the way an unknown fact makes them.

options.outcome: Refused at the overlay line, naming `opts.path`, with the lines to write. In another package's overlay, the message gives the same entry as an `override` in the importing package's own overlay. An entry whose own words already leave its calls unsafe (a TODO word, an uncontracted raw-pointer slot, `retained` on a plain pointer) is not reached.

The line is accepted, but its calls are unsafe because of a header field that the line does not show. Each call outside unsafe code is refused, and inside `unsafe:` L3015 sends the writer back to the overlay.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: both are safe and free at run time; a reads better, with one error at the line to change. 2. Safety: both refuse a safe call. 3. Compile time first: both. 4. A written word only for meaning: under b, a plain overlay line, which says 'safe to call' (GRM-35), would have unsafe calls because of a header field the overlay's reader never sees (verdict 132's lesson). 5. The ordinary program: a gives one error at the overlay line with the lines to write; b gives an error at every call, then L3015. Under a, a dependant that never calls the entry also fails until it writes the override or the dependency is fixed, as with a drifted entry today (FFI-55). 6. Consistency: a matches FFI-10's E5002 for `safe fn` and verdict 136 (no line silently means unsafe). The trigger is what the entry itself says ('whose calls the other rules make safe'), so FFI-11's `retained` row and FFI-11c's TODO words keep deciding their entries.

owner_short.one_line: An overlay line `fn cp_load(opts: borrowed one)` looks complete, but the header's struct holds a `const char*`: refuse the line, or quietly make its calls unsafe?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | overlay writer | writes `fn cp_load(opts: borrowed one)` | refused at this line, naming `opts.path`
2 | overlay writer | writes it unsafe, with what callers must make true | compiles
3 | program | calls `cp_load` in unsafe code with a note | compiles
4 | another package using this overlay | builds before the fix | refused, told the line to write in its own overlay
owner_short.today: The line declares the call safe and is accepted.
options: a: refuse the line, with the unsafe line to write
b: accept it, and make its calls unsafe, as for a fact not yet written
owner_short.recommendation: a: a line means what it says; a plain overlay line means safe to call, so one that cannot be made safe is refused where it is written.

decisions.title: Whether a C++ std::function imported as a callable is limited the same way
decisions.problem: `@ffi(std_function)` turns a C++ `std::function<R(A…)>` into an Ember callable that is safe to call, with no limit on its parameters. Safe code can call it with a raw pointer, or with a struct holding one, and C++ writes through it. Refusing the entry would leave no Ember line that calls the value, because the language has no spelling for an unsafe callable import. A fix also changes what every existing `@ffi(std_function)` entry means.

options.outcome: Calls of a `std::function` value go in `unsafe:` unless its entry says `safe` (`@ffi(std_function, safe)`), and that word is refused when a call would carry a raw pointer, as `@ffi(safe)` is for a C function pointer. Every existing `@ffi(std_function)` entry's calls become unsafe until its entry says `safe`.

options.code:
# the same overlay, as today
fn main():
    fill = f.px.make_filler()
    x: u8 = 7
    fill(f.px.Buf(data=ref_to_ptr(ref mut x), len=4096))   # safe code
options.outcome: Compiles. C++ writes 4,096 bytes from the address of `x`: memory corruption from safe code, for a struct or for a plain `std::function<void(int*)>`.
Refused. The message can only say to remove `@ffi(std_function)`, which leaves `Fill` an opaque object that Ember cannot call at all, so no line it gives makes the program compile (DIA-25).

decisions.chosen: none applied: recommendation a, for the owner
decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: a keeps the callable usable from Ember at C++'s cost and closes the hole; b gives up safety; c refuses correct programs with no Ember way to call them. 2. Safety: a and c are safe; under b, safe code hands C++ a dangling pointer. 3. Compile time first: all three. 4. A written word only for meaning: a's `safe` says who vouches, as `@ffi(safe)` does for a C function pointer. 5. The ordinary program: under a, calls of a `std::function` go in `unsafe:` unless its entry vouches; under c there is no call at all. 6. Consistency: a is FFI-56's rule for C function pointers and the owner's 'C++ too, same rule' (verdict 125). The parameters pick a, but a changes the meaning of a delegated ruling (ODR-199) and of every existing `@ffi(std_function)` program, and it adds the word `safe` to a `std_function` entry. So it goes to the owner, and this change leaves FFI-17a as it is.
decisions.departs_from_verdict: a would change ODR-199 (delegated: `@ffi(std_function)` makes an owned callable value, safe to call); not applied

owner_short.one_line: A C++ `std::function<void(Buf)>`, where `Buf` holds a `uint8_t*`, imported as a callable: safe code can call it with any address. Should calling it be unsafe, as calling a C function pointer is?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | overlay writer | maps `std::function<void(Buf)>` to a callable | today: safe to call
2 | program | calls it with a one-byte address and a length of 4,096 | today: C++ writes past the byte
3 | under a | the call goes in unsafe code with a note, unless the overlay vouches (it cannot vouch here: the struct holds a raw pointer) | the caller vouches
4 | under c | the overlay line is refused | Ember cannot call it at all
owner_short.today: A mapped `std::function` is safe to call whatever its parameters hold.
options: a: unsafe to call unless the overlay says it is safe, which it cannot say for raw pointers (the C function pointer's rule)
b: keep today (C++ can be handed a dangling pointer from safe code)
c: refuse such an overlay line (Ember can then never call it)
owner_short.recommendation: a: the same rule as a C function pointer: unsafe to call unless someone vouches, and never vouched for raw pointers.

responses.objection: S1-7 (the E5002 row's reach disagrees with FFI-2 on FFI-6b's `PAIR_FIRST`)
responses.how: The row now repeats the limit's reach and its trigger: 'a `safe fn`, overlay function entry or `@ffi(safe)` typedef whose calls would otherwise be safe and would carry foreign code a raw pointer from the caller's arguments (one an argument is or holds at any depth, or one an Ember function given to the call returns)', with `[FFI-56]` added to the rule column. `PAIR_FIRST(p: *Pair)`'s calls are unsafe by its own words (an uncontracted raw-pointer slot, FFI-2 p16 33-34), so neither the row nor FFI-2 reaches it. Test 9 keeps `25 4.5 7 7 true false` and its L3015.

responses.objection: E1-1 (the message pushes hand bindings to the raw form, and the line it gives may not compile)
responses.how: Fixed in part: the message now gives a line that compiles under today's rules. For a hand declaration that is the raw form FFI-10 decides ('A raw `*T` can be declared for an unsafe call', p16 82; 'An unsafe raw-pointer declaration keeps its written C ABI parameters', 91-92). For writev it is `@ffi(no_callbacks)` and `@safety("…")` above `unsafe fn writev(fd: c_int, iov: *IoVec, iovcnt: c_int) -> isize`, with the `param(iov, …)` words of the slot written raw dropped, so no type/contract question arises (p16 84). The call line becomes `writev(1, parts.as_span().as_ptr(), parts.len() as c_int)`, in `unsafe:` with a `# SAFETY:` note (DIA-25, p17 474-476). Kept: the hand form and the overlay form of one unsafe function still differ, and the wrapper author writes the pointer and the length conversion by hand. That difference exists today for every unsafe hand declaration (FFI-10 91-92 and 109-110 against FFI-11's count row, p16 291), and E1-1's own program is undecided without this change (nothing says an `unsafe fn` may write `Span[IoVec]`). E1-1's property (contract words decide the Ember signature of `safe fn` and `unsafe fn` alike) is the consistent one (verdict 133: 'as in overlays'). But it rewrites ODR-074's sentence and decides how witnesses, nullable carriers, `out` and `status` behave on unsafe declarations, so it is listed for the owner with that recommendation. Impact: each newly refused hand binding writes `as_ptr()` and a length cast in its wrapper; overlay bindings keep the mapped form.

responses.objection: E1-2 (`@ffi(std_function)` is a fourth assertion; the universal claim is not kept; the FFI-31b cite misleads; the sentence is too long)
responses.how: Rewritten as E1-2 asks, using its fallback. The limit is now its own sentences at the end of FFI-2: the property, the reason, the refusal and its message, the direction. The first sentence names exactly the assertions it decides ('No assertion of the fact — `safe fn`, an overlay function entry not written `unsafe fn`, or `@ffi(safe)` on a function-pointer typedef — covers ...'), so it claims nothing about `@ffi(std_function)`. That spelling (p21 67) has no raw-pointer limit at all, not even for `std::function<void(int*)>`, and its way out needs a spelling the language lacks. It is decision 4, for the owner, with the recommendation to treat it as a C function pointer is treated (FFI-56): unsafe to call, with `safe` asserting within the same limits, using FN-6's `unsafe fn(…) -> R` type (p05 179-183). The `[FFI-31b]` cite is gone, and the reach is defined once in FFI-2's own words. FFI-31b's `char` reach is left as written: it is a separate rule.

responses.objection: E1-3 (the 'reading through it is unsafe already' reason undercuts FFI-10's result refusal)
responses.how: The direction is now scope only: 'A raw pointer that foreign code hands Ember (a result, an `out` value, a callback's parameter) is outside this limit; `[FFI-10]` decides a hand declaration's raw-pointer result.' No reason is given that disagrees with FFI-10 82-84. Listed for the owner: ODR-073's result half (a delegated ruling, p26 361) can only be about the API's shape, since a struct result such as `camera_latest_frame() -> FrameInfo` already brings C's raw pointer into safe code. The owner can keep it as a shape rule or drop it.

responses.objection: E1-4 (read literally, every method of an opaque C++ class with a pointer member is refused)
responses.how: The reach is anchored to the value 'as its Ember type declares it'. An opaque class (FFI-44, p21 43; FFI-32, 76-77), an `extern type` (FFI-8, p16 183) and the bridge types `CppVector[T]` and `CppString` (FFI-17e, p21 69-71) declare no fields in Ember. So nothing in `vertex_count`'s object is reached, and the program prints `3` (test 11).

responses.objection: E1-5 (the impact report undercounts fields holding pointers to opaque types and handle typedefs)
responses.how: The Unchanged row now reads 'an opaque type behind a contracted parameter'. A new programs_changed row lists structs holding a pointer to an opaque type or a pointer typedef (`app_cfg.window`, a field of type `FT_Face`, `VkDescriptorBufferInfo.buffer`) as refused. K46's question, whether `@ffi(handle)` or `@ffi(newtype)` makes such a field something other than a raw pointer, is named for every handle field. `app_start` is test 12 (E5002 naming `cfg.window`) and is in to_verify.

responses.objection: E1-6 (the ordinary call is shown longer than it is; XVI.4 shows no safe layer)
responses.how: Every program now uses `clear(ref mut frame)` (SPN-1, p07 812-814: an `Array[T]` converts to `MutSpan[T]` for a `ref mut` parameter), and test 2 still prints `0 0 4`. One sentence follows XVI.4's example, with no second example: '`vkCreateBuffer` is an `unsafe fn` entry because the structs its call hands Vulkan hold raw pointers (...); a wrapper in an `extend` block of the overlay (`[FFI-13]`) gives safe callers a create call, building those structs from checked views.'

responses.objection: E1-8 (another package's overlay breaks dependants that never call the entry, and the message points at a file they cannot change)
responses.how: For an entry in another package's overlay, the message gives the line the importing package can write: the entry as an `override` in its own overlay, applied after the dependency's (FFI-30c, p16 216-222; ODR-149: 'override before an item'). The build-break scope is in the impact report: once this lands, every build that applies such an overlay fails at the entry, as a build applying an overlay that drifted from its header already does (FFI-55, p16 345-351). That lasts until the dependency writes `unsafe fn` or the dependant writes the override.

responses.objection: I1-1 (X: FFI-11's `retained` row accepts `fn net_keep(cfg: retained one)` with unsafe calls; FFI-2 refused it)
responses.how: The trigger is now a property of what the declaration says: 'a declaration or entry whose calls the other rules make safe, and whose calls would carry such a pointer, is `E5002`'. The other rules leave `net_keep`'s calls unsafe (FFI-11's ownership row, p16 290: 'the call stays `unsafe`, with a raw pointer'), so FFI-2 does not reach it and FFI-11 decides it alone: it compiles and prints `net` (test 10). The same holds for TODO words (FFI-11c, 318-321), for uncontracted raw-pointer slots (FFI-6b's `PAIR_FIRST`), and for any later word that leaves calls unsafe. The two rules no longer decide one entry differently.

responses.objection: I1-2 (the items of an `inout_count` enumeration are filled by C, like an `out` value, and should not be reached)
responses.how: C may read what an enumeration's items hold, so the items are something the call hands C. FFI-11b (p16 313-317) defines the idiom only as 'call once for the count, again to fill'. It does not say that C never reads the items, and no contract word can say so (FFI-30a, 210-212). Vulkan's `vkGetPhysicalDeviceQueueFamilyProperties2(physicalDevice, pQueueFamilyPropertyCount, pQueueFamilyProperties)` is exactly that idiom, and its items `VkQueueFamilyProperties2` hold `pNext`, which the driver reads to find the chained structures it fills. With the items reached, a `pNext` that safe code set to a dead local is refused; with them excluded, the driver writes through it (C++: writing through a dangling pointer). An `out` value is different: Ember passes C no value of its own there. So `font_names` is E5002 naming the elements of `names` (test 13). Its binding writes `unsafe fn` and a wrapper, and the impact report lists two-call enumerations whose items are or hold raw pointers.

responses.objection: I1-3 (the words leave `@ffi(std_function)` undecided; the claim that it is unchanged is unsupported)
responses.how: The words now name only the assertions they cover (`safe fn`, an overlay function entry, `@ffi(safe)` on a typedef), so `@ffi(std_function)` is decided as unchanged by this text, and the impact report and decision 4 say so. I1-3's suggested consequence ('remove `@ffi(std_function)`') would not give a line that compiles in its program (DIA-25, p17 474-475). Without the attribute, `fill` is an opaque object (p21 67), and `fill(…)` has no meaning. The route, with or without a struct, is decision 4 for the owner. The recommended answer applies FFI-56's rule for a C function pointer to C++'s callable: unsafe to call unless the entry says `safe`, within the same limits.

responses.objection: I1-4 (the recommendation claims every route is covered; exports, export tables and overrides are not)
responses.how: The claim is narrowed, in the decision, its owner_short and the impact report, to 'every raw pointer the caller's arguments carry to C', which is what the words reach. Routes where C calls Ember without any call of the program handing it anything stay as they are and are listed for the owner: an `@unsafe(export(...))` function, an `@export_table` field and an override of a C++ class (FFI-52, p16 451-458), whose raw-pointer results C trusts. FFI-26's note vouches only for the name (633-634). These belong to the exports question (K08) and are not caused here (rule E).

responses.objection: I1-5 (`ember bind --init` output and the C++ routes are missing from the impact report; FFI-11 is not unchanged in outcome)
responses.how: CLI-5 (p17 115-116) now says that a declaration the limit keeps from being safe is written `unsafe fn`. So `ember bind --init pixels.h` writes `unsafe fn clear_pixels(buf)`, and its promise 'compiles unchanged' holds; the change is in programs_changed. The C++ routes are listed: a `T&` parameter (FFI-40, p21 161-163), `std::span<S>`, `std::unique_ptr<S>` and `std::optional<S>` (FFI-17a, 58, 63, 64), and a method of a by-value class (FFI-32, 74-80). rules_changed now says that FFI-11's text is unchanged, that its `retained` row keeps its outcome (I1-1), and that two-call enumerations whose items hold raw pointers are newly refused (I1-2).

responses.objection: I1-6 (placement, the general claim, per-spelling messages, FFI-10's naming clause, 'forged', the codes row)
responses.how: (1) The limit is now separate sentences after the DIA-18 sentence, so 'nothing of the kind' stays next to what it refers to. (2) FFI-2's second sentence reads 'makes the call safe, within the limit on raw pointers below'. (3) The message is given for each spelling: the `unsafe fn` line for a declaration or function entry, the typedef's entry without `@ffi(safe)`, and each call outside unsafe code in `unsafe:`. (4) FFI-10's clause reads 'naming the fact that is missing or, under that limit, where the raw pointer is held'. (5) Forging is cited as the spec allows it: a pointer-cast constant (FFI-6a, p16 150-151), beside null, dangling and short pointers (IV.5, SPN-8). (6) The codes row names the reach and cites `[FFI-56]`.

responses.objection: (test2 hole 1, 4) An owned foreign struct holding a pointer (`blob`, `SDL_Surface`, `image_load -> returns_owned(...)`) is refused, and safe code writing `asset.data` before its destructor brings back the invalid free.
responses.how: The words reach only what the caller's arguments carry to C. They do not reach results, `returns_owned` results or `destroys(f)`, so `blob_new`, `image_load` and an `owns SDL_Surface` compile as today. A destructor freeing a field that safe code wrote goes wrong the same way with and without this change, so under rule E it is a gap that already exists; it is listed in notes.

responses.objection: (test2 hole 3) A game loop taking a `ref mut` view of a C struct with pointer fields (ImGui's IO block, `engine_input() -> borrowed one exclusive from(static)`) is refused.
responses.how: A result view is something foreign code hands Ember, which is outside the limit, so `engine_input()` and `engine_begin_frame()` compile as today. The danger the breaker named, safe code writing `input.ini_path`, is the same existing field-write gap, listed for later.

responses.objection: (anticipated) User-data cookies C never dereferences (`SDL_UserEvent.data1`, `VkAllocationCallbacks.pUserData`, `uv_handle_t.data`) are refused although harmless to C.
responses.how: C is unchecked code. The compiler cannot tell a cookie that C hands back from a buffer that C writes, and principle 6 allows no exception where the general rule is not untrue. The cost is one wrapper in the binding. A field word saying 'C never reads through it' belongs to the field-contract feature, which FFI-30a rules out today; it is listed for the owner.

responses.objection: (anticipated) Vulkan cost: every `vkCreate*` create-info has `pNext`, so every create call needs `unsafe fn` and a wrapper.
responses.how: Vulkan walks `pNext` and reads `sType` at each link, so a forged chain from safe code is memory corruption. The safe route is an `extend` wrapper in the overlay (FFI-13), a renderer's checked builder (what vulkano does over ash), or the field-contract feature. The cost falls on the binding, not on code that calls it. It is stated in the readability verdict and in notes.

responses.objection: (anticipated) A wrapper taking the public struct only moves the hole into the wrapper.
responses.how: A sound wrapper builds the struct from checked views (decision 1, option A) or keeps the foreign struct in a private field (MOD-2, p05 19-22; MOD-7, 34-37), so no safe code outside its module can write the pointer. A wrapper that vouches for a struct anyone may fill makes a false `# SAFETY:` claim in unsafe code. That is the unsafe author's error, as in Rust, and `ember tcb` lists it.

out.notes:
The change is rewritten as a whole. The cause stays in FFI-2, where the safe-to-call fact is defined.

The limit is now its own sentences at the end of FFI-2:
- The property: no `safe fn`, overlay function entry or `@ffi(safe)` typedef covers a raw pointer that the caller's arguments carry to foreign code. That means an argument itself, a field or element at any depth of what an argument passes (as its Ember type declares it, a method's object included), or what an Ember function given to the call returns.
- The reason: safe code can make null, dangling, short and constant-address pointers.
- The refusal: E5002 where the declaration or entry is written, but only when the other rules make its calls safe. The message is given for each spelling, with an `override` line for another package's overlay.
- The direction: pointers foreign code hands Ember are outside the limit.

FFI-10 and FFI-56 cite the limit, and FFI-10's E5002 clause names what the message says. The other edits: XVI.4's `vkCreateBuffer` becomes `@safety` plus `unsafe fn`, with one sentence on `extend` wrappers under the example. The E5002 row repeats the limit's reach and adds `[FFI-56]`. CLI-5 writes such declarations `unsafe fn`.

Every open objection is answered: 12 fixed, 1 rebutted (I1-2, which Vulkan's `*2` queries settle), and 1 trade-off kept with a fix (E1-1). The one blocking objection (I1-1, X) is fixed by the trigger 'whose calls the other rules make safe'.

Decisions:
- Decisions 1 to 3 were made by the owner's parameters, with no departure from a verdict: refuse the safe declaration; reach every pointer the caller's arguments carry to C; refuse the overlay line rather than quietly making its calls unsafe.
- Decision 4 (`@ffi(std_function)`) is the owner's. No change is applied and FFI-17a is left as it is. The recommendation is FFI-56's rule for C function pointers: unsafe to call unless the entry says `safe`, within the same limits.

For the owner, besides decision 4:
1. E1-1's property: contract words decide a hand declaration's Ember signature whether it is `safe fn` or `unsafe fn`, as an overlay entry's words already do. It rewrites ODR-074's sentence (FFI-10 91-92, 109-110). Recommended.
2. ODR-073's result half rests on API shape, not safety, since struct results already bring C's raw pointers into safe code (E1-3). Keep it as a shape rule or drop it.
3. Routes where C calls Ember with no call handing it anything: exports, export tables and C++ overrides returning raw pointers (I1-4). These belong to the exports question, K08.
4. Field contracts in overlays, so that create-info and cookie structs could become safe types. This is a whole feature, which FFI-30a forbids today. Undecided cases: Vulkan's `pNext` chains, count fields shared by two pointers, and user-data cookies C never reads through.

Dependencies:
- K46 (J8-14) rewrites the same `vkCreateBuffer` entry and decides whether handle fields count as raw pointers.
- K51 (J2-11) sets the spelling of `ref_to_ptr(ref mut x)`.

Gaps that already exist and are not caused here (rule E):
- Safe code writing pointer or length fields of foreign memory: ImGui-style result views, and `owns` foreign structs whose destructor frees a field.
- A plain overlay entry whose own slot is an uncontracted raw pointer, such as FFI-6b's `PAIR_FIRST`, means unsafe without saying so.
- What an `out` slot holds when C reads it before filling it (Vulkan's `VkPhysicalDeviceFeatures2` reads `sType` and `pNext`).

Read-only work:
- The rules file, the input file, OWNER-DIRECTION.md and JOB.md (verdicts 121, 130-137).
- The part files p16-ffi.md, p04-types.md, p05-declarations.md, p07-ownership.md, p17-toolchain.md, p17a-codes.md and p21-annex-c.md, and p26-appx-h.md for the ODRs.
- compiler-0.9.15/decisions.md and tests/conformance/FFI-6b.

FFI-2 added limit (after p16 42): the property, the reason, the trigger 'whose calls the other rules make safe', the per-spelling message, the override line, and the scope sentence on direction

Trigger against entries already unsafe by their own words: FFI-11 retained row (p16 290), FFI-11c TODO words (318-321), and FFI-6b PAIR_FIRST with its uncontracted *Pair slot. None of them is newly safe and none is newly refused

Routes the reach misses (all gaps that exist today, not caused by the change): C function-pointer fields (FFI-56 field mapping plus an FFI-6a pointer-cast constant, or None), the pointer elements of a bridge container (CppVector[*T] through push_back, excluded by the 'as its Ember type declares it' carve-out), and a callback handing C a pointer through a ref mut parameter (FN-6)

No block S, U or X: every remaining program goes wrong the same way under today's text

previous.objection: S1-7 (the E5002 row's reach disagrees with FFI-2 on FFI-6b's PAIR_FIRST)
previous.why: The row now reads 'a `safe fn`, overlay function entry or `@ffi(safe)` typedef whose calls would otherwise be safe and would carry foreign code a raw pointer from the caller's arguments'. `@ffi(macro_fn) fn PAIR_FIRST(p: *Pair) -> i64` has a raw-pointer slot with no contract facts, so its calls are unsafe under FFI-2 (p16 33-34: 'A call to a foreign function whose contract contains an `unknown` fact requires `unsafe`'). 'Would otherwise be safe' therefore excludes it, and the row and FFI-2 now decide tests/conformance/FFI-6b the same way: the call stays in `unsafe:` and the program prints `25 4.5 7 7 true false`.

objections.walk:
1. `timer_spec` is a complete struct, so it imports as a `@layout(c) struct` (FFI-8, p16 182). Its field `fire` is 'a function pointer that comes from C — a field of an imported struct' and 'imports as `unsafe extern "C" fn(…)`' (FFI-56, p16 590-592; FFI-8 row, p16 188).
2. `TICK_ROM_HANDLER` is a pointer-cast macro. It is 'a `const` of that pointer type holding the address as an integer' (FFI-6a, p16 148-151), so its type is `unsafe extern "C" fn(c_int)`.
3. main.em line 4 builds the struct holding that value in safe code. UNS-1 (p09 266-269) puts only calling 'through a value of an `unsafe` callable type' in unsafe, not holding or storing one.
4. overlays/timer.em line 3 is a function entry, 'which asserts the function safe to call' (GRM-35, p16 278-280). `spec` is a `@layout(c)` value type with no pointer slot, so no fact is unknown (FFI-2, p16 33-35).
5. The added limit covers 'a raw pointer (`*T`, `*mut T`) that the caller's arguments carry to foreign code ... or what an Ember function given to the call ... returns'. `fire` is not `*T` or `*mut T`, and no Ember function is given. The entry stands, line 5 is safe code, and C calls address 0x1FFF0000 (C++: calling through a function pointer cast from an integer).
6. If the importer gives the field `Option[…]` (p16 188: '`Option[…]` when nullable'), `fire=None` hands C a null function pointer from safe code in the same way.
7. Today the same program compiles and fails the same way, so the change does not cause it. But the change's own reason lists 'holds a constant address (`[FFI-6a]`)', which is equally true of a function-pointer constant. Its why_general also claims the limit 'reaches every type that carries a pointer'.
objections.impact: A forged or null C function pointer still reaches C from safe code through a struct argument, which is the same hole J8-08 closes for data pointers. The structs involved are common: hook tables, ops structs and allocator callback structs. The claim that 'every pointer the call's arguments carry to C' is covered does not hold.
objections.suggestion: State the limit by the property, not by a list of types. No assertion covers a pointer value the caller supplies whose target nothing checks. That means a raw pointer, and also a C function pointer value (`unsafe extern "C" fn(…)`, or an `Option` of one), which safe code can hold from a constant or from C. A safe `extern "C" fn` made from an Ember function is checked, and only what it hands back is reached. Then `timer_run` is E5002 naming `spec.fire`, and the binding builds the struct from an Ember function inside a wrapper's `unsafe:` block.

objections.walk:
1. `std::vector<T>` imports as '`CppVector[T]` with `.span()`, `.span_mut()`, `.to_array()`, `push_back`, `len`' (FFI-17a, p21 62). With `T` = `const char*`, that is `*c_char` (FFI-8, p16 180).

3. main.em line 6 is safe code. `null[*c_char]()` 'is safe' (IV.5, p04 347), and `push_back` is a bridge operation, not one of UNS-1's unsafe operations (p09 266-273).

2. FFI-30c (p16 219-222): 'The order is declared where the module is imported: `overlay` takes one file or a list, applied first to last (a dependency's before the package's own); a later file's `override` entry replaces an earlier file's for that name'.

outs.notes:
This round I covered both the specification (integration) and the engineering parts of the job.

Verdict on the change: its core is right and I support it. The cause is in FFI-2, where the safe-to-call fact is defined. The property is type-based, which is the only sound choice; I checked the cheaper alternative under 'checked'. Nothing runs at run time, the ordinary caller's line gets shorter, and every verdict cited holds.

Of the 13 listed objections:
- 11 resolved: E1-1 to E1-6, E1-8, I1-1, I1-4, I1-5 and I1-6.
- 1 withdrawn: I1-2, whose rebuttal about Vulkan's `*2` items is right.
- 1 still open: I1-3. The words still reach `@ffi(std_function)`.

New objections:
1. Block X, and the only blocker. FFI-2's consequence sentence says 'a declaration or entry', not 'such an assertion'. So it refuses `@ffi(std_function) type Fill`, while FFI-17a and the impact report accept it. The fix is a two-word change.
2. Medium (none): `std::vector<S>` elements. The reach is undecided, and the report says they are unchanged while `std::span<S>` is reached.
3. Medium (none): overrides of an object handed to C++ in a call. The report's reason for leaving them out ('no call hands C anything') is untrue for that program.
4. Medium (none): FFI-10's plain-`fn` message and E5012's count hint now lead into the limit's E5002, against verdict 73 and DIA-25.
5. Low: CLI-6 and CLI-7 are missing from the impact report.
6. Low: the other-package `override` message also needs the import's overlay list.
7. Low: the E5002 row leaves out 'a method's object', plus text nits (the XVI.4 edit's before text starts at line 248, not 249; the CLI-5 wording).

A gap that already exists, not caused here: the rewritten XVI.4 `vkCreateBuffer` entry keeps `@ffi(no_callbacks)`, while its own `@safety` says `pAllocator` holds callbacks, which Vulkan runs during the call. FFI-52 (p16 463-464) reads `no_callbacks` as 'a call of it runs none of them'. When the K46 merge rewrites this entry, drop `no_callbacks` or say in the `@safety` that the allocator's functions are not Ember functions.

I agree with the trade-offs kept: Vulkan create-infos, cookie fields, and the dependants' builds breaking as they do for overlay drift (FFI-55). Field contracts belong to the owner as a whole feature.

Read-only work: the part files p16, p17, p17a, p21, p04, p07, p05, p09, p26 and p01; tests/conformance/FFI-6b; OWNER-DIRECTION.md; JOB.md verdicts 73 and 121.

rulings.objection: I1-3 (the words leave `@ffi(std_function)` undecided; the impact report's 'unchanged' is unsupported)
rulings.evidence: The designer fixed sentence 1 so it names three spellings ('No assertion of the fact — `safe fn`, an overlay function entry not written `unsafe fn`, or `@ffi(safe)` on a function-pointer typedef — covers ...'). But the consequence sentence is not tied to them: 'So a declaration or entry whose calls the other rules make safe, and whose calls would carry such a pointer, is `E5002` where it is written.' FFI-17a (p21-annex-c.md 67) makes `@ffi(std_function)` give 'a function value of type `fn(A…) -> R` (`[CLO-3]`), called as any other', so its calls are safe, and `fill(f.px.Buf(...))` carries `Buf.data` by value. The change counts a `type` entry's calls as that entry's calls (test 5: 'E5002 at overlays/mixer.em line 3 (`@ffi(safe)` on `type mix_fn`)'). The designer's own cause text calls std_function 'A fourth assertion'. So the claim that the impact report is not supported still holds against the round-2 text ('`@ffi(std_function)` entries (decision 4) ... Compile exactly as before'). The suggested remedy (refuse, remove the attribute) is rightly rejected: without the attribute `Fill` is 'an opaque object Ember owns' (p21 67) and no compiling line exists (DIA-25, p17 474-475). Block none; the blocking form of this point is E2-1.

rulings.objection: E2-1 (the E5002 consequence reaches `@ffi(std_function)` entries and bridge methods; FFI-17a, the codes row and the impact report say otherwise)
rulings.evidence: Walk: (1) FFI-2 as added, sentence 3: 'So a declaration or entry whose calls the other rules make safe, and whose calls would carry such a pointer, is `E5002` where it is written.' Its subject is any declaration or entry, not the three assertions sentence 1 names. (2) FFI-17a (p21 67): with `@ffi(std_function)` the value is 'a function value of type `fn(A…) -> R` ..., called as any other', so `type Fill` is an entry whose calls the other rules make safe. FFI-2 (p16 35-38) says the safe-to-call fact 'is never derived' and is asserted 'by an overlay entry for the function', so this entry is an assertion. (3) `fill(f.px.Buf(data=ref_to_ptr(ref mut x), len=1))` carries `Buf.data` by value, which is 'a field ... of what an argument passes, by value'. (4) So FFI-2 gives E5002 at overlays/fill.em line 3. The program is correct (len=1, one byte), and without the change it compiles and prints `0`. (5) The unchanged FFI-17a, the edited codes row (p17a 164: 'a `safe fn`, overlay function entry or `@ffi(safe)` typedef whose calls would otherwise be safe') and the impact report ('`@ffi(std_function)` entries (decision 4) ... Compile exactly as before') accept it. Two rules decide one program differently. The designer's own FFI-56 edit admits the pattern: 'Without the cite it would contradict FFI-2's refusal'. FFI-17a has no such cite. (6) The message clause gives no line for this spelling, only '`@safety("…")` above the declaration or entry written `unsafe fn` ... or the typedef's entry without `@ffi(safe)`', so DIA-25 ('The line a message gives compiles', p17 474) cannot be met. In effect the words apply decision 4's option c, which the designer rejected and left to the owner. Caused by the change: X.

rulings.objection: E2-2 (`std::vector<S>` elements: reached or not is unclear; span reached, vector kept)
rulings.evidence: FFI-2 as added reaches 'a field or an element, at any depth, of what an argument passes, by value or behind a contracted pointer, as its Ember type declares it'. FFI-17a (p21 62): `std::vector<T>` is '`CppVector[T]` with `.span()`, `.span_mut()`, `.to_array()`, `push_back`, `len`'. Its Ember type declares elements of type `T`, which Ember code writes. FFI-40 (p21 162): '`const T&` as a plain parameter `x: T`'. The impact report's Unchanged row lists '`CppVector`, `CppString`' on the ground that bridge types 'declare no fields', while programs_changed counts `std::span<S>`, `std::unique_ptr<S>` and `std::optional<S>` as reached. The words do not separate 'declares no fields' from 'declares elements', so `total_spaces(parts)` can be read either way. The limit's own reason ('Safe code can make a raw pointer ... and nothing checks one') applies to vector elements exactly as to span elements. The safety hole itself is old: today and under the designer's reading, C++ reads 64 bytes at null. What the change causes is a reach that depends on the container type and a wrong impact row. Block none.

rulings.objection: E2-3 (an override of a C++ virtual method on an object argument, returning a dangling pointer)
rulings.evidence: FFI-2 as added reaches 'what an Ember function given to the call, as an argument or in one, returns'. The Unchanged row gives as its reason 'C++ overrides returning raw pointers: C calls Ember there, so no call hands C anything'. In E2-3's program, `s.pump(ref mut src, 4096)` hands C++ the object (FFI-40, p21 161: '`T&` parameter imports as `ref mut x: T`'; FFI-39c, p21 139-140: 'a parameter borrowed for the call alone takes the object ... upcast to the C++ base'). FFI-52 (p16 455-457) counts 'every override of an Ember class derived from a C++ class' among what the call may run. So a call does hand C the override's owner, and the stated reason is untrue for this program. `fn pump(src, n)` without `no_callbacks` is still safe to call, since a missing mark 'only refuses a line that the reachable functions' changes would make unsafe' (p16 467). Whether a method of an argument object is 'in one' is not said. Test 6 (`stream_read` with `spare`) is refused while this sibling is not, and the only difference is the construct. Decision 2's owner_short claims 'a C++ object' is covered. The dangling write is old (it compiles today the same way), so this does not block. But the change's words and its report on this route are wrong.

rulings.objection: E2-4 (FFI-10's plain-`fn` message and missing-fact messages give a line that the limit then refuses)
rulings.evidence: FFI-10 (p16 63-66): a plain `fn` is E5002 with a message offering 'or `safe fn lib_step` if a call within its contract cannot break memory safety'. For J8-08's `fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)`, that line is now E5002 under FFI-2's limit, though before the change it compiled. Likewise a missing count fact is E5002 'naming the slot' (p16 84) and the overlay line that supplies it (FFI-2, p16 41-42: 'names each missing fact and the overlay line that supplies it'). Once it is supplied, the trigger 'whose calls the other rules make safe' fires the limit's E5002. DIA-25 (p17 474-475): 'The line a message gives compiles under this document, in that program: its fix never runs into another error'. Verdict 73 (JOB.md 550-555): 'A message's fix must not run into another error'; the owner: 'a rule is supposed to tell how to fix an issue not how to run into another issue'. Caused by the change. The objection is marked block none, so it is weighed.

rulings.objection: E2-5 (`ember bind --check`/`--report` do not know the limit; the impact report lists only CLI-5)
rulings.evidence: CLI-7 (p17 119-121): '`ember bind <header> --check <overlay>` checks `[FFI-12]` and prints how many declarations are safe, still `unsafe`, and skipped'. After the change, `fn cp_load(opts: borrowed one)` passes FFI-12 but the build is E5002, and CLI-7 does not say how such an entry is counted. CLI-6 (p17 117-118) lists 'every declaration still `unsafe` with its unknown facts', and a forced `unsafe fn` has none to give. The impact report lists CLI-5 only. Part refuted: `--merge` records 'the header's declarations as they are now' once the overlay passes FFI-12 (p17 121-122). That record serves drift checking (FFI-55), not safety, so recording it is not wrong. Low.

rulings.objection: E2-6 (the `override` message omits the import line that applies the importer's overlay)
rulings.evidence: FFI-2 as added: 'For an entry in another package's overlay, it gives that entry as an `override` in the importing package's own overlay (`[FFI-30c]`)'. FFI-30c (p16 219-222): 'The order is declared where the module is imported: `overlay` takes one file or a list, applied first to last'. In E2-6's program the import lists only `deps/cparse/overlays/cparse.em`, so an override written in a new file is never applied and the build fails at the same entry. DIA-25 (p17 474-477) requires that the given fix compile and that the message name every line it replaces. The words do not say the message gives the import line or the new file's header. Low, caused by the change.

rulings.objection: E2-7 (codes row omits a method's object; CLI-5 sentence hard to read; XVI.4 line numbers)
rulings.evidence: FFI-2 as added has to say 'a method's object included', since FFI-40 (p21 156-157) says an imported method's 'object is `this`, and it lists no receiver'. The edited E5002 row (p17a 164) says '(one an argument is or holds at any depth, or one an Ember function given to the call returns)' with no method's object, while p17a 3-4 says the registry lists 'Every diagnostic code, what it reports and the rule it enforces'. So `Slice.spaces()`'s refusal is missing from the registry. The XVI.4 edit's before text starts at p16 248 ('    hide vkAllocationFunction'), not 249. The CLI-5 text 'one whose calls `[FFI-2]`'s limit on raw pointers keeps from being safe among them' is hard to read aloud. Text defects; every program is decided the same.

tradeoffs.why: Leaving `@ffi(std_function)` to the owner is sound under B. Refusing the entry leaves no compiling line, because the language has no unsafe-callable spelling for it. Option a would change a delegated ruling (ODR-199) and the meaning of every existing entry. The safety hole it leaves is old, not caused by the change. The designer's intent is justified, but the words must carry it out, and today they do not (E2-1).

The reason given for keeping `CppVector` out ('declare no fields') does not fit a type whose elements Ember writes (`span_mut`, `push_back`). Closing the hole for `std::span<S>` but not `std::vector<S>` makes the rule depend on the type, against D ('a property, never a list of cases') and principle 4. Whichever way it is settled, the owner should see it: either `std::vector<S>` bindings gain a wrapper, or a memory hole stays open for the most common container.

The exclusion rests on 'no call hands C anything', which is untrue when the object is a call's argument. A dangling result is refused through a function pointer and kept through a virtual method. That is a special case by construct, and the owner_short of decision 2 tells the owner a C++ object is covered. The correct split is between objects handed to a call and objects C++ got without one (exports, K08).

The designer has not answered it yet. As written, the change makes existing messages offer a `safe` line or a contract word that the limit then refuses. That departs from verdict 73 and DIA-25 with nothing gained. The fix is a property of the message at no run-time cost.
An omission in the impact report and in the tools' wording. Tools that report safety should decide it as the compiler does. No safety or run-time cost, no verdict at stake.
A message that, when followed, still fails at the same entry falls short of DIA-25. Giving the import line and the new file's header costs nothing.
A registry row that misses one cause, a wrong line range, and one hard sentence. These are text fixes with no trade-off involved.

out.summary: The core of the change holds: a safe C declaration, overlay entry or `@ffi(safe)` typedef whose call would hand C a raw pointer the caller supplied, inside a struct, span, object or callback result, is refused, and a wrapper builds the struct from a checked view. It closes J8-08's memory corruption from safe code at compile time with no run-time cost. One objection blocks (E2-1, a contradiction). FFI-2's new consequence sentence, 'a declaration or entry whose calls the other rules make safe ... is E5002', is not tied to the three spellings sentence 1 names. Read literally, it refuses `@ffi(std_function)` entries, and arguably std.ffi bridge methods, with no compiling line. The unchanged FFI-17a, the edited codes row and the impact report all say these compile. Tying the consequence to the named assertions resolves it and leaves decision 4 with the owner. I1-3 makes the same point, non-blocking. Real but not blocking: E2-2 (`std::vector<S>` elements are reached or not depending on how 'as its Ember type declares it' is read; span reached, vector kept), E2-3 (a C++ override on an object argument returning a dangling pointer is excluded for a reason that is untrue there), E2-4 (FFI-10's plain-fn message and missing-fact messages offer lines the limit then refuses, against verdict 73 and DIA-25), E2-5 (bind --check/--report do not know the limit), E2-6 (the override message omits the import line), E2-7 (the codes row omits a method's object; line 248 not 249; a hard CLI-5 sentence). The holes in E2-2 and E2-3 already exist today; what the change gets wrong there is its reach and its report.

owner_short.one_line: A C function declared safe takes a struct holding a raw `uint8_t*` and a length that safe code filled in. The change refuses such safe declarations, but its refusal sentence also catches imported `std::function` callables it meant to leave for you.
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | binding author | declares `clear_pixels(PixelBuf)` safe | refused, as intended; a wrapper over a checked span is the way
2 | overlay writer | imports a `std::function<void(Buf)>` (Buf holds `uint8_t*`) as a callable | read literally: refused with no line that compiles, though the change says it stays as today
3 | program | passes a `std::vector<Slice>`, or a C++ object whose override returns a dangling pointer | unclear whether refused; the change keeps them open for reasons that do not hold
4 | binding author | follows an existing message's 'or declare it safe' line | the next build refuses that line
owner_short.today: All of these compile, and safe code can hand C or C++ a null, dangling or too-short pointer.
options: Send the change back for one revision: tie the refusal to the three spellings it names (blocking), and also fix the vector, override, message and tool points
Pass it after only the blocking wording fix, with the vector and override routes listed for later
Reject it and keep today (memory corruption from safe code stays)
owner_short.recommendation: Send it back for one revision: the main decision is sound, but one sentence reaches further than intended, and four smaller points are cheap to fix now.

The safety hole itself is old: today and under the designer's reading, C++ reads 64 bytes at null. What the change causes is a reach that depends on the container type and a wrong impact row. Block none.

rulings.objection: E2-3 (an override of a C++ virtual method on an object argument, returning a dangling pointer)
rulings.evidence: FFI-2 as added reaches 'what an Ember function given to the call, as an argument or in one, returns'. The Unchanged row gives as its reason 'C++ overrides returning raw pointers: C calls Ember there, so no call hands C anything'. In E2-3's program, `s.pump(ref mut src, 4096)` hands C++ the object (FFI-40, p21 161: '`T&` parameter imports as `ref mut x: T`'; FFI-39c, p21 139-140: 'a parameter borrowed for the call alone takes the object ... upcast to the C++ base'). FFI-52 (p16 455-457) counts 'every override of an Ember class derived from a C++ class' among what the call may run. So a call does hand C the override's owner, and the stated reason is untrue for this program. `fn pump(src, n)` without `no_callbacks` is still safe to call, since a missing mark 'only refuses a line that the reachable functions' changes would make unsafe' (p16 467). Whether a method of an argument object is 'in one' is not said. Test 6 (`stream_read` with `spare`) is refused while this sibling is not, and the only difference is the construct. Decision 2's owner_short claims 'a C++ object' is covered. The dangling write is old (it compiles today the same way), so this does not block. But the change's words and its report on this route are wrong.

rulings.objection: E2-4 (FFI-10's plain-`fn` message and missing-fact messages give a line that the limit then refuses)
rulings.evidence: FFI-10 (p16 63-66): a plain `fn` is E5002 with a message offering 'or `safe fn lib_step` if a call within its contract cannot break memory safety'. For J8-08's `fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)`, that line is now E5002 under FFI-2's limit, though before the change it compiled. Likewise a missing count fact is E5002 'naming the slot' (p16 84) and the overlay line that supplies it (FFI-2, p16 41-42: 'names each missing fact and the overlay line that supplies it'). Once it is supplied, the trigger 'whose calls the other rules make safe' fires the limit's E5002. DIA-25 (p17 474-475): 'The line a message gives compiles under this document, in that program: its fix never runs into another error'. Verdict 73 (JOB.md 550-555): 'A message's fix must not run into another error'; the owner: 'a rule is supposed to tell how to fix an issue not how to run into another issue'. Caused by the change. The objection is marked block none, so it is weighed.

rulings.objection: E2-5 (`ember bind --check`/`--report` do not know the limit; the impact report lists only CLI-5)
rulings.evidence: CLI-7 (p17 119-121): '`ember bind <header> --check <overlay>` checks `[FFI-12]` and prints how many declarations are safe, still `unsafe`, and skipped'. After the change, `fn cp_load(opts: borrowed one)` passes FFI-12 but the build is E5002, and CLI-7 does not say how such an entry is counted. CLI-6 (p17 117-118) lists 'every declaration still `unsafe` with its unknown facts', and a forced `unsafe fn` has none to give. The impact report lists CLI-5 only. Part refuted: `--merge` records 'the header's declarations as they are now' once the overlay passes FFI-12 (p17 121-122). That record serves drift checking (FFI-55), not safety, so recording it is not wrong. Low.

rulings.objection: E2-6 (the `override` message omits the import line that applies the importer's overlay)
rulings.evidence: FFI-2 as added: 'For an entry in another package's overlay, it gives that entry as an `override` in the importing package's own overlay (`[FFI-30c]`)'. FFI-30c (p16 219-222): 'The order is declared where the module is imported: `overlay` takes one file or a list, applied first to last'. In E2-6's program the import lists only `deps/cparse/overlays/cparse.em`, so an override written in a new file is never applied and the build fails at the same entry. DIA-25 (p17 474-477) requires that the given fix compile and that the message name every line it replaces. The words do not say the message gives the import line or the new file's header. Low, caused by the change.

rulings.objection: E2-7 (codes row omits a method's object; CLI-5 sentence hard to read; XVI.4 line numbers)
rulings.evidence: FFI-2 as added has to say 'a method's object included', since FFI-40 (p21 156-157) says an imported method's 'object is `this`, and it lists no receiver'. The edited E5002 row (p17a 164) says '(one an argument is or holds at any depth, or one an Ember function given to the call returns)' with no method's object, while p17a 3-4 says the registry lists 'Every diagnostic code, what it reports and the rule it enforces'. So `Slice.spaces()`'s refusal is missing from the registry. The XVI.4 edit's before text starts at p16 248 ('    hide vkAllocationFunction'), not 249. The CLI-5 text 'one whose calls `[FFI-2]`'s limit on raw pointers keeps from being safe among them' is hard to read aloud. Text defects; every program is decided the same.

tradeoffs.why: Leaving `@ffi(std_function)` to the owner is sound under B. Refusing the entry leaves no compiling line, because the language has no unsafe-callable spelling for it. Option a would change a delegated ruling (ODR-199) and the meaning of every existing entry. The safety hole it leaves is old, not caused by the change. The designer's intent is justified, but the words must carry it out, and today they do not (E2-1).

The reason given for keeping `CppVector` out ('declare no fields') does not fit a type whose elements Ember writes (`span_mut`, `push_back`). Closing the hole for `std::span<S>` but not `std::vector<S>` makes the rule depend on the type, against D ('a property, never a list of cases') and principle 4. Whichever way it is settled, the owner should see it: either `std::vector<S>` bindings gain a wrapper, or a memory hole stays open for the most common container.

The exclusion rests on 'no call hands C anything', which is untrue when the object is a call's argument. A dangling result is refused through a function pointer and kept through a virtual method. That is a special case by construct, and the owner_short of decision 2 tells the owner a C++ object is covered. The correct split is between objects handed to a call and objects C++ got without one (exports, K08).

The designer has not answered it yet. As written, the change makes existing messages offer a `safe` line or a contract word that the limit then refuses. That departs from verdict 73 and DIA-25 with nothing gained. The fix is a property of the message at no run-time cost.
An omission in the impact report and in the tools' wording. Tools that report safety should decide it as the compiler does. No safety or run-time cost, no verdict at stake.
A message that, when followed, still fails at the same entry falls short of DIA-25. Giving the import line and the new file's header costs nothing.
A registry row that misses one cause, a wrong line range, and one hard sentence. These are text fixes with no trade-off involved.

arbiter.summary: The core of the change holds: a safe C declaration, overlay entry or `@ffi(safe)` typedef whose call would hand C a raw pointer the caller supplied, inside a struct, span, object or callback result, is refused, and a wrapper builds the struct from a checked view. It closes J8-08's memory corruption from safe code at compile time with no run-time cost. One objection blocks (E2-1, a contradiction). FFI-2's new consequence sentence, 'a declaration or entry whose calls the other rules make safe ... is E5002', is not tied to the three spellings sentence 1 names. Read literally, it refuses `@ffi(std_function)` entries, and arguably std.ffi bridge methods, with no compiling line. The unchanged FFI-17a, the edited codes row and the impact report all say these compile. Tying the consequence to the named assertions resolves it and leaves decision 4 with the owner. I1-3 makes the same point, non-blocking. Real but not blocking: E2-2 (`std::vector<S>` elements are reached or not depending on how 'as its Ember type declares it' is read; span reached, vector kept), E2-3 (a C++ override on an object argument returning a dangling pointer is excluded for a reason that is untrue there), E2-4 (FFI-10's plain-fn message and missing-fact messages offer lines the limit then refuses, against verdict 73 and DIA-25), E2-5 (bind --check/--report do not know the limit), E2-6 (the override message omits the import line), E2-7 (the codes row omits a method's object; line 248 not 249; a hard CLI-5 sentence). The holes in E2-2 and E2-3 already exist today; what the change gets wrong there is its reach and its report.

owner_short.one_line: A C function declared safe takes a struct holding a raw `uint8_t*` and a length that safe code filled in. The change refuses such safe declarations, but its refusal sentence also catches imported `std::function` callables it meant to leave for you.
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | binding author | declares `clear_pixels(PixelBuf)` safe | refused, as intended; a wrapper over a checked span is the way
2 | overlay writer | imports a `std::function<void(Buf)>` (Buf holds `uint8_t*`) as a callable | read literally: refused with no line that compiles, though the change says it stays as today
3 | program | passes a `std::vector<Slice>`, or a C++ object whose override returns a dangling pointer | unclear whether refused; the change keeps them open for reasons that do not hold
4 | binding author | follows an existing message's 'or declare it safe' line | the next build refuses that line
owner_short.today: All of these compile, and safe code can hand C or C++ a null, dangling or too-short pointer.
options: Send the change back for one revision: tie the refusal to the three spellings it names (blocking), and also fix the vector, override, message and tool points
Pass it after only the blocking wording fix, with the vector and override routes listed for later
Reject it and keep today (memory corruption from safe code stays)
owner_short.recommendation: Send it back for one revision: the main decision is sound, but one sentence reaches further than intended, and four smaller points are cheap to fix now.

I read: RULES-FOR-THE-TEAM.md (v4); p16-ffi.md lines 18-70, 210-225, 244-252, 448-475 and 594-600; p21-annex-c.md lines 56-80, 118-165; p17-toolchain.md lines 110-125 and 470-478; p17a-codes.md lines 1-6 and 160-166; JOB.md lines 548-556 (verdict 73). The holes behind E2-2 and E2-3 already exist today (rule E). They are real here because of the change's reach and its impact report, not because the change made them.

blockers.objection: E2-1 (the E5002 consequence reaches `@ffi(std_function)` entries and bridge methods; FFI-17a, the codes row and the impact report say otherwise)
blockers.evidence: Walk: (1) FFI-2 as added, sentence 3: 'So a declaration or entry whose calls the other rules make safe, and whose calls would carry such a pointer, is `E5002` where it is written.' Its subject is any declaration or entry, not the three assertions sentence 1 names. (2) FFI-17a (p21 67): with `@ffi(std_function)` the value is 'a function value of type `fn(A…) -> R` ..., called as any other', so `type Fill` is an entry whose calls the other rules make safe. FFI-2 (p16 35-38) says the safe-to-call fact 'is never derived' and is asserted 'by an overlay entry for the function', so this entry is an assertion. (3) `fill(f.px.Buf(data=ref_to_ptr(ref mut x), len=1))` carries `Buf.data` by value, which is 'a field ... of what an argument passes, by value'. (4) So FFI-2 gives E5002 at overlays/fill.em line 3. The program is correct (len=1, one byte), and without the change it compiles and prints `0`. (5) The unchanged FFI-17a, the edited codes row (p17a 164: 'a `safe fn`, overlay function entry or `@ffi(safe)` typedef whose calls would otherwise be safe') and the impact report ('`@ffi(std_function)` entries (decision 4) ... Compile exactly as before') accept it. Two rules decide one program differently. The designer's own FFI-56 edit admits the pattern: 'Without the cite it would contradict FFI-2's refusal'. FFI-17a has no such cite. (6) The message clause gives no line for this spelling, only '`@safety("…")` above the declaration or entry written `unsafe fn` ... or the typedef's entry without `@ffi(safe)`', so DIA-25 ('The line a message gives compiles', p17 474) cannot be met. In effect the words apply decision 4's option c, which the designer rejected and left to the owner. Caused by the change: X.

final.intent: Load a level file on a worker thread and give the main thread either its length or the reason it failed, using the language's default error type (`Result[int]`).

cause.where: Three places, one property each. (1) The definition of `Error`: IV.8's declaration (p04-types.md 676, `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display):`), which ERR-3 describes (p13-errors.md 87-88) and TYP-17 quotes (p04 459). (2) What an object of an `open` or `abstract` class holds: THR-8's list sentence (p11-concurrency.md 47-48, "class objects are `Send` when every component is") and the marker table (p04 577, "a class object is when its fields are") count only the fields of the object's declared class. That is narrower than THR-8's own definition (p11 43-45, "nothing reachable from it ... is a one-thread owner"), because an object of an open class may be an object of any class derived from it (TYP-5 rule 8, p04 86). THR-9 (p11 63-64) has the same gap, and it has no words for a `dyn` either. (3) IFC-3 (p05 411-413) says that implementers meet an interface's parents, but not that an implementation meets them for every type it covers, which takes in each instance of a generic implementation and each derived class.
cause.why_there: Every error is erased through `Error`: `dyn Error`, the box inside `AnyError` (ERR-8), and so the default error type of every `Result[T]` (ERR-9). THR-8's dyn clause is right as it stands (`dyn I` is Send only when `I` requires it). `Error` requires no thread markers, so every erased error is a one-thread value, and the default `Result[T]` cannot leave its thread by any route. ERR-8's `From`, THR-2's routes and THR-10 are each right as written. The missing words belong in what an error is. Once `Error` requires the markers, the requirement is only as sound as the markers of what an error holds. For a class, THR-8's list and the p04 row read the markers from the declared class alone. So a `GameError` that implements `Error` would be judged Send while one of its objects is a `DocError` holding a `shares` owner. That gap already exists for a plain open-class value handed to a thread. The change would carry it into every AnyError. So the class wording is part of the cause. It has to say what THR-8's definition already says. IFC-3 is where the language says what an implementation promises about its interface's parents, so the rule for generic implementations and derived classes goes there, once for every interface, and not in ERR-3 as a case of `Error`.
cause.reported_at: ERR-3, ERR-8, THR-2, THR-8 (it shows through THR-10's "`R` MUST be `Send`", p11 175-176)

existing_rule.rule: THR-8 (its definition and its dyn clause), with IFC-3
existing_rule.words: THR-8: "A type is **`Send`** when a value of it may be handed over to another thread: nothing reachable from it (its fields, its elements, what its `owns` parts hold, a function value's state) is a one-thread owner (`shares T`, `shares mut T`), a `weakref` link to a value that is not `thread_shared`, or bound to the thread that made it" and "`dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs Send:`)". IFC-3: "`interface Ord: needs Eq` requires implementers of `Ord` to implement `Eq`. So a bound brings its parents". Once `Error` requires `Send` and `ThreadShared`, these words reach `dyn Error` and `AnyError` (a struct of `Box[dyn Error]`, `u128` and `Array[String]`, Send and ThreadShared when every component is). They also reach every `E: needs Error` and `type Failure: needs Error` bound, and every implementer. For an open class, "nothing reachable from it" already takes in what a derived object holds.

edits.rule: IV.8 (standard interfaces, the definition ERR-3 cites)
edits.before: interface Error: needs (Debug, Display):
edits.after: interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):
edits.why_general: IV.8 holds "the definitions" of the standard interfaces (p04 600). It is the declaration that every bound, every `dyn Error` and every implementer reads.
edits.why_here: This is the cause. `Error` is the interface that every error is erased through, and it was the only one of ERR-3, ERR-8 and THR-8 that said nothing about threads. std/src/core.em line 80 follows it.

edits.before:
`Error` is the interface of error types:
  `Display + Debug` with `fn source() -> Option[ref dyn Error]` (default `None`) (§IV.8).
edits.after: `Error` is the interface of error types, `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):` with `fn source() -> Option[ref dyn Error]` (default `None`) (§IV.8). Any thread may have and read an error, so `dyn Error` and `AnyError` are `Send` and `ThreadShared` (`[THR-8]`, `[THR-9]`). A type that holds a value that stays on one thread is not an error, and is refused where it implements `Error` or where it is derived from a class that does (`E2040`, `[IFC-3]`; `E2080` at `@derive(Error)`, `[DRV-1]`). It may still be a `Result`'s error that its `Display` prints (`[ERR-1]`, `[ERR-12]`).
edits.why_general: It states one property of what an error is: any thread may have and read it. The general rules then decide the rest. IFC-3 says where an implementation that does not meet the parents is refused and what its message gives. THR-8 and THR-9 say what each part of a type holds. ERR-3 lists no cases and no fixes. ERR-1's "any `E: needs Error`", ERR-8's `From` and ERR-9's "any error" stay true as written. The parents are spelled with `needs`, as verdict 110 spells them, and the old `Display + Debug` spelling goes.
edits.why_here: ERR-3 describes the declaration of p04 676. The two must say the same thing, or the two texts would decide one program differently.

edits.rule: TYP-17 (its example of an interface's parents)
edits.before:
an interface's parents
  (`interface Error: needs (Debug, Display):`)
edits.after:
an interface's parents
  (`interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):`)
edits.why_general: It is the third copy of the declaration. It still serves as the example of several needs in round brackets.
edits.why_here: Left as it was, a reader of the generics chapter would find the old parents, and objection E1-4's `report_later` would compile under one text and be E2040 under the other.

edits.before: Structs, enums, tuples, fixed arrays, collections and class objects are `Send` when every component is;
edits.after: Structs, enums, tuples, fixed arrays, collections and class objects are `Send` when every component is, and an object of an `open` or `abstract` class may be an object of any class the program derives from it, a library's included and each instance of a generic one, whose fields are then among its components (as a call through a `virtual` method counts every override the program has, `[EFF-24]`);
edits.why_general: It makes THR-8's list say what its own definition says ("nothing reachable from it"). This holds for every class hierarchy, error or not: a game's `Script` with an `Enemy` holding a `weakref`, std's ECS `World` holding `Map[u64, AnyStorage]` (std/src/ecs.em 101, 201) whose `[T] AosStorage` holds the program's components, and an error's `GameError` with a `DocError`. Nothing is written: the markers are still inferred from the words of types (TYP-43), here the declarations of the derived classes. A line that needs the marker is refused with E7015, whose message names the derived class and its field (THR-2's "whose message gives the words to write").
edits.why_here: This is where the class markers are stated. Without it, the change's requirement on `Error` would be checked against the declared class alone, and objection S1-1's `DocError` (and an error struct holding a field of a plain open class whose derived object holds a `shares` owner) would cross threads inside an AnyError.

edits.before: Structural types are `ThreadShared` when every component is.
edits.after: Structural types and class objects are `ThreadShared` when every component is (a class object's components as `[THR-8]` counts them), and `dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs (Send, ThreadShared):`), as for `Send` (`[THR-8]`, ODR-255).
edits.why_general: Every interface gets the ThreadShared half of THR-8's dyn clause, a program's own `interface Command: needs (Send, ThreadShared):` as well as `Error`. ODR-255 already ruled it, and the text never said it. Class objects are counted as for Send.
edits.why_here: Without it, `ref r` of a `Result[int]` given to a scoped task (a `ref T` is Send when `T` is ThreadShared, p11 49) and an AnyError inside a thread_shared object's `RwLock` (verdict 165) stay undecided after the ERR-3 change.

edits.rule: Marker table, Send and ThreadShared rows (TYP-43)
edits.before: Send row: "a class object is when its fields are;" / ThreadShared row: "every component is `ThreadShared`;"
edits.after: Send row: "a class object is when its fields are, and those of every class the program derives from its class (`[THR-8]`); `dyn I` when `I` requires it;" / ThreadShared row: "every component is `ThreadShared`, a class object's counted as for `Send`; `dyn I` when `I` requires it;"
edits.why_general: TYP-43 says the table answers the markers (p04 583). It must give the same answer as THR-8 and THR-9.
edits.why_here: The row "a class object is when its fields are" is the narrow reading that lets a base-class value holding a one-thread derived object through. Leaving it would be a contradiction with the edited THR-8.

edits.before: `interface Ord: needs Eq` requires implementers of `Ord` to implement `Eq`. So a bound brings its parents: `T: needs IndexMut[int]` provides `Index[int]`'s methods too, and a binding it writes (`Output = f32`) names the parent's associated type (ODR-042).
edits.after: (unchanged, then:) An implementation meets its interface's parents for every type it covers: each instance of a generic implementation, and each class derived from a class it covers, whose objects are values of that class (`[TYP-5]` rule 8), each instance of a generic one included. One that does not is `E2040`, either at the generic implementation (`extend[T] Tagged[T] implements Ord:` over `extend[T: needs Eq] Tagged[T] implements Eq:` gives `extend[T: needs Eq] Tagged[T] implements Ord:`) or where the derived class is declared, which its own package checks, whichever package declares the base. The message names the part that does not meet a parent and gives a line that compiles. That line either makes the part meet the parent by the rule that decides it (a type parameter's needs, an interface's needs), or holds in its place a copy of what the type uses from it.
edits.why_general: It is one property of every implementation of every interface with parents: `Ord` over `Eq`, `IndexMut` over `Index`, a program's own `interface Command: needs (Send, ThreadShared):`, and `Error`. For a parent the base implements (Eq, Debug), a derived class meets it through the base's implementation, so nothing changes there. For a marker parent, which is inferred from contents, the check falls on the derived class's own fields, at the derived class's own line. A derived class may be in another package, but the check is still local. Rust also requires a supertrait to hold for every type an impl covers. The message rule is a property, not a list: it gives a needs line where one exists and a copy line otherwise. That is principle 12, and verdict 73's "how to fix an issue not how to run into another", so `thread_shared` is offered only where it compiles.
edits.why_here: Decision 2 (a generic error implementation) and objection S1-1 (a derived error class) are both about what an implementation covers. Stating it in ERR-3 would make it a case of `Error` (objection I1-1), and `Command`, `Ord` and every later interface with marker parents would stay undecided.

edits.before: A derive whose requirement a field does not meet is `E2080`, naming the field.
edits.after: (unchanged, then:) On a generic type, a requirement that a field meets only for some arguments of the type's parameters is written as their needs in the generated `extend`, so the derive implements the interface for those instances (`@derive(Copy)` above `[T]` and `pub struct Range:` is `Copy` when `T` is, ODR-027; `[STR-5]`).
edits.why_general: Every derive works this way, which is how STR-5 ("when every field implements the interface"), ODR-027 and std's own `@derive(Copy)` above `[T] pub struct Range` (std/src/core.em 1850-1853) already read it. E2080 stays for a field whose own written type fails. The generated code stays what `ember inspect --expand` prints.
edits.why_here: With Error's new parents, `@derive(Error)` on a generic error type (`SpawnError[T]` holding `rejected: T`) must be decided. Read the other way it would be refused even when only `SpawnError[int]` is used, unlike every other derive (objection E1-3).

edits.after: | `E2080` | a derive whose requirement a field does not meet, naming the field (`@derive(Copy)` with a field that is not `Copy`; `@derive(Error)` on a type holding a value that stays on one thread) | `[STR-3]`, `[DRV-1]`, `[ERR-3]` |

edits.why_here: ERR-3 now names E2080 for `@derive(Error)`.
