impact.rules_changed: IV.8 (p04 676), ERR-3 (p13 87-88) and TYP-17's example (p04 459): Error requires Debug, Display, Send and ThreadShared, and a type holding a one-thread part is not an error. THR-8 (p11 47-48), THR-9 (p11 63-64) and the marker rows (p04 577-578): an object of an open or abstract class counts the fields of every class the program derives from it, and THR-9 gains the dyn clause. IFC-3 (p05 411-413): an implementation meets its interface's parents for every type it covers (generic instances, derived classes), with the refusal placed and the message's line stated as a property. DRV-1 (p14 138): a derive on a generic type holds per instance and writes those needs. p17a 59 and 71: the code rows. ERR-1, ERR-8, ERR-9, ERR-12, THR-1, THR-2, THR-10 and CLS-12 are unchanged and stay true.

readability.verdict: Better. No word is added to ordinary code. The worker loses an import, a concrete error type and, with two kinds of failure, a whole error enum. Generic error code (`type Failure: needs Error`), wrappers holding `owns dyn Error`, and class hierarchies whose derived classes hold plain data stay exactly as they are today. Words are added in two places only. A hand-written generic error implementation whose parameter holds the caller's value writes `T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)` (a derive writes it itself). An interface whose values an error holds as `owns dyn I` gets `Send` and `ThreadShared` in its needs, which then holds every implementer of that interface to them, or else the error holds a copy of the data. Under option A, the bound would be written instead in every pub generic function that uses `?` on such an error. Refusals fall on the type that holds the one-thread part: an error type at its declaration, a derived error class at its own line, and a plain open-class value at the line that sends it.

impact.cost: Compile time: Send and ThreadShared are inferred as today. For each open or abstract class, the program build collects the classes derived from it (a library's included, and each generic instance made). That is one walk of the class declarations, which EFF-24 already makes for virtual calls. Each implementation of an interface with parents is checked once per instance and once per derived class. A `?` into AnyError is checked as today. Run time: the class rule adds nothing. AnyError keeps its layout (the boxed error's data and table pointers, a 16-byte identity, the context list) and its one allocation on the failure path (ERR-11). The success path costs nothing, as in C, and handing an AnyError to another thread moves it, as C passes an error pointer. Two costs are stated. (1) CLS-12 (p05 380): a `@cached` method of a class that implements Error is filled under the once-flag, because its objects may now be read by several threads. Per call, the flag test becomes an acquire load (on x86-64 the same `mov` as a plain load; on ARM64 an `ldar`), and the first call fills under the flag with one compare-and-swap. This is already the duty today for any ThreadShared class given by `ref` to scoped tasks. (2) THR-2's hand-over check (verdict 114, "every object the handed object owns") reaches objects the boxed error owns whose class has weakref links, through the error's table: one indirect call per AnyError handed over. Nothing runs in a program where no error type converted into AnyError owns such an object. To measure: AnyError's size and its failure-path time against today's build; the `@cached` once-flag against a plain flag on ARM64 and x86-64; and the hand-over check's time.

verdicts.verdict: 61 (`thread_shared fn()`: the type says which threads may run it, not a whole-program search)
verdicts.how: The Error interface says which threads may have an error, and option C (a search through the `?` lines of the whole program) is turned down for verdict 61's reason. The class rule reads the declarations of derived classes, which are the words of types that TYP-43 infers markers from. It does not read bodies to find which functions a field is given, which is what 61 turned down. Listed for the owner as the nearest tension (decision 3).

import std.thread

class Level:
    name: String = String("forest")

decisions.title: Where the thread markers of an erased error come from
decisions.problem: AnyError is the default error type, and it holds any error behind `owns dyn Error`. By THR-8 it is one-thread unless `Error` requires Send, so a worker's `Result[int]`, a channel of results, a task's view of one and a thread_shared table of them are all refused. Making AnyError Send without a requirement would let an error holding a one-thread owner (a plain refcount) cross threads.

options.code:
pub struct AnyError:
    error: owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared   # a spelling the language does not have
extend[E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)] AnyError implements From[E]:
    ...
[S: needs Source]
pub fn count_lines(src: S) -> Result[int] where S.Failure: needs (Send, ThreadShared):
    text = src.read_all()?
options.outcome: The worker compiles. A one-thread error is refused at each `?` into AnyError, even with one thread. Generic error code and wrappers holding `owns dyn Error` must write thread words, and `source()` needs a conversion from a marked dyn to `dyn Error` that no rule states. A one-thread error that is only matched, never put into AnyError, compiles.

options.code: fn load(path: StrView) -> Result[int, io.Error]:   # today's rules
options.outcome: The `Result[int]` worker stays refused at the spawn line (E7015). A worker names a concrete error type, with an error enum when it can fail two ways.

options.code:
## std unchanged; the compiler collects every type converted into AnyError in the whole program
fn load(path: StrView) -> Result[int]:
options.outcome: The worker compiles until some `?` anywhere converts a one-thread error. From then on every spawn, channel and thread_shared holder of AnyError is refused, with a message naming a distant line. It contradicts THR-8's dyn clause (by requirement, ODR-255) and is the search verdict 61 turned down.

The worker, channels, task views and thread_shared holders of results compile. Generic `needs Error` code and `owns dyn Error` wrappers write nothing. An error type holding a one-thread part (a shares owner, a weakref to a one-thread value, a sharedref mut link, a Cell, a plain fn(), an `owns dyn I` whose I lacks the markers) is refused where it implements Error, even if it never leaves its thread, with a line that compiles. A hand-written generic one writes `T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)`. This is Swift's choice (`Error` refines `Sendable`).

options.code: pub interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send):   # or the same bound on AnyError's From
options.outcome: Results may be sent, but AnyError is not ThreadShared: `ref r` to scoped tasks and `thread_shared Assets(sizes=RwLock([...]))` stay refused. In exchange it accepts error types that hold a Cell or a vouched raw pointer.

options.code:
## AnyError records whether its error may cross; every hand-over checks it while running
h = thread.spawn(owns fn() => load("level1.cfg"))   # stops the program if the error may not cross
options.outcome: Everything compiles. A one-thread error that reaches another thread stops the program at the hand-over, on the failure path. Each hand-over of an AnyError costs a compare and a list of results costs a walk, and views given to scoped tasks and writes into thread_shared holders cannot be checked cheaply.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once. B fails 'easy to write': every worker grows its own error type, and an enum when it can fail two ways. A and E fail it for generic error code and wrappers, which grow thread words. C, D and F keep ordinary code as it is today. 2. Safety: A to E all refuse before a one-thread value crosses, and F stops the program. D is sound only with the class components counted as THR-8's definition reads them (decision 3) and with derived classes checked (IFC-3), both in this change. 3. Compile time first: A to E are decided when compiling. F's run-time check cannot make the refused program work: a shares owner inside the error cannot be moved away from its other owners, so F can only stop it. A compile-time refusal with a line to write would become a crash on the least-tested path (checklist 8), so F is out. 4. A written word only for meaning: A and E write markers in bounds and after `dyn`, and B writes a concrete error type. D writes a bound only on a hand-written generic error implementation (the library's promise, verdict 108), and the markers on an interface only when an error holds its values, where they state which threads may have those values. 5. The ordinary program no longer or harder: C lets an edit anywhere break a spawn far away. D refuses only an error type holding a one-thread part, at its own declaration, even in a one-thread program, and the fix is to hold a copy. A refuses the same errors at their `?`, which nearly every error reaches because main returns `Result[void]`. A accepts an error that is only matched, as in objection E1-1's renderer, which D refuses. 6. Consistency: D uses THR-8's own dyn clause, IFC-3, ODR-255, verdict 110's spelling, verdict 61 (the type says which threads may have it) and verdict 165 (refused where it is made). It matches Swift (`Error: Sendable`) and Rust's anyhow (`Send + Sync`). So D.
decisions.recommendation: D: Error needs Debug, Display, Send and ThreadShared, so AnyError goes to and is read by any thread with nothing written. An error type holding a one-thread part is refused where it is made an error, with a line that compiles.

owner_short.one_line: Should every error type be safe to hand to and read from any thread (as Swift's errors are), so the catch-all error (like C++'s `std::exception_ptr`; Ember's `AnyError`) can come back from a worker thread?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | error type's author | declares an error of plain values (a code, a text) | allowed: it may go to any thread
2 | worker thread | `fs.read_to_string(path)?` puts the file error into the catch-all | allowed, nothing written
3 | worker thread | returns `Result[int]` (a count or the catch-all error) | allowed: every error may cross threads
4 | main thread | `n = h.join()?` | gets the count, or passes the error on
5 | error type's author | declares an error holding a one-thread shared owner, or an object of an interface that does not say threads may have it | refused at that declaration, with the line to write
owner_short.today: The worker returning `Result[int]` is refused at `thread.spawn`, the text never says so, and the worker must name its own error type.
options: A: the catch-all checks each error where `?` puts it in; generic error code and error wrappers must add thread words
B: keep today: the catch-all stays on its thread; every worker names its own error type
C: the compiler searches the whole program; one one-thread error anywhere breaks every thread hand-off, far from that line
D: every error type is safe for every thread, checked where the type is declared an error; nothing written anywhere else
E: the catch-all may be sent but not read by two threads at once; a shared table of results is refused
F: check while running and stop the program when a one-thread error crosses
owner_short.recommendation: D: ordinary worker, server and library code compile with nothing written; only an error holding a one-thread part is refused, at its own line, with the fix.

decisions.title: A generic implementation whose interface has parents (a generic error that holds the caller's value)
decisions.problem: Under D, a generic error such as `PoolFull[T]` (like Rust's `SendError<T>`) is Send only when `T` is. The text left open whether `extend[T] PoolFull[T] implements Error:` is refused or quietly holds only for some `T`. The same question arises for every interface with parents (`extend[T] Echo[T] implements Command:` with `interface Command: needs (Send, ThreadShared):`, `extend[T] Tagged[T] implements Ord:` over a bounded `Eq`), and for a derive on a generic type (`@derive(Error)` above `[T] enum SpawnError:` with `Full(rejected: T)`).

options.code:
extend[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)] PoolFull[T] implements Error:
    pass
## written without the bound: E2040 at this line, giving the line above
@derive(Error)
[T]
enum SpawnError:
    @error("the spawn point is full")
    Full(rejected: T)
## the derive writes extend[T: needs (Debug, Send, ThreadShared)] itself, as @derive(Copy) on Range does
options.outcome: Each written line means what it says. `PoolFull[int]` and `SpawnError[int]` are Errors. `PoolFull[shares Enemy]` is not, and its `?` into AnyError is E2040 at the `?` or at the call. A derive implements the interface per instance, as every derive already does (STR-5, ODR-027).

options.code:
extend[T] PoolFull[T] implements Error:
    pass
## holds only for the T that are Send and ThreadShared, with nothing said
options.outcome: No word is written, but the line claims every `T` and means fewer. The refusal appears at a distant `?` with no line of the declaration saying why.
A generic error type used only with plain values is refused until it is bounded, and the bound limits what the type may hold, not only where it is an Error, unlike every other derive.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: all are equal for ordinary code, because generic error types holding a caller's value are rare. (iii) is harder: a type used only as `SpawnError[int]` is refused. 2. Safety: all three are safe. 3. Compile time: all three. 4. A written word only for meaning: the bound on a hand-written implementation is the library's promise of which values it is an error for (verdicts 108, 111). A derive is the compiler writing the implementation, so it writes the bound itself and `ember inspect --expand` shows it (principle 1). 5. The ordinary program: unchanged under (i). 6. Consistency: IFC-3 says implementers implement the parents, Rust requires a supertrait to hold for every type an impl covers, verdict 132 says a declaration's meaning comes only from what it says, and STR-5, ODR-027 and std's `@derive(Copy)` on `[T] pub struct Range` make derives per instance. So (i), stated once in IFC-3 for every interface and in DRV-1 for every derive.
decisions.recommendation: (i): a hand-written generic implementation writes the bound its interface's parents need, or the compiler refuses it and gives that line; a derive writes the bound itself.

owner_short.one_line: A generic error that hands the caller's value back (like Rust's `SendError<T>`): is it an error for every `T`, or only for the `T`s any thread may have, and who writes that?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | library author | writes `extend[T] PoolFull[T] implements Error:` | refused, with the line to write
2 | library author | writes `extend[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)] PoolFull[T] implements Error:` | allowed
3 | library author | writes `@derive(Error)` on a generic enum | allowed; the derive writes the bound itself
4 | program | `insert(...)?` with `PoolFull[int]` into the catch-all | allowed
5 | one-thread game | `insert(...)?` with `PoolFull[shares Enemy]` into the catch-all | refused at that line: name the error type instead
owner_short.today: Nothing says; the implementation covers every `T`, because errors need no thread markers today.
options: (i) a hand-written implementation writes the bound, or is refused with the line to write; a derive writes it itself
(ii) the implementation quietly holds only for the safe `T`s
(iii) a generic error type must bound its parameter on the type itself
owner_short.recommendation: (i): the line says what it means, the compiler gives the line to write, and derives keep working per instance as they already do.

decisions.title: What an object of an open class may hold, for the thread markers
decisions.problem: A base-class value may be an object of any derived class (C++'s `Base*` to a `Derived`). THR-8's definition says a type is Send when nothing reachable from it is a one-thread owner, but its list and the p04 table judge a class object by its declared class's fields alone. So a `Script` value that is an `Enemy` holding a `shares` owner may go to another thread today. Under D, a `GameError` that is a `DocError` holding one would also go inside every AnyError.

options.code:
open class Script:
    entity: int
class Enemy(Script):
    level: shares Level
## a Script's components include Enemy's fields: thread.spawn(owns fn() owns s: ...) is E7015 naming Enemy.level
## a class derived from an Error class is checked where it is declared (IFC-3)
options.outcome: Every program whose derived classes hold only thread-safe parts is accepted, with nothing written: Door(Script) crosses, and std's ECS World crosses when its components do. A refusal falls on the line that sends the value, naming the derived class. A library's line may depend on a class the program derives, as a virtual call's effects already do.

options.code:
interface Task: needs (Send, ThreadShared):
    pass
extend Script implements Task:   # without this, no Script value ever goes to another thread
    pass
options.outcome: An open class's values never cross threads unless it promises the markers through an interface, and then every derived class is checked (Swift: a non-final class is never Sendable). Std's ECS World (`Map[u64, AnyStorage]`) could then never go to another thread or be read by tasks, unless std bounds every component to be Send and ThreadShared.

options.code:

    level: shares Level   # refused: Script is Send by its fields, so every derived class must be

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: (iii) refuses ordinary class hierarchies. (ii) refuses every open-class value crossing threads or read by tasks unless an interface is written only to carry the markers, and it breaks std's own ECS World. (i) and (iv) keep ordinary code. 2. Safety: (iv) lets a one-thread owner cross, so it is out. 3. Compile time: (i), (ii) and (iii) are all decided when compiling. 4. A written word only for meaning: (i) writes nothing, and (ii) writes an interface that says nothing a declaration does not already say. 5. The ordinary program: (i) accepts every program whose derived classes are thread-safe. Its refusal is at the line that sends the value and names the derived class, the cost verdict 86 accepted for effects. 6. Consistency: (i) is what THR-8's own definition says ("nothing reachable from it"). It is how the language already treats an open class's virtual calls (EFF-24, p10 94: "from every function the program can put there"; verdict 122) and its views (p07 713). And it infers markers from the words of types, as TYP-43 says. (ii) matches THR-8's dyn clause and Swift, but a class has no needs list, and (ii) loses on parameters 1 and 5 first. Where a base does promise the markers, by implementing an interface that needs them (Error), each derived class is checked at its own line (IFC-3, decision 2's property). So (i).
decisions.recommendation: (i): a base-class value is judged by every class the program derives from it, with nothing written; a class derived from an error class is checked where it is declared.

owner_short.one_line: When a base-class object (C++'s `Base*` that may point at a `Derived`) is handed to another thread, should the compiler look at every derived class the program declares?

owner_short.today: The compiler looks only at the base class's own fields, so a Script that is an Enemy goes to another thread and its shared count races.
options: (i) look at every derived class the program declares; nothing written
(ii) a base class's objects never go to another thread unless the base promises it through an interface (Swift)
(iii) every derived class must be as thread-safe as its base's own fields
(iv) keep today
owner_short.recommendation: (i): correct hierarchies keep working with nothing written, and only the class that holds the one-thread part is named.

responses.objection: S1-1 (safety, block S): an open error class `GameError` implements Error, and its subclass `DocError` holds a `shares Doc`. Upcast to GameError and put into an AnyError, it reaches another thread, and its plain count races.
responses.how: The cause is what an object of an open class holds, so the change now fixes it there. THR-8's list (p11 47-48), THR-9 (p11 63-64) and the p04 rows (577-578) now say what THR-8's definition already says ("nothing reachable from it"): an object of an open or abstract class counts the fields of every class the program derives from it. IFC-3 (p05 411-413) now says that an implementation covers each class derived from a class it covers, and refuses one that does not meet the parents where that derived class is declared, in its own package. Walk of the objection's program: line 17 passes (GameError's own `code: int`). Line 20, `class DocError(GameError):`, is E2040 naming `doc`, even when GameError is in a library compiled earlier. So no DocError object exists, and nothing one-thread is reachable from the AnyError at line 38. The same words close the existing gap for a plain `owns b: GameError`, and for a plain open class: an `Enemy(Script)` holding a `shares` owner makes a Script hand-over E7015, naming Enemy's field. They also cover an error struct holding a field of a plain open class. The earlier premise, "the one place its contents are known", is withdrawn. For an open class, contents are also declared at each derived class, which is where the check now goes. Tests k20_derived_error_class_refused, k20_open_class_one_thread_subclass_refused and k20_open_class_plain_subclasses_runs.

responses.objection: S1-3: a `@cached` method on an error class is now filled from two threads through AnyError, and the impact said nothing is added at run time.
responses.how: CLS-12 decides it as written (p05 380: "On an object several threads reach, the kept result is filled once under a once-flag"). After the change, every object of a class that implements Error is such an object, because Error requires ThreadShared and AnyError is ThreadShared, and the compiler knows this from the type. The impact now states the duty and its cost. Per call, the flag test is an acquire load (on x86-64 the same `mov` as a plain load; on ARM64 an `ldar`), and the first call fills under the flag (one compare-and-swap), to be measured. It is the same duty today for any ThreadShared class given by `ref` to scoped tasks. The objection's program prints 68.

responses.objection: E1-1: an error holding `owns dyn Shape` (Shape needing only Debug) is refused, ERR-3's closed list of fixes gives no line that compiles, and the readability verdict's 'only one place' was false.
responses.how: ERR-3 no longer lists fixes. IFC-3 states the message as a property: it names the part and gives a line that compiles, either one that makes the part meet the parent by the rule that decides it (here `interface Shape: needs (Debug, Send, ThreadShared):` in place of line 1), or one that holds a copy of what the type uses (`TooLarge(area: int)`). programs_changed now has the row for `owns dyn I` fields, including that the interface's needs then hold every implementer (a `Sprite` holding `shares Texture` becomes E2040), and that under A a one-thread renderer matching `Result[int, DrawError]` compiles. The readability verdict now names both places where words are added. The trade-off itself is kept, because an error that any thread may read cannot hold an object only one thread may read. The copy line keeps `Shape` as it is. Test k20_error_holding_dyn_interface_refused.

responses.objection: E1-2: the offered fix 'make the value thread_shared' for a `shares mut Doc` field leads into E7014 when the program changes the document directly.
responses.how: The same message property in IFC-3: only a line that compiles is given. `thread_shared` is offered only where no line then changes the value directly. Here the message gives `ReadOnly(path: String)` in place of line 7 and `e = SaveError.ReadOnly(path=copy of doc.path)` in place of line 12 (verdict 73).

responses.objection: E1-3: refusing `@derive(Error)` on a generic type with a `T` field gives derives two rules (per instance for Copy, Eq, Debug and Clone, refused for Error), and the help bounds the type itself.
responses.how: DRV-1 (p14 138) now says, for every derive, that a requirement a field meets only for some arguments of the type's parameters is written as their needs in the generated `extend`, so the derive holds per instance, as STR-5, ODR-027 and std's `@derive(Copy)` on `[T] pub struct Range` already do. The objection's program runs and prints `the spawn point is full`. E2080 stays for a field whose own written type fails. A hand-written unbounded `extend[T] X[T] implements Error:` stays refused (decision 2 (i), verdict 132). This settles the previous notes' gap (1) for every derive. Test k20_generic_derive_error_per_instance.

responses.objection: E1-4: TYP-17 (p04 459) still quotes `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display):`.
responses.how: p04 458-459 is edited to the new declaration in the same change. It stays the example of several needs in round brackets. `report_later` then compiles under every text.

responses.objection: E1-5: the THR-9 sentence ('which an interface writes among its needs as a bound does') reads as if it attached to `dyn I`, and decides nothing more.
responses.how: THR-9 now reads: "Structural types and class objects are `ThreadShared` when every component is (a class object's components as `[THR-8]` counts them), and `dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs (Send, ThreadShared):`), as for `Send` (`[THR-8]`, ODR-255)." The objection's program prints 4.

responses.objection: I1-1: 'an implementation meets all four for every type it covers' was written as a fact about Error. `extend[T] Echo[T] implements Command:` with `interface Command: needs (Send, ThreadShared):` stays undecided, and TYP-43's per-instance reading may be carried over.
responses.how: The property is now stated once in IFC-3 for every interface: an implementation meets its interface's parents for every type it covers (each instance of a generic implementation, each derived class), otherwise E2040 at the implementation, with the bounded line given. ERR-3 states only Error's four parents and cites IFC-3. Line 10 of the objection's program is E2040, giving `extend[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)] Echo[T] implements Command:`. `Tagged[T]`'s Ord gives `extend[T: needs Eq] Tagged[T] implements Ord:`. TYP-43's per-instance words are about a vouched generic Send whose parameters are bounded, so they do not apply to an unbounded implementation. Test k20_interface_parents_generic_extend.

responses.objection: I1-2: ERR-3's closed list of fixes gives no compiling line for an `owns dyn Note` field, a Cell field or a plain function.
responses.how: The list is gone, and the message rule in IFC-3 is a property (a line that makes the part meet the parent by the rule that decides it, or a copy). For the objection's program, the message gives `interface Note: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):` in place of line 3. For a `Cell[int]` it gives `Atomic[int]`, as verdict 165's message does.

responses.objection: I1-3: programs_changed missed error types holding a plain `fn()` or an `owns dyn I`, and whether the offered `thread_shared fn()` is ThreadShared is undecided.
responses.how: Both rows are now in programs_changed. For a plain `fn()` field, the message gives a copy line (the data the function would read) and does not offer `thread_shared fn()`. Whether a `thread_shared fn()` is ThreadShared (THR-9 names no function type, and a `fn() owns n: n += 1` changes its own state when called) is a gap that exists today: it shows in verdict 165's rule for a `thread_shared Bus` holding an unguarded `Array[thread_shared fn()]`, which THR-1's own message offers (p11 84-85). It is not caused by this change and is listed in notes beside J7-06.

responses.objection: I1-4: the impact missed TYP-17's copy of the declaration and the p17a code rows.
responses.how: p04 459 is edited, and p17a 71 (E2080: a derive whose requirement a field does not meet, `@derive(Error)` included, citing DRV-1 and ERR-3) and p17a 59 (E2040: an implementation that does not meet its parents, citing IFC-3 and ERR-3) are edited. All three are listed under rules changed.

Regression scan over tests/, examples/ and the spec's examples: list every error type now refused (holding shares, shares mut, a weakref to a one-thread value, sharedref mut, Cell, a plain fn(), an owns dyn I whose I lacks the markers, or a raw pointer), and every hand-over, scoped `ref`, channel or thread_shared holder of an open-class value now refused because a derived class holds a one-thread part. The class rule on separate packages: a library's `pub open class` with a derived class in the program. The program's build counts the derived class. A derived class of a library's Error class is refused at its own line. A library line that sends a base value is reported in the program's build, at the line that passes the value, naming the derived class.
Every std implementation of an interface with parents meets them for every type it covers (search `implements Ord`, `implements IndexMut`, `implements Error`): no generic one needs a new bound.

`@derive(Copy)` on `[T] pub struct Range` and the other range types still gives `Copy` per instance, and `@derive(Error)` on a generic enum writes `extend[T: needs (Debug, Send, ThreadShared)]` in `ember inspect --expand`.
The sixteen tests above give exactly the stated results, including the E2080, E2040 and E7015 messages. Each message's offered line must compile.

A type that is Send only by `unsafe extend X implements Send` (a raw pointer) and implements Error is E2040 at its implementation, with a message that does not offer a vouch for ThreadShared (pending J7-06).
Verdict 114's hand-over check reaches objects owned inside an AnyError's box (through the error's table) when an AnyError is returned from a thread or sent on a channel.

To measure: AnyError's size and the failure-path time of a `?` into it, against today's build; a `@cached` call on an error class with the once-flag against a plain flag, on x86-64 and ARM64; and the time of the hand-over check for an AnyError in a program where an error type owns an object of a class with weakref links.
final.notes:
This revision keeps direction D and rewrites the change as a whole. Objection S1-1 showed that D is sound only if the markers of what an error holds are sound, and for an object of an open class they were not: THR-8's list and the p04 row counted the declared class's fields, while THR-8's own definition says \"nothing reachable from it\". So the change now also fixes the class wording (THR-8, THR-9, p04 577-578) at that cause. It states once in IFC-3 that an implementation meets its interface's parents for every type it covers (generic instances, derived classes), with the refusal's place and its message's line given as properties. That replaces ERR-3's closed list of fixes. DRV-1 now says derives on generic types are per instance, as STR-5, ODR-027 and std's Range already read it. TYP-17's copy of the declaration and the p17a rows are edited. Decision 3 (open classes) is new. The nearest tension is with verdict 61, which turned down a whole-program search through bodies. Option (i) reads the declarations of derived classes, as the language already does for an open class's virtual calls (EFF-24, verdict 122). It is listed for the owner with option (ii), Swift's rule, which would stop std's ECS World from ever going to another thread or being read by tasks.

Existing gaps found on the way, not caused by this change, listed for later:
(1) Whether a `thread_shared fn()` is ThreadShared. THR-9 names no function type, and a `fn() owns n: n += 1` changes its own state when called. It shows today in verdict 165's rule for a thread_shared Bus holding an unguarded `Array[thread_shared fn()]`, which THR-1's own E7015 message offers (p11 84-85). Until it is decided, the message for an error holding a function gives a copy line. Present it beside J7-06.
(2) A ThreadShared vouch for types holding raw pointers (P04, J7-06). Until it is settled, an error type holding a raw pointer cannot be an Error.
(3) Verdict 114's hand-over check through any `owns dyn I` whose interface needs Send. THR-2's words ('every object the handed object owns') cover it, but the table mechanism is not stated.
(4) std/src/thread.em still uses the old spawn signature (implementation, not spec).

Precedents: Swift's `Error` refines `Sendable` (SE-0302), and a non-final Swift class cannot be Sendable. Rust's anyhow::Error requires `Send + Sync + 'static`, and a Rust impl must meet its supertraits for every type it covers.

All work was read-only. The repository's start-up reading (AUTOPILOT, HANDOFF) was skipped, as the team rules direct.

# file gamekit/ember.toml
#   [package]

from std.fmt import Formatter, FmtError

pub open class Script:
    let entity: int

    pub fn init(entity: int):
        this.entity = entity

pub struct LoadError:
    pub script: Script

extend LoadError implements Display:
    fn fmt(ref mut f: Formatter) -> Result[void, FmtError]:
        return f.write_str("the script could not load")

extend LoadError implements Debug:
    fn fmt_debug(ref mut f: Formatter) -> Result[void, FmtError]:
        return f.write_str("LoadError")

extend LoadError implements Error:
    pass
# file game/ember.toml
#   [package]
#   name = "game"
#   version = "0.1.0"
#   language = "0.9.15"
#   [dependencies]
#   gamekit = { path = "../gamekit" }
# file game/src/main.em (line numbers below count from its first line)
import std.thread
from gamekit import Script, LoadError

class Level:
    name: String = String("forest")

class Enemy(Script):
    level: shares Level

    fn init(entity: int, owns level: shares Level):
        this.level = level
        super.init(entity)

fn make_enemy(entity: int, owns level: shares Level) -> Result[int, LoadError]:
    return Err(LoadError(script=Enemy(entity, owns level)))   # an Enemy, upcast to Script

fn load(entity: int, owns level: shares Level) -> Result[int]:
    return Ok(make_enemy(entity, owns level)?)                # LoadError -> AnyError

fn main():
    level = shares Level()
    r = load(1, shares level)                                  # r's error holds a second owner of the Level
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns r: r.is_err())             # r goes to another thread, which ends it
    for i in 0..100000:
        other = shares level                                   # +1, then -1 at the end of the round: plain adds
        println(i, other.name.len())
    println(h.join())
open.walk:
In C++ terms: an engine library's exception type holds a `Base*`. The game's `Derived` holds a non-atomic refcounted pointer. A type-erased `std::exception_ptr` carries it to another thread.
(1) gamekit/src/lib.em line 20, `extend LoadError implements Error:`, in gamekit's build. p04 676 after reads `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):`. IFC-3 after (p05 411-413) reads "An implementation meets its interface's parents for every type it covers". LoadError's one component is `script: Script` (line 10). THR-8 after (p11 47-48) reads "an object of an `open` or `abstract` class may be an object of any class the program derives from it, a library's included". gamekit derives nothing from Script, so in its build Script's components are `entity: int`, and LoadError is Send and ThreadShared (THR-9 after, p11 63-64). Display is line 12 and Debug is line 16. Line 20 passes, and gamekit is done. MOD-9 (p05 38-46): "What a dependant may rely on is what the package's `pub` items write and what the compiler works out from their code ... recorded in the package's interface file".
(2) game/src/main.em line 7, `class Enemy(Script):`, with `level: shares Level` on line 8. CLS-4 (p05 335) lets an open class be subclassed. The new IFC-3 sentence checks a derived class only when it is "derived from a class it covers". ERR-3 after (p13 87-88) says the same: "refused where it implements `Error` or where it is derived from a class that does". The Error implementation covers LoadError, not Script, and Script implements nothing. So nothing checks line 7, and it compiles.
(3) Line 15. TYP-5 rule 8 (p04 86) gives "a class object to a base class (upcast)" at a field initialiser, a coercion site (p04 71). The LoadError now holds an Enemy, and the Enemy holds a second owner of main's Level.
(4) Line 18. ERR-2 (p13 51-52) "returns `Err(F.from(err))`". ERR-8 (p13 95) says AnyError "implements `From[E]` for every `E: needs Error`". LoadError meets that bound through gamekit's line 20 (IFC-3: "So a bound brings its parents"). The edited E2040 row (p17a 59 after) places the parent refusal "at the generic implementation or at the derived class". Line 18 is neither, and so is every other line of game.
(5) Line 23. THR-10 (p11 176) says "`R` MUST be `Send`". R is Result[int, AnyError]. AnyError's `Box[dyn Error]` is Send by THR-8's dyn clause (p11 51), "`dyn I` when `I` requires it", which reads the interface and never the implementers. So line 23 compiles. The changed THR-8 does make LoadError itself not Send in game's build, because Script now counts Enemy's fields. But no line of game checks LoadError's markers. They were checked once, at gamekit's line 20, in gamekit's build, which game's build only relies on (MOD-9).
(6) The worker ends `r`. The box ends the LoadError, which ends the Enemy (CLS-6, p05 353), which ends `level`. RC-4 (p08 155-156) says the counts of a value that is not thread_shared "are changed with plain adds and subtracts, and never cross threads". That -1 on the worker races with main's +1/-1 on lines 25-26. A lost update either leaks the Level, or brings its count to 0 while `other.name` is read: a use after free, then a double free at the last end.
Today the same program is E7015 at line 23. Error needs only Debug and Display (p04 676, p13 88), so by p11 51 `dyn Error` is not Send, and neither is r.
Read the other way, game's build would check gamekit's line 20 again and refuse it with E2040. Then the refusal falls on a dependency's line, which the game's author cannot change, and the text places it nowhere (the 'either ... or' of IFC-3 after). The program is let through or refused depending on which reading is taken.
Route 2, hot reload. Take the same two packages, with game reloadable and Enemy at first holding only `angle: int`. A reload adds `target: Option[weakref Level] = None` to Enemy. # package engine (a library): engine/src/lib.em
from std.fmt import Formatter, FmtError

pub open class Script:
    pub entity: int

    pub fn init(entity: int):
        this.entity = entity

pub struct ScriptError:
    pub script: Script

extend ScriptError implements Display:
    fn fmt(ref mut f: Formatter) -> Result[void, FmtError]:
        return f.write_str("the script failed")

extend ScriptError implements Debug:
    fn fmt_debug(ref mut f: Formatter) -> Result[void, FmtError]:
        return f.write_str("ScriptError")

extend ScriptError implements Error:
    pass

pub fn fail(owns s: Script) -> Result[int, ScriptError]:
    return Err(ScriptError(script=s))

# package game (uses engine): game/src/main.em
import std.thread
from std.sync import Sender, channel
from engine import Script, fail

class Level:
    name: String = String("forest")

class Enemy(Script):
    level: shares Level

    fn init(entity: int, owns level: shares Level):
        this.level = level
        super.init(entity)

fn tick(owns s: Script) -> Result[int]:
    return Ok(fail(owns s)?)                         # ScriptError -> AnyError

fn work(tx: Sender[Result[int]]):
    level = shares Level()
    tx.send(owns tick(owns Enemy(1, shares level))).expect("receiver is gone")
    n = 0
    for _ in 0..1000000:
        extra = shares level                         # plain add and sub on this thread
        n += extra.name.len()
    println(n)

fn main():
    tx, rx = channel[Result[int]](capacity=1)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns tx: work(tx))
    for r in rx:
        match r:
            Ok(n) => println(n)
            Err(e) => println(e)                     # the Enemy ends here: a plain sub on the main thread
    h.join()

closed.suggestion: Use one property for every derive (DRV-1). closed.walk: The property that decides decision 2 is written as a fact about one interface. p13-errors.md 88 (after): "An implementation of `Error` meets all four for every type it covers. One that does not is `E2040` where it implements `Error`". Those words reach only Error. The general rule is IFC-3 (p05-declarations.md 411-412): "`interface Ord: needs Eq` requires implementers of `Ord` to implement `Eq`. So a bound brings its parents". IFC-3 says what implementers must meet. It does not say whether a generic implementation that meets the parents for only some `T` is refused or holds per instance, and no other rule says it (grep of p04/p05/p14 for 'parent': only p04 458 and p05 412). The change's own THR-9 edit (p11 63-64 after) presents `interface I: needs (Send, ThreadShared):` as the way to write such an interface. In the program, line 10 `extend[T] Echo[T] implements Command:` covers every `T`, but `Echo[T]` is Send and ThreadShared only when `T` is (p11 47-48, "Structs ... are `Send` when every component is"; p11 63-64). ERR-3 does not reach `Command`, and IFC-3 decides nothing. TYP-43 (p04 591-592) states the per-instance reading for generic marker vouches ("holds for each instance whose arguments meet the markers its parameters are bounded by"), which a reader may carry over. So line 10 is undecided, while the same shape with `Error` is E2040. The same holds for `extend[T] Tagged[T] implements Ord:` over `extend[T: needs Eq] Tagged[T] implements Eq:`.

new_gaps.walk:
The danger in C++ terms: a weak_ptr's control block is updated without atomics while another thread destroys the object it points at.
The change relies on verdict 114 for class errors (cost: "THR-2's existing hand-over check ... reaches objects the boxed error owns ... through the error's table"). THR-2 (p11 112-114) runs that check only when "An object handed whole to another thread leaves its `weakref` links behind ... At the hand-over the program reads the object's weak count".
Line 31, `thread_shared Log(...)`. THR-1 (p11 69-72) allows thread_shared before a new value. Its check that "everything reachable from it is `Send`" (p11 82) passes, because AnyError is Send after the change (p11 51; p04 676 after). Verdict 165's ThreadShared check passes, because THR-9 (p11 66) makes "`Mutex[T]` for a `Send` `T`" ThreadShared. Nothing is handed to a thread at this line: the object is moved into a new value. So THR-2's move does not run, and `w` still points at the LoadError object, which the worker can now reach through the Mutex.
Line 32: the worker gets one more owner of `log` (THR-17, p11 186). On the worker, `g.clear()` (line 26) ends the LoadError object: OBJ-3 (p08 83-86) runs its field drops, which free `path`'s String, and decrements its weak count. RC-4 (p08 155-156) says that count is changed with plain adds and subtracts.
Lines 33-34 on main: WK-12 (p08 346-348) says opening the link "tests the target's header". RC-5 point 1 (p08 196-204) checks only lines and calls of this thread. RC-5 point 2 (p08 215) counts only for "A view of a `thread_shared` object". So main tests the header and reads `p.path` while the worker ends the object and frees the String: a data race on the weak count, and a read after free.
Not caused by the change: the same program with `class Enemy` in a `Mutex[Array[Enemy]]` (Enemy is Send by its fields, p11 47-48) compiles today and goes wrong the same way. The change routes the default error type through this route (its game sibling is exactly this shape) while counting on verdict 114's check, which does not run here.
new_gaps.impact: A use-after-free reached by storing a result into a lock of a thread_shared object while a link on this thread points at the error object. It is the same for any class object in a thread_shared container today.
new_gaps.suggestion: This is a gap for the list, in THR-2, not a reason to block this change. The property: an object becomes reachable from another thread by any route THR-2 already lists (handed over, sent, or stored into a thread_shared value or a lock of one), and by any such route it leaves its weakref links behind, as verdict 114's hand-over does: one compare at that line. With that, line 31 moves the object, `w` finds it ended, and the program prints `done`. Also correct the change's cost line, which currently implies verdict 114 covers every route a boxed error takes to another thread.

new_gaps.walk:
The danger in C++ terms: a non-atomic refcount (an Rc-like shared_ptr) pushed through a thread-safe queue to another thread.
The change's impact gives, for its server program, "before: E7015 at the spawn line (the Sender holds AnyErrors, which are not Send)", and its sibling relies on "a Sender is Send when its element is". The text does not say that. THR-15 (p11 336-337) says "`Sender` is `Send`, `ThreadShared` and `Clone` ... `Receiver` is `Send`", with no condition on the element.
So in this program, line 19 hands `rx` (a Receiver, Send by p11 337) to a thread. Each `shares doc` sent on line 15 is a one-thread owner, which the worker ends with a plain -1 (RC-4, p08 155-156) while main makes the next owner with a plain +1: a data race on the count, and then a read after free of `d.path`. This compiles today. It is J7-07, the group's open lead fix, and it exists without the change. The change does close it for AnyError, by accident, since AnyError becomes Send.
new_gaps.impact: The change's 'before' column claims a refusal where today's text has a hole. The owner would read the server case as safe today when it is not. The change does not add any risk here.
new_gaps.suggestion: Correct the server row's 'before' to: "compiles by THR-15's words (Sender and Receiver are Send whatever the element); the J7-07 fix (a channel end is Send only for a Send element) is what makes it E7015". Keep J7-07 on the list.

new_gaps.walk: Three statements in the report are not what the text says. (1) Server sibling, before: the report gives "E7015 at the spawn line (the Sender holds AnyErrors, which are not Send)", and its walk quotes "a Sender is Send when its element is". THR-15 (p11 335-336) instead says "`Sender` is `Send`, `ThreadShared` and `Clone`" with no condition. By THR-15 the spawn line holds a Send `tx` and compiles today. By THR-8 (p11 44-48) it does not. That clash exists already (J7-07). After the change both rules accept this program. (2) Generic-library sibling: R is `Result[int, AnyError]` whatever `S.Failure` is (ERR-9 p13 48-49). So what decides it is p11 51 through AnyError's box, not "IFC-3 carries Send and ThreadShared into `S.Failure`". (3) Cost: "which the compiler knows from the From instances". An `owns dyn Error` is also made outside AnyError's From (a wrapper's `cause: owns dyn Error` field, an `@from` variant's `source`). The condition for verdict 114's check to run is that some type implementing Error owns an object of a class that `weakref` links point at.
new_gaps.impact: The before/after table and the cost line that the owner reads quote words the specification does not have. No outcome after the change is wrong.
new_gaps.suggestion: Server before: write 'THR-15 says it compiles and THR-8 says E7015 (J7-07, a clash that exists already)'. Generic library: cite p11 51 through AnyError. Cost: state the condition as 'a type implementing Error owns an object whose class a weakref is made to'.

new_gaps.walk: The change's tests k20_worker_failure_reaches_main and k20_server_channel_of_results expect `the text is not a value of this type`. That text is std/src/string.em line 22, not the specification. p15-stdlib.md 158-159 says only "`ParseError`, in `std.string`, is a unit-only enum, `Empty`, `Invalid` or `Overflow`". By DRV-1 p14 130, a derived Display of a unit-only enum is "the variant name". So the specification decides neither text, and the expected stderr is not one the specification fixes (rule E: "an error code the specification names ... or the exact text the program prints").
new_gaps.impact: Two of the change's tests follow the implementation, not the specification (memory rule: tests follow the spec). If std's text changes, they fail with nothing in the specification having changed.
new_gaps.suggestion: Make the failure come from text the specification fixes: `AnyError.msg(f"not a level: {text}")` (ERR-8 p13 98-100), or the test's own `@derive(Error)` enum with an `@error(...)` text (ERR-3). See the replacement tests below.

tests.name: error_wrapper_with_boxed_cause_crosses_threads
tests.program:
# a mesh importer's wrapper error returned from a worker; the danger in C++ terms: a
# std::unique_ptr<std::exception> holding any exception, moved to another thread
import std.thread
from std.fmt import Formatter, FmtError

struct ImportError:
    file: String
    cause: owns dyn Error

extend ImportError implements Display:
    fn fmt(ref mut f: Formatter) -> Result[void, FmtError]:
        return f.write_str(f"cannot import {this.file}")

extend ImportError implements Debug:
    fn fmt_debug(ref mut f: Formatter) -> Result[void, FmtError]:
        return f.write_str("ImportError")

extend ImportError implements Error:
    pass

fn import_mesh(file: StrView, text: StrView) -> Result[int, ImportError]:
    match text.parse[int]():
        Ok(n):
            return Ok(n)
        Err(e):
            return Err(ImportError(file=String(file), cause=owns e))

fn main():
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() => import_mesh("tree.mesh", "many"))
    match h.join():
        Ok(n):
            println(n)
        Err(e):
            println(e)
tests.expected: stdout: `cannot import tree.mesh` (one line); exit status 0

out.intent: Load a level file on a worker thread and give the main thread its length, or the reason the load failed.

cause.where: ERR-3 and the declaration it cites in IV.8: p13-errors.md 87-88 ("`Error` is the interface of error types: `Display + Debug` with `fn source() ...`") and p04-types.md 676 (`interface Error: needs (Debug, Display):`). `Error` requires nothing about threads.
cause.why_there: The rules that showed the problem are right as written. THR-8 (p11 51) makes an erased value `Send` by what its interface requires: "`dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs Send:`)". THR-10 (p11 176) is right to require a `Send` result. ERR-8 (p13 93-95) is right to hold an error as `owns dyn Error`, and THR-2's routes are complete. What is missing is a statement about what an error is. Because `Error` says nothing about threads, `dyn Error` may hold a one-thread owner, so every erased error stays on its thread. That includes `AnyError`, the default error type of every `Result[T]` (ERR-9 p13 48-50), and also a wrapper's boxed cause and a list of errors. Fixing it in ERR-8, by bounding `AnyError`'s `From`, would leave every other `owns dyn Error` on one thread and would need a second spelling for a `Send` dyn. Fixing it in THR-8 or THR-2 would make a dyn `Send` by something other than its interface: a search of the whole program, which verdict 61 turned down for function values.
cause.reported_at: ERR-3, ERR-8, THR-2, THR-8 (the question's citations: THR-10 p11 175-176, THR-8 p11 51, ERR-3 p13 87-88, ERR-8 p13 93-95)

existing_rule.words: THR-8: "Structs, enums, tuples, fixed arrays, collections and class objects are `Send` when every component is; an `owns T` when `T` is; ... `dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs Send:`)." IFC-3: "`interface Ord: needs Eq` requires implementers of `Ord` to implement `Eq`. So a bound brings its parents". (Also DRV-1 p14 138: "A derive whose requirement a field does not meet is `E2080`, naming the field"; and ODR-255, p26 542: "`dyn I` is `Send`/`Sync` when `I` requires it".)

edits.before: `Error` is the interface of error types: `Display + Debug` with `fn source() -> Option[ref dyn Error]` (default `None`) (§IV.8).
edits.after: `Error` is the interface of error types: `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):` with `fn source() -> Option[ref dyn Error]` (default `None`) (§IV.8). Any thread may have and read an error, so `dyn Error`, and `AnyError`, which holds one (`[ERR-8]`), are `Send` and `ThreadShared` (`[THR-8]`, `[THR-9]`).
edits.why_general: The property is stated once, on what an error is: any thread may have it and read it. THR-8's existing words then carry it to every holder with nothing written: `dyn Error`, an `owns dyn Error` in any wrapper or list, `AnyError`, and every bound `E: needs Error` or `type Failure: needs Error` (IFC-3: a bound brings its parents). So every route is covered at once: a thread's result, a job's result, a channel, a `thread_shared` holder, an `RwLock`, a `ref` given to a scoped task. ERR-1's "any `E: needs Error`", ERR-8's `From` and ERR-9's "any error" stay true as written. The old `Display + Debug` becomes verdict 110's `needs` spelling.
edits.why_here: This is where the cause is. `Error` said nothing about threads, so every erased error, with `AnyError` (the default of `Result[T]`) first, was confined to its thread without the text ever saying so.

edits.before: A variant marked `@from` whose single field is an error type gets `From` for that type and returns it from `source`.
edits.after: A variant marked `@from` whose single field is an error type gets `From` for that type and returns it from `source`. A type implements `Error` only when it is `Send` and `ThreadShared` (`[IFC-3]`). A written implementation for a type that is not is `E2040`; a derived one is `E2080` at the field (`[DRV-1]`). Each message names what stays on one thread and the words to write: a copy, `path: String`, in place of a `shares SourceFile` field; `extend[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)]` for a generic type that holds its `T`. `@derive(Error)` on a generic type implements `Error` for the instances that are both.
edits.why_general: This is IFC-3's property (an implementer meets the interface's parents) applied to `Error`'s new parents, with the codes the specification already uses: `E2040` for a written implementation, as tests/conformance/THR-8 gives for `extend Handle implements Sendable`, and `E2080` for a derive's field (DRV-1 p14 138). A derive's reach on a generic type is its instances, as `@derive(Zeroable)` is judged per instance (tests/conformance/ARN-11) and as STR-5's derives and TYP-36's "if `T`" work. It decides every error type, written or derived, plain or generic, with no list of cases.
edits.why_here: Without it, a generic error type (a pool's `PoolFull[T]`, a loader's `LoadError[T]`) is left undecided between a refusal and a per-instance implementation. That is the third round's 'undecided' hole.

edits.rule: IV.8 standard interfaces (the declaration ERR-3 cites)
edits.before: interface Error: needs (Debug, Display):
edits.after: interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):    # any thread may have and read an error (`[ERR-3]`)
edits.why_general: This is the normative declaration that ERR-3 states. Both change together, so no two texts disagree about what an error requires. std/src/core.em line 80 follows after review.
edits.why_here: p04 676 is the declaration ERR-3 points to (§IV.8). Leaving it unchanged was the third round's 'clash' hole.

edits.before: Structural types are `ThreadShared` when every component is.
edits.after: Structural types are `ThreadShared` when every component is, and `dyn I` is when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs (Send, ThreadShared):`), as for `Send` (`[THR-8]`, ODR-255).
edits.why_general: ODR-255 already ruled that a dyn has a marker when its interface requires it. THR-8 says this for `Send`, but THR-9 says only "inferred like `Send`". This one clause makes it explicit for every interface, a program's own included, and shows that `ThreadShared` may be written in an interface's `needs`, as THR-8 writes `Send`.
edits.why_here: `AnyError` being `ThreadShared` depends on `dyn Error` being `ThreadShared`: a `thread_shared` cache of results (verdict 165), and a `ref` to an error given to a scoped task (THR-8 p11 49).

impact.rules_changed: ERR-3: p13-errors.md 87-88 changed (Error's declaration gains Send and ThreadShared; dyn Error and AnyError follow), 91-92 added (who implements Error; a derive on a generic type). readability.verdict: Better. The threaded program reads like the one-thread one, and no word is added to ordinary error code. impact.cost: Compile time: Send and ThreadShared are inferred as today, plus one check per type that implements Error. Run time on one thread: no change. AnyError keeps its layout (the boxed error's data and table pointers, its identity, its list of context messages) and its one allocation on the failure path (ERR-11). A `?` costs what it costs today, and the success path costs nothing, as in C. Handing an error to another thread (a join, a channel, a thread_shared holder) moves those words, as C passes a struct by value. Where some error type owns an object of a class that a weakref is made to anywhere, verdict 114's hand-over check runs through the error's table: one indirect call per error handed over, and one compare per such object. Nothing runs when no error type owns such an object. C copies a pointer and checks nothing. To measure: AnyError's size and the failure-path time of `?` against today's build, and the time of the hand-over check where it applies.

sibling_cases.program:
# a generic text tool; the danger in C++ terms: a template that copies an exception type it
# knows nothing about to another thread
import std.io

interface Source:
    type Failure: needs Error
    fn read_all() -> Result[String, Failure]

struct Fixed:
    text: String

extend Fixed implements Source:
    type Failure = io.Error
    fn read_all() -> Result[String, io.Error]:
        return Ok(copy of this.text)

[S: needs Source]
pub fn count_lines(src: S) -> Result[int]:
    text = src.read_all()?            # S.Failure -> AnyError
    return Ok(text.lines().count())

fn main() -> Result[void]:

    return Ok(())

decisions.title: Where the thread requirement of errors sits: on what an error is, on the catch-all's conversion, or nowhere
decisions.problem: `Result[T]`'s default error type, AnyError, holds `owns dyn Error`. Error requires nothing about threads, so by THR-8 AnyError is not Send, and a worker thread cannot return `Result[T]`. Making it Send needs some rule to keep one-thread errors out of it.

options.code:
## std.core
interface SendableError: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared):
    pass
pub struct AnyError:
    error: owns dyn SendableError
    ...
extend[E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)] AnyError implements From[E]:
    ...
## user code
struct ImportError:
    cause: owns dyn Error        # not Send
options.outcome: The worker compiles. A one-thread error is refused at its `?` into AnyError (E2040), even with one thread. A wrapper holding `owns dyn Error` is not Send, so its `?` into AnyError is refused too; fixing it needs a second error interface (or `dyn Error + Send`, a spelling Ember does not have). A pub generic function that `?`s `E: needs Error` must also write `needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)`. Only refusals, no change in meaning.

Today's rules, written down. The `Result[int]` worker is E7015 at the spawn line. A worker must name a concrete error type, and an `@derive(Error)` enum with `@from` variants when it can fail two ways. A thread_shared cache of results and a wrapper with a boxed cause stay on one thread.

options.code:
## std unchanged; the compiler collects every error put into any AnyError anywhere in the program
fn load(path: StrView) -> Result[int]:
    ...
h = thread.spawn(owns fn() => load("level1.cfg"))
options.outcome: The worker compiles until a `?` anywhere in the program, even in code that never meets a thread, puts a one-thread error into an AnyError. From then on every spawn, channel or thread_shared holder of AnyError is refused, naming that distant line.

The worker compiles. Wrappers holding `owns dyn Error`, generic `needs Error` code, channels and shared caches of results compile with nothing written. An error type holding a one-thread part is refused where it implements Error (E2040 written, E2080 derived), with the words to write, even if it never leaves its thread. A generic error type's written implementation names its bound. This is Swift's choice: its Error refines Sendable.

The worker and the channel compile. AnyError is Send but not ThreadShared, so `cache = thread_shared ShaderCache()` holding `RwLock[Array[Result[int]]]` is E7015 at its line (verdict 165), and a `ref` to an error cannot reach a scoped task.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals. B fails 'easy to read and write': the ordinary worker grows a concrete error type, and an error enum when it can fail two ways. A fails it for error wrappers and generic error code, which need a second error interface and extra bounds. E keeps the worker but refuses a shared cache of results. C and D keep ordinary code as it is. 2. Safety: every option refuses before a one-thread value crosses, so none is preferred. 3. Compile time first: all are decided when compiling, but under C the answer for a spawn depends on code anywhere in the program. 4. A written word only for meaning: D writes the requirement once, where an error is defined. A writes it on AnyError's field, in pub generic bounds and in every wrapper. B writes concrete types. 5. The ordinary program no longer or harder: D refuses only an error holding a one-thread part, at its own line with the fix. C lets a far edit break a spawn. 6. Consistency: D uses THR-8's own spelling (`interface I: needs Send:`) with ODR-255, IFC-3 (a bound brings its parents), verdict 110's `needs`, verdict 61 (the type says which threads may have it; no whole-program search) and verdict 165 (refused where it is made). It keeps ERR-1, ERR-8 and ERR-9 true as written. So D.
decisions.departs_from_verdict: No owner verdict is departed from. It departs from phase 2's recommendation (A), which is not a verdict, for the reasons in parameters 1, 4 and 6.
decisions.recommendation: D. `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):`; nothing else is written in ordinary code.

owner_short.one_line: Should every error type be safe to hand to and read from any thread (like requiring every exception type to be thread-safe so a catch-all std::exception_ptr can always cross threads), so a worker thread can return the catch-all error?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | worker thread | a file read fails; `?` puts the error into the catch-all error | allowed, nothing written
2 | worker thread | returns the count or the catch-all error | allowed: every error may go to any thread
3 | main thread | `n = h.join()?` | gets the count, or passes the error on
4 | an error type's author | declares an error holding a one-thread shared owner | refused at that declaration, with the line to write (hold a copy)
owner_short.today: A worker returning the default error type is refused at the thread start, the text never says so, and the worker must name a concrete error type.
options: A: the catch-all checks each error where `?` puts it in; error wrappers holding a boxed cause, and generic code, need extra thread words and a second error interface
B: keep today: the catch-all stays on its thread; workers name their own error types
C: the compiler searches the whole program; one one-thread error anywhere breaks every hand-off far away
D: every error type is safe for every thread (Swift's choice), checked where the type is made an error
E: the catch-all may be sent but not read by two threads at once; a shared cache of results is refused
owner_short.recommendation: D: ordinary worker, wrapper and library error code compile with nothing written; only an error holding a one-thread part is refused, at its own line, with the fix.

decisions.title: What `@derive(Error)` on a generic error type covers once errors must be thread-safe
decisions.problem: A derived error on a generic type holding its T (`[T]` above `enum LoadError` with `Refused(item: T)`) is thread-safe for some T and not for others. The rules must decide whether the derive is refused, or covers only the thread-safe instances.

options.outcome: The library writes the bound on its type. `LoadError[shares Asset]` is then refused wherever it is written, even as a plain value that a one-thread program matches. Nothing changes meaning.

Nothing is written. `LoadError[int]` is an Error. `LoadError[shares Asset]` is a plain value with Display and Debug: a `?` of it into AnyError, or a `needs Error` bound, is E2040 naming the field. A `main` that returns it prints it without its `caused by:` lines.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. Goals: (b) writes nothing and keeps a generic error type usable with one-thread arguments as a plain value; (a) makes the library write a bound and refuses one-thread users outright. 2. Safety: equal; both refuse before a one-thread value enters an error. 3. Compile time: equal. 4. A written word only for meaning: (b) writes none. 5. The ordinary program: neither is harder for ordinary code, and (a) refuses a one-thread program that matches its own pool error. 6. Consistency: (b) is how derives already reach a generic type's instances (`@derive(Zeroable)` in tests/conformance/ARN-11, STR-5's derives, TYP-36's 'if T'). A written `extend[T]` still means 'for every T' (checklist 15), so it is refused without its bound. The cost of (b), a `main` returning a one-thread instance printing without its `caused by:` lines, is listed for the owner. So (b).
decisions.recommendation: b. A derived generic error is an Error for its thread-safe instances; a written one states its bound.

owner_short.one_line: When a generic error template (like `template<class T> struct PoolFull { T rejected; }`) is made an error by a derive, is it an error for a one-thread T?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | library author | derives the error on a generic error type holding its T | allowed, nothing written
2 | thread-safe user | uses it with a number | it is an error: `?` puts it into the catch-all
3 | one-thread user | uses it with a one-thread shared owner and matches it | allowed: it is a plain value
4 | one-thread user | `?` of it into the catch-all | refused at that line, naming the field
owner_short.today: Every instance is an error; nothing decides this once errors must be thread-safe.
options: (a) refuse the derive unless T is bounded to thread-safe types: the library writes one bound, and one-thread users cannot use the type at all
(b) the derive covers the thread-safe instances only, as other derives do; the one-thread instance stays a plain value, and a `main` returning it prints it without its 'caused by' lines
owner_short.recommendation: (b): nothing is written, more correct programs are accepted, as with every other derive; the one changed program prints one line less and is listed for you.

responses.objection: (Third round, regression) A generic error type that hands the caller's value back (`PoolFull[T]`) needs thread words under D, so the claim 'adds no word anywhere' is false, and the one-thread pool game (`Pool[shares Enemy]`, `fill(...)?`) is refused.
responses.how: The account is corrected. D writes `extend[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)]` once on a generic error type's written implementation (IFC-3, verdict 111; test generic_error_without_bound_refused). It writes nothing with `@derive(Error)` (decision 2). A pub generic `fill[T]` that `?`s `PoolFull[T]` into AnyError writes `[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)]` under D, exactly as it must under A (verdict 108), so the game is refused under both. Under D the game may still match its `PoolFull[shares Enemy]` as a plain value.

responses.objection: (Third round, undecided) `@derive(Error)` on `LoadError[T]` is undecided between a refusal and a silent change in what main prints.
responses.how: ERR-3's added sentence decides it: the derive covers the instances that are Send and ThreadShared (decision 2). `?` of `LoadError[shares Asset]` into AnyError is E2040 (test derived_generic_error_one_thread_instance). The one changed output, a main report without its `caused by:` line, is a listed trade-off with an exact test (main_report_of_a_one_thread_instance).

responses.objection: (Third round, cross-rule clash) ERR-3 and IV.8's declaration (p04 676) can disagree, so a test can be written to either.
responses.how: Both are edited in the same change (p13 87-88 and p04 676), with the same words. std/src/core.em line 80 follows after review.

responses.objection: A refuses fewer correct programs: a one-thread error that never goes into AnyError compiles under A and is refused under D.
responses.how: This is true. But such an error reaches AnyError in nearly every program (main returns `Result[void]`, ERR-9 p13 48, FN-8), and A refuses it there too. A also refuses every wrapper holding `owns dyn Error` and needs a second spelling for a Send dyn, against THR-8's one spelling (p11 51) and checklist 11. D's message gives a one-line fix (hold a copy).

responses.objection: An error that holds a raw pointer can no longer be an Error, because ThreadShared cannot be vouched (TYP-43 p04 592-593: ThreadShared written by hand is E2040).
responses.how: Listed for the owner. Under A such an error could not enter AnyError either. The pending vouch question (P04, J7-06) decides it for every type at once; until then the message gives a copy to hold (a String).

responses.objection: Requiring ThreadShared, not only Send, refuses an error that holds a Cell.
responses.how: With Send alone (option E), a thread_shared cache of results is refused where it is made (verdict 165), and a `ref` to an error cannot reach a scoped task (THR-8 p11 49: `ref T` is Send when T is ThreadShared). An error that changes itself while it is shown is not an ordinary error, and Rust's anyhow requires both markers for the same reason.

responses.objection: (Safety) An AnyError returned from a worker may own a class object that a weakref on the worker points at. The main thread then ends it while the worker's link counts with plain adds.
responses.how: THR-2 (p11 112-121) already says that at a hand-over, every object the handed object owns whose class a weakref is made to anywhere is checked (one compare). With a link, its contents move and the old block stays on the giving thread. The rule already applies to every `owns dyn I` with `I: needs Send` (tests/conformance/THR-8 moves `Box[dyn Shape]` to a thread). D adds no route, only more values on an existing one. That the check runs through the error's table is in to_verify.

responses.objection: (Contradiction) A written generic implementation is refused while a derived one covers its instances: two answers for one case.
responses.how: These are two declarations, each decided by its own words. A written `extend[T] PoolFull[T] implements Error` says 'for every T' and means what it says (OWNER-DIRECTION checklist 15; IFC-3). A derive writes no bounds and covers the instances its fields allow, as `@derive(Zeroable)` does (tests/conformance/ARN-11) and as STR-5's derives do. No program is decided two ways.

tests.name: error_wrapper_with_boxed_cause_crosses_threads
tests.program:
# a mesh importer's wrapper error returned from a worker; the danger in C++ terms: a
# std::unique_ptr<std::exception> holding any exception, moved to another thread
import std.thread
from std.fmt import Formatter, FmtError

struct ImportError:
    file: String

existing_rule.words: THR-8: "`dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs Send:`)". IFC-3: "`interface Ord: needs Eq` requires implementers of `Ord` to implement `Eq`. Once `Error` requires `Send` and `ThreadShared`, these existing words reach `dyn Error`, `AnyError` (a struct of `Box[dyn Error]`, `u128`, `Array[String]`, Send and ThreadShared when every component is), every `E: needs Error` and `type Failure: needs Error` bound, and every implementer, which must meet the parents.

An implementation of `Error` meets all four for every type it covers. One that does not is `E2040` where it implements `Error` (`E2080` at `@derive(Error)`, `[DRV-1]`). Its message names what in the type stays on one thread and the words to write: the error holds a copy of it, or the value is made `thread_shared`, or, for a type parameter, the bound `T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)`.

With nothing written, every place that names an error then carries it (IFC-3, a bound brings its parents): `E: needs Error`, `type Failure: needs Error`, a field `owns dyn Error`, and `AnyError` itself through THR-8's existing dyn clause. That covers every route at once: a thread's or task's result, a channel element, a job's data, a thread_shared holder, an `RwLock`, a `ref` given to a scoped task. There is one check, where a type is made an error, which is the one place its contents are known, and the existing marker rules decide every one-thread part (a shares owner, a weakref link, a sharedref mut link, a Cell) without a list of cases. "For every type it covers" also decides generic implementations, with no clause of their own. ERR-1's "any `E: needs Error`", ERR-8's `From` and ERR-9's "any error" stay true as written. The parents are spelled with `needs`, as verdict 110 spells them (the old `Display + Debug` spelling goes).
edits.why_here: This is the cause. `Error` is the interface every error is erased through, and it was the only one of the three rules (ERR-3, ERR-8, THR-8) that said nothing about threads. Putting the requirement on AnyError's `From` instead (option A) would leave `dyn Error` one-thread for every wrapper and generic bound, and would need a spelling for a dyn that carries markers, which the language does not have.
