decisions.title: Where the thread markers of an erased error come from
decisions.problem: AnyError is the default error type, and it holds any error behind `owns dyn Error`. By THR-8 it is one-thread unless `Error` requires Send, so a worker's `Result[int]`, a channel of results, a task's view of one and a thread_shared table of them are all refused. Making AnyError Send without a requirement would let an error holding a one-thread owner (a plain refcount) cross threads.

options.code:
pub struct AnyError:
    error: owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared   # a spelling the language does not have
extend[E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)] AnyError implements From[E]:
    ...
[S: needs Source]
pub fn count_lines(src: S) -> Result[int] where S.Failure: needs (Send, ThreadShared):
    text = src.read_all()?
options.outcome: The worker compiles. A one-thread error is refused at each `?` into AnyError, even with one thread. Generic error code and wrappers holding `owns dyn Error` must write thread words, and `source()` needs a conversion from a marked dyn to `dyn Error` that no rule states.

options.code: fn load(path: StrView) -> Result[int, io.Error]:   # today's rules
options.outcome: The `Result[int]` worker stays refused at the spawn line (E7015). A worker names a concrete error type, with an error enum when it can fail two ways.

options.code:
## std unchanged; the compiler collects every type converted into AnyError in the whole program
fn load(path: StrView) -> Result[int]:
options.outcome: The worker compiles until some `?` anywhere converts a one-thread error. From then on every spawn, channel and thread_shared holder of AnyError is refused, with a message naming a distant line. A library's `pub` function compiles or not depending on the importing program. This is the search verdict 61 turned down.

The worker, channels, task views and thread_shared holders of results compile. Generic `needs Error` code and `owns dyn Error` wrappers write nothing. An error type holding a one-thread part is refused where it implements Error (E2040, or E2080 at the derive), even if it never leaves its thread. A generic one writes `T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)`. This is Swift's choice (`Error` refines `Sendable`).

options.code: pub interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send):   # or the same bound on AnyError's From
options.outcome: Results may be sent, but AnyError is not ThreadShared: `ref r` to scoped tasks and `thread_shared Assets(sizes=RwLock([...]))` stay refused. In exchange it accepts error types that hold a Cell or a vouched raw pointer.

options.code:
## AnyError records whether its error may cross; every hand-over checks it while running
h = thread.spawn(owns fn() => load("level1.cfg"))   # stops the program if the error may not cross
options.outcome: Everything compiles. A one-thread error that reaches another thread stops the program at the hand-over, on the failure path. Each hand-over of an AnyError costs a compare, and a list of results costs a walk. Views given to scoped tasks and writes into thread_shared holders cannot be checked cheaply.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once. B fails 'easy to write': every worker grows its own error type, and an enum when it can fail two ways. A and E fail it for generic error code and wrappers, which grow thread words. C, D and F keep ordinary code as it is today. 2. Safety: A to E all refuse before a one-thread value crosses, and F stops the program. A also rests on a dyn conversion no rule states. D needs only THR-8's existing dyn clause. 3. Compile time first: A to E are decided when compiling. F runs a check at every hand-over, and the run time cannot make the refused program work: a shares owner inside the error cannot be moved away from its other owners, so F can only stop it. A compile-time refusal with a line to write therefore becomes a crash on the least-tested path, with a walk for every list of results (checklist 8). F is out. 4. A written word only for meaning: A and E write markers in bounds and after `dyn`, B writes a concrete error type, and C and D write nothing in ordinary code. D's only word is the bound on a generic error implementation, which states the library's promise (verdict 108). 5. The ordinary program no longer or harder: C lets an edit anywhere break a spawn far away. D refuses only an error type holding a one-thread part, at its own declaration, even in a one-thread program, and the fix is to hold a copy. Those are the same errors A refuses at their `?`, which nearly every error reaches because main returns `Result[void]`. 6. Consistency: D uses THR-8's own clause (a dyn is Send by what its interface requires), IFC-3 (a bound brings its parents), ODR-255, verdict 110's spelling, verdict 61 (the type says which threads may have it, which also rules out C), and verdict 165 (refused where it is made). It matches Swift (`Error: Sendable`) and Rust's anyhow (`Send + Sync`). So D.
decisions.recommendation: D: Error needs Debug, Display, Send and ThreadShared, so AnyError goes to and is read by any thread with nothing written. An error type holding a one-thread part is refused where it implements Error, with the line to write.

owner_short.one_line: Should every error type be safe to hand to and read from any thread (as Swift's errors are), so the catch-all error (like C++'s `std::exception_ptr`; Ember's `AnyError`) can come back from a worker thread?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | error type's author | declares an error of plain values (a code, a text) | allowed: it may go to any thread
2 | worker thread | `fs.read_to_string(path)?` puts the file error into the catch-all | allowed, nothing written
3 | worker thread | returns `Result[int]` (a count or the catch-all error) | allowed: every error may cross threads
4 | main thread | `n = h.join()?` | gets the count, or passes the error on
5 | error type's author | declares an error holding a one-thread shared owner | refused at that declaration: hold a copy instead
owner_short.today: The worker returning `Result[int]` is refused at `thread.spawn`, the text never says so, and the worker must name its own error type.
options: A: the catch-all checks each error where `?` puts it in; generic error code and error wrappers must add thread words
B: keep today: the catch-all stays on its thread; every worker names its own error type
C: the compiler searches the whole program; one one-thread error anywhere breaks every thread hand-off, far from that line
D: every error type is safe for every thread, checked where the type is declared an error; nothing written anywhere else
E: the catch-all may be sent but not read by two threads at once; a shared table of results is refused
F: check while running and stop the program when a one-thread error crosses
owner_short.recommendation: D: ordinary worker, server and library code compile with nothing written; only an error holding a one-thread part is refused, at its own line, with the fix.

decisions.problem: Under D, a generic error such as `PoolFull[T]` (like Rust's `SendError<T>`) is Send only when `T` is. The previous round found the text left open whether `extend[T] PoolFull[T] implements Error:` is refused or quietly holds only for some `T`.

    pass
## written without the bound: E2040 at this line, giving the line above

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: both are equal for ordinary code, because generic error types holding a caller's value are rare. 2. Safety: both are safe. 3. Compile time: both. 4. A written word only for meaning: the bound is the library's promise of which values it is an error for (verdicts 108, 111). 5. The ordinary program: unchanged. 6. Consistency: IFC-3 already says "requires implementers ... to implement" the parents, TYP-43 says a generic marker implementation "holds for each instance whose arguments meet the markers its parameters are bounded by", and verdict 132 says a declaration's meaning comes only from what it says. So (i), which ERR-3's words "for every type it covers" now state.
decisions.recommendation: (i): the generic implementation writes `T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)`; without it, the compiler refuses and gives that line.

owner_short.one_line: A generic error that hands the caller's value back (like `std::future_error` carrying a payload, or Rust's `SendError<T>`): is it an error for every `T`, or only for the `T`s any thread may have?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | library author | writes `extend[T] PoolFull[T] implements Error:` | refused, with the line to write
2 | library author | writes `extend[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)] PoolFull[T] implements Error:` | allowed
3 | program | `insert(...)?` with `PoolFull[int]` into the catch-all | allowed
4 | one-thread game | `insert(...)?` with `PoolFull[shares Enemy]` into the catch-all | refused at that line: name the error type instead
owner_short.today: Nothing says; the implementation covers every `T`, because errors need no thread markers today.
options: (i) the implementation writes the bound; without it, refused with the line to write
(ii) the implementation quietly holds only for the safe `T`s
owner_short.recommendation: (i): the line says what it means, and the compiler gives the line to write.

responses.objection: Previous round, hole 1 (regression): a generic error that hands the caller's value back (`PoolFull[T]`, std's `SendError[T]`) needs thread words under D, and a one-thread game whose pool holds `shares` owners is refused at its call. The claim that D 'adds no word anywhere' was false, so the owner would compare A and D on a wrong account.
responses.how: The account is now corrected in the readability verdict and in decision 2. D writes `T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)` on such an implementation, and nothing anywhere else. The one-thread game's `pool.insert(owns x)?` into AnyError is refused under D and under A alike: `pub fn fill[T]` must write the same bound (IFC-6), and main's call with `T = shares Enemy` is E2040. A additionally writes thread words in every pub generic function forwarding a `needs Error` error, which is far more common than generic error types holding a caller's value. The game's fix is to name the error type (`-> Result[void, PoolFull[T]]`; main's error then needs only Display, ERR-12) or to keep handles in the pool. The trade-off is kept by parameters 4 and 5.

responses.objection: Previous round, hole 2 (undecided): `@derive(Error)` on a generic `enum LoadError[T]` with `Refused(item: T)` is left between a refusal and a silent per-instance implementation.
responses.how: ERR-3's new words, "An implementation of `Error` meets all four for every type it covers", decide it. With DRV-1's existing words (p14 136, "A derive whose requirement a field does not meet is `E2080`, naming the field"), the derive is E2080 naming `Refused.item`, with the help `[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)]` above `enum LoadError:`. It is never quietly per instance (verdict 132). Whether derives on generic types bound their parameters in general is a gap that exists today for Debug and Hash too, and is listed in the notes for later.

responses.objection: Previous round, hole 3 (cross-rule clash): ERR-3 was changed while IV.8's declaration (p04 676) still said `needs (Debug, Display)`, so two rules decided one program differently.
responses.how: p04-types.md 676 is edited in the same change to `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):`. std/src/core.em line 80 is in to_verify.

responses.objection: Critic's note on the input: the chosen design refuses a one-thread error even in a program with one thread; state that cost.
responses.how: This is stated in programs_changed, the decision and the editor sibling. Such a type is refused where it implements Error, even in a one-thread program. It can still be a `Result` error shown with Display, and the fix is a copy or `thread_shared`. A run-time check (F) would accept it but cannot make a crossing one safe (it can only stop the program, on the failure path), and C's whole-program search makes the default error's markers depend on distant code. Swift took D.

responses.objection: Parameter 3 says run time only where compile time would refuse correct programs, and D refuses correct one-thread programs, so the run-time option F should win.
responses.how: Parameter 3 sends the decision to run time where run time can make the correct program work, as verdict 114 moves the object so that nothing stops. Here it cannot: a shares owner inside an error that crosses threads keeps its other owners on this thread, so F can only stop the program at the hand-over. That is a crash on the failure path where a refusal with a line to write is possible (checklist 8). F also needs a walk for each list of results handed over, and checks that cannot be made cheap for views given to scoped tasks and writes into thread_shared holders, so it is not the cheapest way either.

out.notes:
Previous round (v3 test2) chose the same direction (D) but was left unresolved with three holes. This revision answers each of them in `responses`: the cost accounting for generic errors is corrected, the generic derive and extend are decided by ERR-3's 'for every type it covers', and IV.8's declaration is edited with ERR-3. Option F (a run-time check) is added so that parameter 3 is visibly weighed.

Existing gaps found on the way, not caused by this change, listed for later:
(1) Whether a derive on a generic type bounds its parameters or refuses (DRV-1, p14 136). This already applies to Debug and Hash; read as written, a field of type T that fails the derive's requirement is E2080.
(2) Verdict 114's hand-over check through any `owns dyn I` whose interface needs Send. THR-2's words ('every object the handed object owns') cover it, but the table mechanism is not stated.
(3) A ThreadShared vouch for types holding raw pointers (P04, J7-06). Until it is settled, an error type holding a raw pointer cannot be an Error.
(4) The p04 marker table rows for Send and ThreadShared (577-578) do not mention dyn. THR-8 and THR-9 decide it.
(5) std/src/thread.em still uses the old spawn signature (implementation, not spec).

Precedents: Swift's `Error` refines `Sendable` (SE-0302); Rust's anyhow::Error requires `Send + Sync + 'static`.

All work was read-only. The repository's start-up reading (AUTOPILOT, HANDOFF) was skipped, as the team rules direct.

checked: ERR-3 as changed (p13 88) with IV.8's declaration (p04 676): every implementation of Error is checked for Send and ThreadShared where it implements Error, and for every type it covers. Generic implementations are refused unless bounded, which is safe. @derive(Error) gives E2080 by DRV-1 (p14 138). A raw-pointer type vouched only for Send is refused as an Error, which is the safe direction (TYP-43, p04 587-593).

THR-8's dyn clause (p11 51) and the clause added to THR-9 (p11 63-64): a dyn is Send and ThreadShared only by what its interface requires. A sub-interface of Error brings both through IFC-3 (p05 411-413). Whether a generic implementation of a user interface that needs markers is refused or applies only to some instances, the result is safe either way, because IFC-3 'requires implementers ... to implement' the parents. shares dyn I and shares mut dyn I (IFC-5, p05 430-432) stay one-thread owners.

Class hierarchies: open classes (CLS-4, p05 335), implicit upcast (TYP-5 rule 8, p04 84-86), nominal implementations (TYP-40, p04 478-481), and the order of destruction (CLS-6, p05 353-355). This finds objection 1, a block S.

THR-2's hand-over move (verdict 114, p11 112-122) for class error objects inside an AnyError's box, and the view-across-hand-over rule (RC-5 point 1, p08 196-204, which covers 'owns dyn I whose value's state owns one'). Both are covered on hand-over routes. The thread_shared-holder route, which this change opens for AnyError, bypasses the move: objection 2, a gap that exists today.
@cached methods (CLS-12, p05 376-381; p10 339) on error classes read through a ThreadShared dyn by several threads: objection 3, a missing impact entry.

Cell inside an error (CELL-1, p09 442-444; CELL-3, p09 449): it is not ThreadShared, so the derive is refused (test). Setting a Cell needs a name that may change its holder, so it cannot be set through a shared ref anyway.

Methods called through ref dyn Error that change `this` are refused through read-only names (E3023, TYP-4 resolution step 3 at p04 860-863; DSP-5 at p08 313-316, every implementation counted). No race through a ThreadShared AnyError without a ThreadShared interior.

Making, ending or opening a weakref link to an object inside an AnyError from a scoped task or a thread: refused for a target that is not thread_shared (THR-2, p11 107-110; THR-11, p11 405-406; WK-11, p08 338-339).
Drops on another thread: EFF-24 (p10 96-97) counts the drops of owns dyn I state, and THR-20 (p11 296-301) gives E7012 for main-thread module variables reached by a drop that may run elsewhere.

Views inside errors (TYP-15, p04 311-317; TYP-34, p04 303-305): an AnyError holding a view lives no longer than the view, and THR-2 (p11 105-106) keeps it from unscoped threads. Any gap here exists today for every view type.
thread_shared owners inside errors travelling inside another object (RC-4 points 4-5, p08 173-182): designed for.

sharedref mut: verdict 164 is not yet in THR-8's or THR-9's text (p11 43-68), so the change's claim that an error holding one 'is not Send' rests on a verdict waiting for the next hardening. This is K01 and exists today.
Channel ends: THR-15 (p11 336-337) makes Sender and Receiver Send with no condition on the element (J7-07), so the impact's 'before' for the server program is not what the text says: objection 4.
Memory managers (`using`, TYP-46): an error holding arena memory freed on another thread is P02 and exists today. CppError holds strings only (annex C p21 100-101).

Safety guarantees of today's specification removed by the change: none found. ERR-1, ERR-8, ERR-9, ERR-12, THR-2, THR-8 and THR-10 keep their words. Every refusal the change adds is in the safe direction.
The change's ten tests: none of them lets a one-thread value cross. Their expected results are consistent with the changed words.

previous.objection: Previous round, hole 1: the cost account for generic errors that hold the caller's value (PoolFull[T]) was wrong.
previous.why: On the safety side, the bounded `extend[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)]` and the refusal of the unbounded line mean no instance with a one-thread T becomes an Error. The account is now corrected in the readability verdict and in decision 2.

previous.objection: Previous round, hole 2: @derive(Error) on a generic enum with a T payload was left between a refusal and a quiet per-instance implementation.
previous.why: ERR-3's new words 'meets all four for every type it covers', with DRV-1's 'A derive whose requirement a field does not meet is E2080, naming the field' (p14 138), decide it as a refusal. That is safe.

previous.objection: Previous round, hole 3: ERR-3 was changed while IV.8's declaration (p04 676) was not.
previous.why: p04 676 is edited in the same change, so the two say the same thing.

objections.walk:
The danger in C++ terms: a derived exception class holds a non-atomic refcounted pointer, and a base-class std::exception_ptr carries it to another thread.
(1) Line 17, `extend GameError implements Error:`. The changed ERR-3 (p13 88) says "An implementation of `Error` meets all four for every type it covers. One that does not is `E2040` where it implements `Error`". GameError's components are its written fields, `code: int`. THR-8 (p11 47-48) says "class objects are `Send` when every component is". THR-9 (p11 63-64) says "Structural types are `ThreadShared` when every component is". TYP-43 (p04 583) says "`Send` and `ThreadShared` are inferred from what a type holds, which its words say". Debug is given for class objects (TYP-36 table, p04 716), and Display is line 13. So line 17 passes.
(2) Line 20, `class DocError(GameError):`, with `doc: shares Doc` on line 21. CLS-4 (p05 335) lets an open class be subclassed. TYP-40 (p04 478-479) says "A type implements an interface only through an `implements` clause or an `extend … implements` block", and DocError writes neither. So no implementation of Error is at line 20, ERR-3's check has nothing to check there, and no other rule checks a derived class against what its base implements. Line 20 compiles.
(3) Line 29: TYP-5 rule 8 (p04 86) allows "a class object to a base class (upcast)". The `Err` holds a GameError value that is a DocError object owning a second owner of main's Doc.
(4) Line 33: ERR-2 (p13 51-52) says `?` "returns `Err(F.from(err))`". ERR-8 (p13 95) says AnyError "implements `From[E]` for every `E: needs Error`", here with E = GameError, so the AnyError holds an `owns dyn Error` (p13 94) of that DocError object.
(5) Line 38: THR-10 (p11 175) takes a `thread_shared fn()`, which by THR-1 (p11 86-87) "holds only `thread_shared` owners, values handed over to it and copies". `r` is handed over (`owns r`, THR-17 p11 185). r's type is Result[int, AnyError]. AnyError's `owns dyn Error` is Send by THR-8 (p11 51), "`dyn I` when `I` requires it", because Error now needs Send (p04 676, after the change). Nothing in the type the compiler sees holds a `shares`, so line 38 compiles.
(6) The thread ends `r`. CLS-6 (p05 353-354) says "Destruction runs the derived `drop`, then the base's, then ends the fields", so DocError's `doc` ends on the worker. RC-4 (p08 155-156) says the counts of a value that is not thread_shared "are changed with plain adds and subtracts, and never cross threads". That is a plain -1 on the worker, while lines 40-41 do a plain +1 and -1 on main at the same time. A lost update either leaks the Doc, or lets its count reach 0 while `other` still reads it: `other.path` is then read after it is freed, and the last end frees it a second time.
Today the same program is E7015 at line 38. Error needs only Debug and Display (p13 88, p04 676), so by p11 51 `dyn Error` is not Send and neither is r. The change makes `dyn Error` Send on the strength of a check that never sees derived classes.
If instead an implementation for GameError is read as covering every GameError object, DocError's included, ERR-3 puts the refusal "where it implements Error", which is line 17. When GameError is a `pub open class` in a library compiled before a program subclasses it, line 17 cannot be refused, and the program's line 20 is checked by nothing.
The same gap in THR-8's class clause lets `owns b` of a plain `b: GameError` that holds a DocError reach a thread today, and also an `owns dyn Job` with `interface Job: needs Send:`. The change makes the gap reach the default error type of every program. It also states as its premise "There is one check, where a type is made an error, which is the one place its contents are known", which is false for an open class: derived classes add contents later, possibly in other packages.
objections.impact: A use-after-free and a double free of a one-thread shared value, through the default error type, in a program that writes no thread word beyond `thread.spawn`. Any open error class (a game's `GameError` base with subclasses per subsystem is ordinary) lets a subclass with a `shares`, `weakref`, `sharedref mut` or `Cell` field into every AnyError that crosses threads. The ThreadShared half breaks the same way: a Cell or a one-thread count in a subclass, read through `ref r` by scoped tasks or through a thread_shared RwLock.
objections.suggestion: Fix it at the cause, what a class object holds, as a property: the fields of every class derived from a class are among that class's components, because a value of an open class may be any of them. So a derived class is one of the types its base's implementations cover. A class derived from one that implements an interface needing Send or ThreadShared (Error among them) meets those markers too, checked where the derived class is declared. Here that is E2040 at line 20 naming `doc`, with the copy to write. This is the change's own 'for every type it covers', with the derived class named as a covered type and the refusal placed at the derived class's line, which every package can check. Swift's precedent is stricter (a non-final class cannot conform to Sendable). Checking each subclass keeps open classes and still refuses only the class that holds the one-thread part. The same property closes the existing gap for a plain open-class value captured by a thread.

objections.walk:
The danger in C++ terms: a weak_ptr's control block is updated without atomics while another thread destroys the object it points at.
The change relies on verdict 114 for class errors (cost: "THR-2's existing hand-over check ... reaches objects the boxed error owns ... through the error's table"). THR-2 (p11 112-114) runs that check only when "An object handed whole to another thread leaves its `weakref` links behind ... At the hand-over the program reads the object's weak count".
Line 31, `thread_shared Log(...)`. THR-1 (p11 69-72) allows thread_shared before a new value. Its check that "everything reachable from it is `Send`" (p11 82) passes, because AnyError is Send after the change (p11 51; p04 676 after). Verdict 165's ThreadShared check passes, because THR-9 (p11 66) makes "`Mutex[T]` for a `Send` `T`" ThreadShared. Nothing is handed to a thread at this line: the object is moved into a new value. So THR-2's move does not run, and `w` still points at the LoadError object, which the worker can now reach through the Mutex.
Line 32: the worker gets one more owner of `log` (THR-17, p11 186). On the worker, `g.clear()` (line 26) ends the LoadError object: OBJ-3 (p08 83-86) runs its field drops, which free `path`'s String, and decrements its weak count. RC-4 (p08 155-156) says that count is changed with plain adds and subtracts.
Lines 33-34 on main: WK-12 (p08 346-348) says opening the link "tests the target's header". RC-5 point 1 (p08 196-204) checks only lines and calls of this thread. RC-5 point 2 (p08 215) counts only for "A view of a `thread_shared` object". So main tests the header and reads `p.path` while the worker ends the object and frees the String: a data race on the weak count, and a read after free.
Not caused by the change: the same program with `class Enemy` in a `Mutex[Array[Enemy]]` (Enemy is Send by its fields, p11 47-48) compiles today and goes wrong the same way. The change routes the default error type through this route (its game sibling is exactly this shape) while counting on verdict 114's check, which does not run here.
objections.impact: A use-after-free reached by storing a result into a lock of a thread_shared object while a link on this thread points at the error object. It is the same for any class object in a thread_shared container today.
objections.suggestion: This is a gap for the list, in THR-2, not a reason to block this change. The property: an object becomes reachable from another thread by any route THR-2 already lists (handed over, sent, or stored into a thread_shared value or a lock of one), and by any such route it leaves its weakref links behind, as verdict 114's hand-over does: one compare at that line. With that, line 31 moves the object, `w` finds it ended, and the program prints `done`. Also correct the change's cost line, which currently implies verdict 114 covers every route a boxed error takes to another thread.

objections.walk:
The danger in C++ terms: a lazily filled `mutable std::string` cache inside an exception's what(), read from two threads.
CLS-12 (p05 376-380) says a @cached method "keeps the method's result after the first call ... any other as a `ref T` view into the kept value ... On an object several threads reach, the kept result is filled once under a once-flag". The cost table (p10 339) says the same.
LoadError's fields are a String, so it is Send and ThreadShared (p11 47-48, 63-64), and line 15 passes the changed ERR-3. AnyError is ThreadShared by the added THR-9 clause (p11 63-64 after) with p04 676 after. So `ref r` reaches two scoped tasks (THR-17, p11 196-199; THR-8, p11 49: `ref T` is Send when T is ThreadShared). Both tasks run LoadError.fmt through the error's table on the same object, and the first call fills the kept String.
Whether 'several threads reach' a LoadError object has to be decided where `message` is compiled. No line of thread code names LoadError, only AnyError. Before the change no dyn was ThreadShared in the text, so an object behind `dyn Error` was never read by two threads. After it, every object of every Error class may be.
Read as written, CLS-12 requires the once-flag, so the words decide the case. But the change's impact says "Run time: nothing is added" and lists no such duty. A compiler that decides 'several threads reach' from the concrete type's own uses fills the cache with a plain flag: two tasks store into one place, and one frees the String whose `ref` view the other is reading.
objections.impact: The program must print 68. With a plain flag it has a data race and a read after free. The once-flag is a run-time cost per call of every @cached method on an error class (and on any class behind a ThreadShared dyn), and the change does not state it.
objections.suggestion: State the duty and its cost in the impact as a property of the type: an object of a type that may be reached through a ThreadShared dyn (every implementer of an interface that requires ThreadShared, every Error) is 'an object several threads reach' for CLS-12. Its @cached methods are filled under the once-flag. To measure: the time of one @cached call on an error class with the once-flag against a plain flag.

objections.walk:
The danger in C++ terms: a non-atomic refcount (an Rc-like shared_ptr) pushed through a thread-safe queue to another thread.
The change's impact gives, for its server program, "before: E7015 at the spawn line (the Sender holds AnyErrors, which are not Send)", and its sibling relies on "a Sender is Send when its element is". The text does not say that. THR-15 (p11 336-337) says "`Sender` is `Send`, `ThreadShared` and `Clone` ... `Receiver` is `Send`", with no condition on the element.
So in this program, line 19 hands `rx` (a Receiver, Send by p11 337) to a thread. Each `shares doc` sent on line 15 is a one-thread owner, which the worker ends with a plain -1 (RC-4, p08 155-156) while main makes the next owner with a plain +1: a data race on the count, and then a read after free of `d.path`. This compiles today. It is J7-07, the group's open lead fix, and it exists without the change. The change does close it for AnyError, by accident, since AnyError becomes Send.
objections.impact: The change's 'before' column claims a refusal where today's text has a hole. The owner would read the server case as safe today when it is not. The change does not add any risk here.
objections.suggestion: Correct the server row's 'before' to: "compiles by THR-15's words (Sender and Receiver are Send whatever the element); the J7-07 fix (a channel end is Send only for a Send element) is what makes it E7015". Keep J7-07 on the list.

outs.notes:
I am the safety engineer. I read RULES-FOR-THE-TEAM.md and OWNER-DIRECTION.md in full, and the K20 input in full. In the part files I read: p13 (all), p11 (all), p04 (IV.6, IV.6a, IV.7, IV.8, IV.9 dyn, IV.11), p05 (FN-1 words, CLS-1 to CLS-12, IFC-1 to IFC-6, STA-1), p08 (OBJ, RC-1 to RC-5, DSP-5/6, WK-1 to WK-17), p09 (CELL-1 to CELL-3), p10 (EFF-1, EFF-2, EFF-4, EFF-24 to EFF-27, cost table) and p14 (DRV-1), plus the ODR-255 and ODR-050 rows in p26. All work was read-only, and I skipped the repository's start-up reading as the team rules direct.

Result. The change removes no safety guarantee of today's specification. Its refusals (shares, weakref, Cell, unbounded generics, raw pointers vouched only for Send) all fall on the safe side, and the ThreadShared half is decided by THR-9's added clause.

One block S: objection 1, open classes. The change makes `dyn Error`, and so AnyError, Send and ThreadShared on the strength of a check made 'where a type is made an error'. A class derived from an open error class adds fields that check never sees. Upcast to the base and `?` then put a one-thread owner into an AnyError that crosses threads, giving a use-after-free and a double free of a non-atomic count. The same program is E7015 today. The underlying gap in THR-8's class clause also exists today for a direct capture of an open-class value and for `owns dyn Job` with `interface Job: needs Send:`. The fix is a property: a derived class is one of the types its base's implementations cover, checked where the derived class is declared.

Not blocking:
- Objection 2: a gap that exists today. Verdict 114's move does not run when an object is stored into a thread_shared holder; the change relies on that move and opens this route for AnyError.
- Objection 3: the impact omits the @cached once-flag duty for error classes reached through a ThreadShared dyn. CLS-12's words decide the case, but the cost of nothing added is untrue.
- Objection 4: the server row's 'before' contradicts THR-15's words. That is J7-07, which exists today.

For to_verify:
- The 'one indirect call per AnyError handed over' must be emitted at every hand-over site in a library compiled without the final program (EFF-4). So 'Nothing runs in a program where no error type ... owns such an object' holds only for whole-program builds.
- Verdict 164's sharedref mut wording is not yet in THR-8 or THR-9, and the change's claim for that field kind rests on it.

objections.walk: A renderer error hands back the shape it refused, as SendError hands back its value. Today it compiles and prints 9. After the change, ERR-3 (p13 88, new words) requires Send and ThreadShared. The field is `owns dyn Shape`, and THR-8 (p11 48) makes 'an `owns T` [Send] when `T` is'. THR-8 (p11 51) makes '`dyn I` [Send] when `I` requires it', and the new THR-9 clause says the same for ThreadShared. `Shape` requires only `Debug`, so the result is E2080 at line 11 (DRV-1, p14 138). ERR-3's new message words are a closed list: 'the error holds a copy of it, or the value is made `thread_shared`, or, for a type parameter, the bound `T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)`'. None of the three compiles here. (a) A copy: TYP-36 (p04 690) makes `owns dyn I` Clone only 'when `I` requires `Clone`', and the copy would again be an `owns dyn Shape`, still not Send. (b) `thread_shared`: THR-8 (p11 50) makes 'a `thread_shared T` ... [Send] when `T` is `Send` and `ThreadShared`', and `dyn Shape` is neither. (c) There is no type parameter. A plain `fn()` field is a fourth case the list does not cover, because THR-8 (p11 51-52) says that of the function types only `thread_shared fn()` is Send. The lines that do compile are `interface Shape: needs (Debug, Send, ThreadShared):` in place of line 1, or holding what the error reports (`TooLarge(area: int)`). OWNER-DIRECTION's checklist 9 ('Does every message give a line that compiles?') and principle 12 require such a line.
objections.impact: Errors that hold an interface value are refused, and their message offers no line that compiles. The impact report also misses this case. The readability verdict says 'Words are added in only one place: a generic error implementation', but here the words go on the interface `Shape`. Every implementer of `Shape` in the program then must be Send and ThreadShared: a `Sprite` holding `texture: shares Texture` becomes E2040 at its `implements Shape`. So one error's thread requirement spreads to an unrelated interface. Under option A, only a `?` into AnyError is refused, and a one-thread renderer that matches `Result[int, DrawError]` compiles. programs_changed should say this, so that the owner compares A and D on a correct account. That was the point of the previous round's hole 1.
objections.suggestion: Replace the closed list in ERR-3's message words with the property: 'Its message names the part that is not Send or ThreadShared and gives a line that compiles: one that makes that part meet them by the rule that decides it ([THR-8], [THR-9]), or one that holds a copy of what the error reports.' Add to programs_changed: an error holding `owns dyn I`, or a plain `fn()`, whose interface or type does not require the markers. Before the change it compiles. After it is E2080 at the derive, and the fix either goes on the interface (constraining every implementer) or holds a copy of the data. Correct the readability verdict's 'only one place' to say so.

objections.walk: Today this compiles and prints `the document is read-only`. After the change it is E2080 at line 4, because a `shares mut` owner is neither Send nor ThreadShared (THR-8 p11 44-46, THR-9 p11 64-65). ERR-3's new words offer 'or the value is made `thread_shared`'. Following that offer gives `doc = thread_shared Doc()`, and then line 11 (`doc.path = String("notes.em")`) is E7014: THR-1 (p11 77) says 'no owner changes a `thread_shared` value directly'. The message would then lead into another error. Verdict 73 (OWNER-DIRECTION principle 12) says a rule 'is supposed to tell how to fix an issue not how to run into another'.
objections.impact: In an editor or game where the object is changed directly, an offered fix sends the programmer into E7014. Making a document `thread_shared` also changes the whole program's ownership model, just to report an error.
objections.suggestion: This is decided by the same property as objection 1: the message gives only lines that compile. `thread_shared` is offered only where no line changes the value directly; otherwise the message offers the copy of what the error reports (`ReadOnly(path: String)` in place of line 7, `e = SaveError.ReadOnly(path=copy of doc.path)` in place of line 12).

objections.walk: The change's answer to hole 2 reads ERR-3's new 'An implementation of `Error` meets all four for every type it covers' with DRV-1 (p14 138: 'A derive whose requirement a field does not meet is `E2080`, naming the field'). The result is that `@derive(Error)` on a generic type with a `T` field is E2080 at line 3, and the help writes `[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)]` above `enum SpawnError:`. This program only ever uses `SpawnError[int]`, yet it is refused. Everywhere else, the language decides a derive on a generic type per instance. STR-5 (p05 239-240): 'A struct or enum implements `Eq`, `Debug` and `Clone` field-wise, automatically, when every field implements the interface'. ODR-027 (p26 315): the range types are '`Copy` when the bound is', which std writes as `@derive(Copy)` above `[T] pub struct Range` (std/src/core.em 1845-1853). By the change's reading, that `@derive(Copy)` would also be E2080 naming `start`. The help also bounds the type itself, not the implementation. `SpawnError[shares Enemy]` could then not be written even as a Display-only `Result` error, which decision 2's (i) keeps legal (there only the implementation is bounded).
objections.impact: Derives on generic types get two rules: per instance for Copy, Eq, Debug and Clone, refused for Error. The help line changes what the type may hold, not only where it is an Error. A generic error enum used only with plain values is refused. The notes list 'whether a derive on a generic type bounds its parameters' as an existing gap (1), but the answer to hole 2 settles that gap for Error alone, and in the opposite direction from STR-5 and ODR-027.
objections.suggestion: Use one property for every derive (DRV-1). A derive on a generic type implements the interface for the instances whose fields meet the derive's requirement, as STR-5 and ODR-027 already do. Its generated `extend` writes those needs, which `ember inspect --expand` prints (DRV-1 p14 138-139). E2080 stays for a field whose own written type fails the requirement. A `?` of a `SpawnError[shares Enemy]` into AnyError is then E2040 at the `?`, and its message names the derive's needs. A hand-written unbounded `extend[T] X[T] implements Error:` stays refused under decision 2's (i), because there the programmer's own declaration says 'every T' (verdict 132). List the DRV-1 wording beside the D question, because it settles gap (1) for every derive.

objections.walk: After the change, p04 676 and p13 88 declare `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):`. IFC-3 (p05 411-412, 'a bound brings its parents') gives `E` the Send that the spawn's `owns e` capture needs (THR-8, THR-10), so the program compiles and prints `connection reset`. TYP-17 (p04 457-459) still quotes the declaration as 'an interface's parents (`interface Error: needs (Debug, Display):`)'. Read with that declaration, `E` has only Debug and Display. The `pub` function must then write its bound (IFC-6 p05 449-453), and line 10 is E2040. Two texts give `Error` different parents, which is the shape of the previous round's hole 3, at another line.
objections.impact: A reader of the generics chapter learns the wrong parents for `Error`, and the two texts decide this program differently. The fix is one line.
objections.suggestion: Edit p04 459 to the new declaration, or take another interface for the spelling example, such as `interface IndexMut[Idx]: needs Index[Idx]:` from p04 670.

objections.program:
import std.thread

interface Command: needs (Send, ThreadShared):
    fn name() -> String

struct Quit:
    code: int

extend Quit implements Command:
    fn name() -> String:
        return String("quit")

fn main():
    cmds: Array[owns dyn Command] = [owns Quit(code=0)]
    total = 0
    with scope = thread.scope():
        for c in cmds:
            scope.spawn(owns fn() ref c: total += c.name().len())
    println(total)
objections.walk: The new THR-9 clause decides this program: `ref c` reaches a scoped task only if `owns dyn Command` is ThreadShared (THR-8 p11 49). It reads: '... and `dyn I` when `I` requires it, which an interface writes among its needs as a bound does (`interface I: needs (Send, ThreadShared):`, `[THR-8]`, ODR-255)'. The relative clause 'which an interface writes among its needs as a bound does' attaches to `dyn I` when read aloud, but it is meant to say that an interface's parent list counts as a bound under THR-9's 'written only in bounds' (p11 60). That is already settled elsewhere. TYP-17 (p04 457-459) lists 'an interface's parents' among the places a `needs` list is written. THR-8 (p11 51) already writes `interface I: needs Send:` under the same 'written only in bounds' (p11 53-54).
objections.impact: A rule sentence becomes hard to read and decides nothing more. The program's outcome (it prints 4) is the same either way.
objections.suggestion: Write: 'Structural types are `ThreadShared` when every component is, and `dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs (Send, ThreadShared):`), as for `Send` (`[THR-8]`, ODR-255).'

outs.notes:
I agree with D and with decision 2's (i) for a hand-written `extend[T]`, judged on the owner's parameters. Neither ordinary nor generic `needs Error` code writes a word, everything is decided at compile time, and the design matches Swift's Error: Sendable and anyhow's Send + Sync. I found no safety hole, so nothing is blocked. My five objections are all weighed.
(1) The ERR-3 message list gives no compiling line for an error that holds an `owns dyn I`, and the account of words added misses this case: the words go onto the interface, and from there to every implementer.
(2) The `thread_shared` offer can lead to E7014.
(3) The answer to hole 2 decides derives on generic types for Error in the opposite direction from STR-5 and ODR-027 (std's `@derive(Copy)` above `[T] Range`), and its help bounds the type itself.
(4) p04 459 still quotes the old declaration of Error.
(5) THR-9's added clause is hard to read.

Existing gaps found on the way, not caused by the change:
(a) p17a-codes.md 71 describes E2080 only for `@derive(Copy)`, while DRV-1 (p14 138) uses it for every derive.
(b) Through EFF-2's whole-program reading of dyn, an Error implementer's `drop` that touches a main-thread `static mut` already makes any thread that drops an AnyError E7012 (THR-20). That is a distant-line refusal that exists today, because workers already make and drop AnyErrors.
(c) std's SendError[T] (std/src/sync.em 122-127) implements no Error, so `tx.send(...)?` into AnyError is refused today and stays refused. Decision 2 cites it as an analogy, not as a std change.

All work was read-only, using Read, Grep and `sed -n`/`cat`/`grep` in a shell. I skipped the repository's start-up reading, as the team rules direct.

import std.thread

interface Command: needs (Send, ThreadShared):
    fn run() -> int

[T]
struct Echo:
    payload: T

extend[T] Echo[T] implements Command:
    fn run() -> int:

objections.walk: The property that decides decision 2 is written as a fact about one interface. p13-errors.md 88 (after): "An implementation of `Error` meets all four for every type it covers. One that does not is `E2040` where it implements `Error`". Those words reach only Error. The general rule is IFC-3 (p05-declarations.md 411-412): "`interface Ord: needs Eq` requires implementers of `Ord` to implement `Eq`. So a bound brings its parents". IFC-3 says what implementers must meet. It does not say whether a generic implementation that meets the parents for only some `T` is refused or holds per instance, and no other rule says it (grep of p04/p05/p14 for 'parent': only p04 458 and p05 412). The change's own THR-9 edit (p11 63-64 after) presents `interface I: needs (Send, ThreadShared):` as the way to write such an interface. In the program, line 10 `extend[T] Echo[T] implements Command:` covers every `T`, but `Echo[T]` is Send and ThreadShared only when `T` is (p11 47-48, "Structs ... are `Send` when every component is"; p11 63-64). ERR-3 does not reach `Command`, and IFC-3 decides nothing. TYP-43 (p04 591-592) states the per-instance reading for generic marker vouches ("holds for each instance whose arguments meet the markers its parameters are bounded by"), which a reader may carry over. out.intent: Load a level file on a worker thread and give the main thread either its length or the reason it failed, using the language's default error type (`Result[int]`).

cause.where: Three places, one property each. (1) The definition of `Error`: IV.8's declaration (p04-types.md 676, `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display):`), which ERR-3 describes (p13-errors.md 87-88) and TYP-17 quotes (p04 459). (2) What an object of an `open` or `abstract` class holds: THR-8's list sentence (p11-concurrency.md 47-48, "class objects are `Send` when every component is") and the marker table (p04 577, "a class object is when its fields are") count only the fields of the object's declared class. That is narrower than THR-8's own definition (p11 43-45, "nothing reachable from it ... is a one-thread owner"), because an object of an open class may be an object of any class derived from it (TYP-5 rule 8, p04 86). THR-9 (p11 63-64) has the same gap, and it has no words for a `dyn` either. (3) IFC-3 (p05 411-413) says that implementers meet an interface's parents, but not that an implementation meets them for every type it covers, which takes in each instance of a generic implementation and each derived class.
cause.why_there: Every error is erased through `Error`: `dyn Error`, the box inside `AnyError` (ERR-8), and so the default error type of every `Result[T]` (ERR-9). THR-8's dyn clause is right as it stands (`dyn I` is Send only when `I` requires it). `Error` requires no thread markers, so every erased error is a one-thread value, and the default `Result[T]` cannot leave its thread by any route. ERR-8's `From`, THR-2's routes and THR-10 are each right as written. The missing words belong in what an error is. Once `Error` requires the markers, the requirement is only as sound as the markers of what an error holds. For a class, THR-8's list and the p04 row read the markers from the declared class alone. So a `GameError` that implements `Error` would be judged Send while one of its objects is a `DocError` holding a `shares` owner. That gap already exists for a plain open-class value handed to a thread. The change would carry it into every AnyError. So the class wording is part of the cause. It has to say what THR-8's definition already says. IFC-3 is where the language says what an implementation promises about its interface's parents, so the rule for generic implementations and derived classes goes there, once for every interface, and not in ERR-3 as a case of `Error`.
cause.reported_at: ERR-3, ERR-8, THR-2, THR-8 (it shows through THR-10's "`R` MUST be `Send`", p11 175-176)

existing_rule.rule: THR-8 (its definition and its dyn clause), with IFC-3
existing_rule.words: THR-8: "A type is **`Send`** when a value of it may be handed over to another thread: nothing reachable from it (its fields, its elements, what its `owns` parts hold, a function value's state) is a one-thread owner (`shares T`, `shares mut T`), a `weakref` link to a value that is not `thread_shared`, or bound to the thread that made it" and "`dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs Send:`)". IFC-3: "`interface Ord: needs Eq` requires implementers of `Ord` to implement `Eq`. So a bound brings its parents". Once `Error` requires `Send` and `ThreadShared`, these words reach `dyn Error` and `AnyError` (a struct of `Box[dyn Error]`, `u128` and `Array[String]`, Send and ThreadShared when every component is). They also reach every `E: needs Error` and `type Failure: needs Error` bound, and every implementer. For an open class, "nothing reachable from it" already takes in what a derived object holds.

edits.rule: IV.8 (standard interfaces, the definition ERR-3 cites)
edits.before: interface Error: needs (Debug, Display):
edits.after: interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):
edits.why_general: IV.8 holds "the definitions" of the standard interfaces (p04 600). It is the declaration that every bound, every `dyn Error` and every implementer reads.
edits.why_here: This is the cause. `Error` is the interface that every error is erased through, and it was the only one of ERR-3, ERR-8 and THR-8 that said nothing about threads. std/src/core.em line 80 follows it.

edits.before:
`Error` is the interface of error types:
  `Display + Debug` with `fn source() -> Option[ref dyn Error]` (default `None`) (§IV.8).
edits.after: `Error` is the interface of error types, `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):` with `fn source() -> Option[ref dyn Error]` (default `None`) (§IV.8). Any thread may have and read an error, so `dyn Error` and `AnyError` are `Send` and `ThreadShared` (`[THR-8]`, `[THR-9]`). A type that holds a value that stays on one thread is not an error, and is refused where it implements `Error` or where it is derived from a class that does (`E2040`, `[IFC-3]`; `E2080` at `@derive(Error)`, `[DRV-1]`). It may still be a `Result`'s error that its `Display` prints (`[ERR-1]`, `[ERR-12]`).
edits.why_general: It states one property of what an error is: any thread may have and read it. The general rules then decide the rest. IFC-3 says where an implementation that does not meet the parents is refused and what its message gives. THR-8 and THR-9 say what each part of a type holds. ERR-3 lists no cases and no fixes. ERR-1's "any `E: needs Error`", ERR-8's `From` and ERR-9's "any error" stay true as written. The parents are spelled with `needs`, as verdict 110 spells them, and the old `Display + Debug` spelling goes.
edits.why_here: ERR-3 describes the declaration of p04 676. The two must say the same thing, or the two texts would decide one program differently.

edits.rule: TYP-17 (its example of an interface's parents)
edits.before:
an interface's parents
  (`interface Error: needs (Debug, Display):`)
edits.after:
an interface's parents
  (`interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):`)

edits.why_here: Left as it was, a reader of the generics chapter would find the old parents, and objection E1-4's `report_later` would compile under one text and be E2040 under the other.

edits.before: Structs, enums, tuples, fixed arrays, collections and class objects are `Send` when every component is;
edits.after: Structs, enums, tuples, fixed arrays, collections and class objects are `Send` when every component is, and an object of an `open` or `abstract` class may be an object of any class the program derives from it, a library's included and each instance of a generic one, whose fields are then among its components (as a call through a `virtual` method counts every override the program has, `[EFF-24]`);
edits.why_general: It makes THR-8's list say what its own definition says ("nothing reachable from it"). This holds for every class hierarchy, error or not: a game's `Script` with an `Enemy` holding a `weakref`, std's ECS `World` holding `Map[u64, AnyStorage]` (std/src/ecs.em 101, 201) whose `[T] AosStorage` holds the program's components, and an error's `GameError` with a `DocError`. Nothing is written: the markers are still inferred from the words of types (TYP-43), here the declarations of the derived classes. A line that needs the marker is refused with E7015, whose message names the derived class and its field (THR-2's "whose message gives the words to write").
edits.why_here: This is where the class markers are stated. Without it, the change's requirement on `Error` would be checked against the declared class alone, and objection S1-1's `DocError` (and an error struct holding a field of a plain open class whose derived object holds a `shares` owner) would cross threads inside an AnyError.

edits.after: Structural types and class objects are `ThreadShared` when every component is (a class object's components as `[THR-8]` counts them), and `dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs (Send, ThreadShared):`), as for `Send` (`[THR-8]`, ODR-255).
edits.why_general: Every interface gets the ThreadShared half of THR-8's dyn clause, a program's own `interface Command: needs (Send, ThreadShared):` as well as `Error`. ODR-255 already ruled it, and the text never said it. Class objects are counted as for Send.
edits.why_here: Without it, `ref r` of a `Result[int]` given to a scoped task (a `ref T` is Send when `T` is ThreadShared, p11 49) and an AnyError inside a thread_shared object's `RwLock` (verdict 165) stay undecided after the ERR-3 change.

edits.rule: Marker table, Send and ThreadShared rows (TYP-43)
edits.before: Send row: "a class object is when its fields are;" / ThreadShared row: "every component is `ThreadShared`;"
edits.after: Send row: "a class object is when its fields are, and those of every class the program derives from its class (`[THR-8]`); `dyn I` when `I` requires it;" / ThreadShared row: "every component is `ThreadShared`, a class object's counted as for `Send`; `dyn I` when `I` requires it;"
edits.why_general: TYP-43 says the table answers the markers (p04 583). It must give the same answer as THR-8 and THR-9.
edits.why_here: The row "a class object is when its fields are" is the narrow reading that lets a base-class value holding a one-thread derived object through. Leaving it would be a contradiction with the edited THR-8.

edits.before: `interface Ord: needs Eq` requires implementers of `Ord` to implement `Eq`. So a bound brings its parents: `T: needs IndexMut[int]` provides `Index[int]`'s methods too, and a binding it writes (`Output = f32`) names the parent's associated type (ODR-042).
edits.after: (unchanged, then:) An implementation meets its interface's parents for every type it covers: each instance of a generic implementation, and each class derived from a class it covers, whose objects are values of that class (`[TYP-5]` rule 8), each instance of a generic one included. One that does not is `E2040`, either at the generic implementation (`extend[T] Tagged[T] implements Ord:` over `extend[T: needs Eq] Tagged[T] implements Eq:` gives `extend[T: needs Eq] Tagged[T] implements Ord:`) or where the derived class is declared, which its own package checks, whichever package declares the base. The message names the part that does not meet a parent and gives a line that compiles. That line either makes the part meet the parent by the rule that decides it (a type parameter's needs, an interface's needs), or holds in its place a copy of what the type uses from it.
edits.why_general: It is one property of every implementation of every interface with parents: `Ord` over `Eq`, `IndexMut` over `Index`, a program's own `interface Command: needs (Send, ThreadShared):`, and `Error`. For a parent the base implements (Eq, Debug), a derived class meets it through the base's implementation, so nothing changes there. For a marker parent, which is inferred from contents, the check falls on the derived class's own fields, at the derived class's own line. A derived class may be in another package, but the check is still local. Rust also requires a supertrait to hold for every type an impl covers. The message rule is a property, not a list: it gives a needs line where one exists and a copy line otherwise. That is principle 12, and verdict 73's "how to fix an issue not how to run into another", so `thread_shared` is offered only where it compiles.
edits.why_here: Decision 2 (a generic error implementation) and objection S1-1 (a derived error class) are both about what an implementation covers. Stating it in ERR-3 would make it a case of `Error` (objection I1-1), and `Command`, `Ord` and every later interface with marker parents would stay undecided.

edits.before: A derive whose requirement a field does not meet is `E2080`, naming the field.
edits.after: (unchanged, then:) On a generic type, a requirement that a field meets only for some arguments of the type's parameters is written as their needs in the generated `extend`, so the derive implements the interface for those instances (`@derive(Copy)` above `[T]` and `pub struct Range:` is `Copy` when `T` is, ODR-027; `[STR-5]`).
edits.why_general: Every derive works this way, which is how STR-5 ("when every field implements the interface"), ODR-027 and std's own `@derive(Copy)` above `[T] pub struct Range` (std/src/core.em 1850-1853) already read it. E2080 stays for a field whose own written type fails. The generated code stays what `ember inspect --expand` prints.
edits.why_here: With Error's new parents, `@derive(Error)` on a generic error type (`SpawnError[T]` holding `rejected: T`) must be decided. Read the other way it would be refused even when only `SpawnError[int]` is used, unlike every other derive (objection E1-3).

readability.verdict: Better. No word is added to ordinary code. The worker loses an import, a concrete error type and, with two kinds of failure, a whole error enum. Generic error code (`type Failure: needs Error`), wrappers holding `owns dyn Error`, and class hierarchies whose derived classes hold plain data stay exactly as they are today. Words are added in two places only. A hand-written generic error implementation whose parameter holds the caller's value writes `T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)` (a derive writes it itself). An interface whose values an error holds as `owns dyn I` gets `Send` and `ThreadShared` in its needs, which then holds every implementer of that interface to them, or else the error holds a copy of the data. Under option A, the bound would be written instead in every pub generic function that uses `?` on such an error. Refusals fall on the type that holds the one-thread part: an error type at its declaration, a derived error class at its own line, and a plain open-class value at the line that sends it.

impact.cost: Compile time: Send and ThreadShared are inferred as today. For each open or abstract class, the program build collects the classes derived from it (a library's included, and each generic instance made). That is one walk of the class declarations, which EFF-24 already makes for virtual calls. Each implementation of an interface with parents is checked once per instance and once per derived class. A `?` into AnyError is checked as today. Run time: the class rule adds nothing. AnyError keeps its layout (the boxed error's data and table pointers, a 16-byte identity, the context list) and its one allocation on the failure path (ERR-11). The success path costs nothing, as in C, and handing an AnyError to another thread moves it, as C passes an error pointer. Two costs are stated. (1) CLS-12 (p05 380): a `@cached` method of a class that implements Error is filled under the once-flag, because its objects may now be read by several threads. Per call, the flag test becomes an acquire load (on x86-64 the same `mov` as a plain load; on ARM64 an `ldar`), and the first call fills under the flag with one compare-and-swap. This is already the duty today for any ThreadShared class given by `ref` to scoped tasks. (2) THR-2's hand-over check (verdict 114, "every object the handed object owns") reaches objects the boxed error owns whose class has weakref links, through the error's table: one indirect call per AnyError handed over. Nothing runs in a program where no error type converted into AnyError owns such an object. To measure: AnyError's size and its failure-path time against today's build; the `@cached` once-flag against a plain flag on ARM64 and x86-64; and the hand-over check's time.

verdicts.verdict: 61 (`thread_shared fn()`: the type says which threads may run it, not a whole-program search)
verdicts.how: The Error interface says which threads may have an error, and option C (a search through the `?` lines of the whole program) is turned down for verdict 61's reason. The class rule reads the declarations of derived classes, which are the words of types that TYP-43 infers markers from. It does not read bodies to find which functions a field is given, which is what 61 turned down. Listed for the owner as the nearest tension (decision 3).

decisions.title: Where the thread markers of an erased error come from
decisions.problem: AnyError is the default error type, and it holds any error behind `owns dyn Error`. By THR-8 it is one-thread unless `Error` requires Send, so a worker's `Result[int]`, a channel of results, a task's view of one and a thread_shared table of them are all refused. Making AnyError Send without a requirement would let an error holding a one-thread owner (a plain refcount) cross threads.

options.code:
pub struct AnyError:
    error: owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared   # a spelling the language does not have
extend[E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)] AnyError implements From[E]:
    ...
[S: needs Source]
pub fn count_lines(src: S) -> Result[int] where S.Failure: needs (Send, ThreadShared):
    text = src.read_all()?
options.outcome: The worker compiles. A one-thread error is refused at each `?` into AnyError, even with one thread. Generic error code and wrappers holding `owns dyn Error` must write thread words, and `source()` needs a conversion from a marked dyn to `dyn Error` that no rule states. A one-thread error that is only matched, never put into AnyError, compiles.

options.code: fn load(path: StrView) -> Result[int, io.Error]:   # today's rules
options.outcome: The `Result[int]` worker stays refused at the spawn line (E7015). A worker names a concrete error type, with an error enum when it can fail two ways.

options.code:
## std unchanged; the compiler collects every type converted into AnyError in the whole program
fn load(path: StrView) -> Result[int]:
options.outcome: The worker compiles until some `?` anywhere converts a one-thread error. From then on every spawn, channel and thread_shared holder of AnyError is refused, with a message naming a distant line. It contradicts THR-8's dyn clause (by requirement, ODR-255) and is the search verdict 61 turned down.

The worker, channels, task views and thread_shared holders of results compile. Generic `needs Error` code and `owns dyn Error` wrappers write nothing. An error type holding a one-thread part (a shares owner, a weakref to a one-thread value, a sharedref mut link, a Cell, a plain fn(), an `owns dyn I` whose I lacks the markers) is refused where it implements Error, even if it never leaves its thread, with a line that compiles. A hand-written generic one writes `T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)`. This is Swift's choice (`Error` refines `Sendable`).

options.code: pub interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send):   # or the same bound on AnyError's From
options.outcome: Results may be sent, but AnyError is not ThreadShared: `ref r` to scoped tasks and `thread_shared Assets(sizes=RwLock([...]))` stay refused. In exchange it accepts error types that hold a Cell or a vouched raw pointer.

options.code:
## AnyError records whether its error may cross; every hand-over checks it while running
h = thread.spawn(owns fn() => load("level1.cfg"))   # stops the program if the error may not cross
options.outcome: Everything compiles. A one-thread error that reaches another thread stops the program at the hand-over, on the failure path. Each hand-over of an AnyError costs a compare and a list of results costs a walk, and views given to scoped tasks and writes into thread_shared holders cannot be checked cheaply.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once. B fails 'easy to write': every worker grows its own error type, and an enum when it can fail two ways. A and E fail it for generic error code and wrappers, which grow thread words. C, D and F keep ordinary code as it is today. 2. Safety: A to E all refuse before a one-thread value crosses, and F stops the program. D is sound only with the class components counted as THR-8's definition reads them (decision 3) and with derived classes checked (IFC-3), both in this change. 3. Compile time first: A to E are decided when compiling. F's run-time check cannot make the refused program work: a shares owner inside the error cannot be moved away from its other owners, so F can only stop it. A compile-time refusal with a line to write would become a crash on the least-tested path (checklist 8), so F is out. 4. A written word only for meaning: A and E write markers in bounds and after `dyn`, and B writes a concrete error type. D writes a bound only on a hand-written generic error implementation (the library's promise, verdict 108), and the markers on an interface only when an error holds its values, where they state which threads may have those values. 5. The ordinary program no longer or harder: C lets an edit anywhere break a spawn far away. D refuses only an error type holding a one-thread part, at its own declaration, even in a one-thread program, and the fix is to hold a copy. A refuses the same errors at their `?`, which nearly every error reaches because main returns `Result[void]`. A accepts an error that is only matched, as in objection E1-1's renderer, which D refuses. 6. Consistency: D uses THR-8's own dyn clause, IFC-3, ODR-255, verdict 110's spelling, verdict 61 (the type says which threads may have it) and verdict 165 (refused where it is made). It matches Swift (`Error: Sendable`) and Rust's anyhow (`Send + Sync`). So D.
decisions.recommendation: D: Error needs Debug, Display, Send and ThreadShared, so AnyError goes to and is read by any thread with nothing written. An error type holding a one-thread part is refused where it is made an error, with a line that compiles.

owner_short.one_line: Should every error type be safe to hand to and read from any thread (as Swift's errors are), so the catch-all error (like C++'s `std::exception_ptr`; Ember's `AnyError`) can come back from a worker thread?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | error type's author | declares an error of plain values (a code, a text) | allowed: it may go to any thread
2 | worker thread | `fs.read_to_string(path)?` puts the file error into the catch-all | allowed, nothing written
3 | worker thread | returns `Result[int]` (a count or the catch-all error) | allowed: every error may cross threads
4 | main thread | `n = h.join()?` | gets the count, or passes the error on
5 | error type's author | declares an error holding a one-thread shared owner, or an object of an interface that does not say threads may have it | refused at that declaration, with the line to write
owner_short.today: The worker returning `Result[int]` is refused at `thread.spawn`, the text never says so, and the worker must name its own error type.
options: A: the catch-all checks each error where `?` puts it in; generic error code and error wrappers must add thread words
B: keep today: the catch-all stays on its thread; every worker names its own error type
C: the compiler searches the whole program; one one-thread error anywhere breaks every thread hand-off, far from that line
D: every error type is safe for every thread, checked where the type is declared an error; nothing written anywhere else
E: the catch-all may be sent but not read by two threads at once; a shared table of results is refused
F: check while running and stop the program when a one-thread error crosses
owner_short.recommendation: D: ordinary worker, server and library code compile with nothing written; only an error holding a one-thread part is refused, at its own line, with the fix.

decisions.title: A generic implementation whose interface has parents (a generic error that holds the caller's value)
decisions.problem: Under D, a generic error such as `PoolFull[T]` (like Rust's `SendError<T>`) is Send only when `T` is. The text left open whether `extend[T] PoolFull[T] implements Error:` is refused or quietly holds only for some `T`. The same question arises for every interface with parents (`extend[T] Echo[T] implements Command:` with `interface Command: needs (Send, ThreadShared):`, `extend[T] Tagged[T] implements Ord:` over a bounded `Eq`), and for a derive on a generic type (`@derive(Error)` above `[T] enum SpawnError:` with `Full(rejected: T)`).

options.code:
extend[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)] PoolFull[T] implements Error:
    pass
## written without the bound: E2040 at this line, giving the line above
@derive(Error)
[T]
enum SpawnError:
    @error("the spawn point is full")
    Full(rejected: T)
## the derive writes extend[T: needs (Debug, Send, ThreadShared)] itself, as @derive(Copy) on Range does
options.outcome: Each written line means what it says. `PoolFull[int]` and `SpawnError[int]` are Errors. `PoolFull[shares Enemy]` is not, and its `?` into AnyError is E2040 at the `?` or at the call. A derive implements the interface per instance, as every derive already does (STR-5, ODR-027).

options.code:
extend[T] PoolFull[T] implements Error:
    pass
## holds only for the T that are Send and ThreadShared, with nothing said
options.outcome: No word is written, but the line claims every `T` and means fewer. The refusal appears at a distant `?` with no line of the declaration saying why.
A generic error type used only with plain values is refused until it is bounded, and the bound limits what the type may hold, not only where it is an Error, unlike every other derive.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: all are equal for ordinary code, because generic error types holding a caller's value are rare. (iii) is harder: a type used only as `SpawnError[int]` is refused. 2. Safety: all three are safe. 3. Compile time: all three. 4. A written word only for meaning: the bound on a hand-written implementation is the library's promise of which values it is an error for (verdicts 108, 111). A derive is the compiler writing the implementation, so it writes the bound itself and `ember inspect --expand` shows it (principle 1). 5. The ordinary program: unchanged under (i). 6. Consistency: IFC-3 says implementers implement the parents, Rust requires a supertrait to hold for every type an impl covers, verdict 132 says a declaration's meaning comes only from what it says, and STR-5, ODR-027 and std's `@derive(Copy)` on `[T] pub struct Range` make derives per instance. So (i), stated once in IFC-3 for every interface and in DRV-1 for every derive.
decisions.recommendation: (i): a hand-written generic implementation writes the bound its interface's parents need, or the compiler refuses it and gives that line; a derive writes the bound itself.

owner_short.one_line: A generic error that hands the caller's value back (like Rust's `SendError<T>`): is it an error for every `T`, or only for the `T`s any thread may have, and who writes that?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | library author | writes `extend[T] PoolFull[T] implements Error:` | refused, with the line to write
2 | library author | writes `extend[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)] PoolFull[T] implements Error:` | allowed
3 | library author | writes `@derive(Error)` on a generic enum | allowed; the derive writes the bound itself
4 | program | `insert(...)?` with `PoolFull[int]` into the catch-all | allowed
5 | one-thread game | `insert(...)?` with `PoolFull[shares Enemy]` into the catch-all | refused at that line: name the error type instead
owner_short.today: Nothing says; the implementation covers every `T`, because errors need no thread markers today.
options: (i) a hand-written implementation writes the bound, or is refused with the line to write; a derive writes it itself
(ii) the implementation quietly holds only for the safe `T`s
(iii) a generic error type must bound its parameter on the type itself
owner_short.recommendation: (i): the line says what it means, the compiler gives the line to write, and derives keep working per instance as they already do.

decisions.title: What an object of an open class may hold, for the thread markers
decisions.problem: A base-class value may be an object of any derived class (C++'s `Base*` to a `Derived`). THR-8's definition says a type is Send when nothing reachable from it is a one-thread owner, but its list and the p04 table judge a class object by its declared class's fields alone. So a `Script` value that is an `Enemy` holding a `shares` owner may go to another thread today. Under D, a `GameError` that is a `DocError` holding one would also go inside every AnyError.

options.code:
open class Script:
    entity: int
class Enemy(Script):
    level: shares Level
## a Script's components include Enemy's fields: thread.spawn(owns fn() owns s: ...) is E7015 naming Enemy.level
## a class derived from an Error class is checked where it is declared (IFC-3)
options.outcome: Every program whose derived classes hold only thread-safe parts is accepted, with nothing written: Door(Script) crosses, and std's ECS World crosses when its components do. A refusal falls on the line that sends the value, naming the derived class. A library's line may depend on a class the program derives, as a virtual call's effects already do.

options.code:
interface Task: needs (Send, ThreadShared):
    pass
extend Script implements Task:   # without this, no Script value ever goes to another thread
    pass
options.outcome: An open class's values never cross threads unless it promises the markers through an interface, and then every derived class is checked (Swift: a non-final class is never Sendable). Std's ECS World (`Map[u64, AnyStorage]`) could then never go to another thread or be read by tasks, unless std bounds every component to be Send and ThreadShared.

options.code:
class Enemy(Script):
    level: shares Level   # refused: Script is Send by its fields, so every derived class must be
options.outcome: Every derived class adding a one-thread field to a plain base is refused, even with one thread: an `Enemy` holding a `weakref` target, the ordinary game-engine pattern.

options.code:
## today: a Script value is judged by Script's own fields
