decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: (iii) refuses ordinary class hierarchies. (ii) refuses every open-class value crossing threads or read by tasks unless an interface is written only to carry the markers, and it breaks std's own ECS World. (i) and (iv) keep ordinary code. 2. Safety: (iv) lets a one-thread owner cross, so it is out. 3. Compile time: (i), (ii) and (iii) are all decided when compiling. 4. A written word only for meaning: (i) writes nothing, and (ii) writes an interface that says nothing a declaration does not already say. 5. The ordinary program: (i) accepts every program whose derived classes are thread-safe. Its refusal is at the line that sends the value and names the derived class, the cost verdict 86 accepted for effects. 6. Consistency: (i) is what THR-8's own definition says ("nothing reachable from it"). It is how the language already treats an open class's virtual calls (EFF-24, p10 94: "from every function the program can put there"; verdict 122) and its views (p07 713). And it infers markers from the words of types, as TYP-43 says. (ii) matches THR-8's dyn clause and Swift, but a class has no needs list, and (ii) loses on parameters 1 and 5 first. Where a base does promise the markers, by implementing an interface that needs them (Error), each derived class is checked at its own line (IFC-3, decision 2's property). So (i).
decisions.recommendation: (i): a base-class value is judged by every class the program derives from it, with nothing written; a class derived from an error class is checked where it is declared.

owner_short.one_line: When a base-class object (C++'s `Base*` that may point at a `Derived`) is handed to another thread, should the compiler look at every derived class the program declares?
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | game author | `open class Script`, and `class Door(Script)` with plain fields | a Script may go to another thread
2 | game author | adds `class Enemy(Script)` holding a one-thread shared owner | allowed
3 | worker | `thread.spawn(owns fn() owns s: ...)` with `s: Script` | refused at that line, naming Enemy's field
4 | error author | `class DocError(GameError)` holding a one-thread shared owner, GameError being an error | refused at DocError's line
owner_short.today: The compiler looks only at the base class's own fields, so a Script that is an Enemy goes to another thread and its shared count races.
options: (i) look at every derived class the program declares; nothing written
(ii) a base class's objects never go to another thread unless the base promises it through an interface (Swift)
(iii) every derived class must be as thread-safe as its base's own fields
(iv) keep today
owner_short.recommendation: (i): correct hierarchies keep working with nothing written, and only the class that holds the one-thread part is named.

responses.objection: S1-1 (safety, block S): an open error class `GameError` implements Error, and its subclass `DocError` holds a `shares Doc`. Upcast to GameError and put into an AnyError, it reaches another thread, and its plain count races.
responses.how: The cause is what an object of an open class holds, so the change now fixes it there. THR-8's list (p11 47-48), THR-9 (p11 63-64) and the p04 rows (577-578) now say what THR-8's definition already says ("nothing reachable from it"): an object of an open or abstract class counts the fields of every class the program derives from it. IFC-3 (p05 411-413) now says that an implementation covers each class derived from a class it covers, and refuses one that does not meet the parents where that derived class is declared, in its own package. Walk of the objection's program: line 17 passes (GameError's own `code: int`). Line 20, `class DocError(GameError):`, is E2040 naming `doc`, even when GameError is in a library compiled earlier. So no DocError object exists, and nothing one-thread is reachable from the AnyError at line 38. The same words close the existing gap for a plain `owns b: GameError`, and for a plain open class: an `Enemy(Script)` holding a `shares` owner makes a Script hand-over E7015, naming Enemy's field. They also cover an error struct holding a field of a plain open class. The earlier premise, "the one place its contents are known", is withdrawn. For an open class, contents are also declared at each derived class, which is where the check now goes. Tests k20_derived_error_class_refused, k20_open_class_one_thread_subclass_refused and k20_open_class_plain_subclasses_runs.

responses.objection: S1-3: a `@cached` method on an error class is now filled from two threads through AnyError, and the impact said nothing is added at run time.
responses.how: CLS-12 decides it as written (p05 380: "On an object several threads reach, the kept result is filled once under a once-flag"). After the change, every object of a class that implements Error is such an object, because Error requires ThreadShared and AnyError is ThreadShared, and the compiler knows this from the type. The impact now states the duty and its cost. Per call, the flag test is an acquire load (on x86-64 the same `mov` as a plain load; on ARM64 an `ldar`), and the first call fills under the flag (one compare-and-swap), to be measured. It is the same duty today for any ThreadShared class given by `ref` to scoped tasks. The objection's program prints 68.

responses.objection: E1-1: an error holding `owns dyn Shape` (Shape needing only Debug) is refused, ERR-3's closed list of fixes gives no line that compiles, and the readability verdict's 'only one place' was false.
responses.how: ERR-3 no longer lists fixes. IFC-3 states the message as a property: it names the part and gives a line that compiles, either one that makes the part meet the parent by the rule that decides it (here `interface Shape: needs (Debug, Send, ThreadShared):` in place of line 1), or one that holds a copy of what the type uses (`TooLarge(area: int)`). programs_changed now has the row for `owns dyn I` fields, including that the interface's needs then hold every implementer (a `Sprite` holding `shares Texture` becomes E2040), and that under A a one-thread renderer matching `Result[int, DrawError]` compiles. The readability verdict now names both places where words are added. The trade-off itself is kept, because an error that any thread may read cannot hold an object only one thread may read. The copy line keeps `Shape` as it is. Test k20_error_holding_dyn_interface_refused.

responses.objection: E1-2: the offered fix 'make the value thread_shared' for a `shares mut Doc` field leads into E7014 when the program changes the document directly.
responses.how: The same message property in IFC-3: only a line that compiles is given. `thread_shared` is offered only where no line then changes the value directly. Here the message gives `ReadOnly(path: String)` in place of line 7 and `e = SaveError.ReadOnly(path=copy of doc.path)` in place of line 12 (verdict 73).

responses.objection: E1-3: refusing `@derive(Error)` on a generic type with a `T` field gives derives two rules (per instance for Copy, Eq, Debug and Clone, refused for Error), and the help bounds the type itself.
responses.how: DRV-1 (p14 138) now says, for every derive, that a requirement a field meets only for some arguments of the type's parameters is written as their needs in the generated `extend`, so the derive holds per instance, as STR-5, ODR-027 and std's `@derive(Copy)` on `[T] pub struct Range` already do. The objection's program runs and prints `the spawn point is full`. E2080 stays for a field whose own written type fails. A hand-written unbounded `extend[T] X[T] implements Error:` stays refused (decision 2 (i), verdict 132). This settles the previous notes' gap (1) for every derive. Test k20_generic_derive_error_per_instance.

responses.objection: E1-4: TYP-17 (p04 459) still quotes `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display):`.
responses.how: p04 458-459 is edited to the new declaration in the same change. It stays the example of several needs in round brackets. `report_later` then compiles under every text.

responses.objection: E1-5: the THR-9 sentence ('which an interface writes among its needs as a bound does') reads as if it attached to `dyn I`, and decides nothing more.
responses.how: THR-9 now reads: "Structural types and class objects are `ThreadShared` when every component is (a class object's components as `[THR-8]` counts them), and `dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs (Send, ThreadShared):`), as for `Send` (`[THR-8]`, ODR-255)." The objection's program prints 4.

responses.objection: I1-1: 'an implementation meets all four for every type it covers' was written as a fact about Error. `extend[T] Echo[T] implements Command:` with `interface Command: needs (Send, ThreadShared):` stays undecided, and TYP-43's per-instance reading may be carried over.
responses.how: The property is now stated once in IFC-3 for every interface: an implementation meets its interface's parents for every type it covers (each instance of a generic implementation, each derived class), otherwise E2040 at the implementation, with the bounded line given. ERR-3 states only Error's four parents and cites IFC-3. Line 10 of the objection's program is E2040, giving `extend[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)] Echo[T] implements Command:`. `Tagged[T]`'s Ord gives `extend[T: needs Eq] Tagged[T] implements Ord:`. TYP-43's per-instance words are about a vouched generic Send whose parameters are bounded, so they do not apply to an unbounded implementation. Test k20_interface_parents_generic_extend.

responses.objection: I1-2: ERR-3's closed list of fixes gives no compiling line for an `owns dyn Note` field, a Cell field or a plain function.
responses.how: The list is gone, and the message rule in IFC-3 is a property (a line that makes the part meet the parent by the rule that decides it, or a copy). For the objection's program, the message gives `interface Note: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):` in place of line 3. For a `Cell[int]` it gives `Atomic[int]`, as verdict 165's message does.

responses.objection: I1-3: programs_changed missed error types holding a plain `fn()` or an `owns dyn I`, and whether the offered `thread_shared fn()` is ThreadShared is undecided.
responses.how: Both rows are now in programs_changed. For a plain `fn()` field, the message gives a copy line (the data the function would read) and does not offer `thread_shared fn()`. Whether a `thread_shared fn()` is ThreadShared (THR-9 names no function type, and a `fn() owns n: n += 1` changes its own state when called) is a gap that exists today: it shows in verdict 165's rule for a `thread_shared Bus` holding an unguarded `Array[thread_shared fn()]`, which THR-1's own message offers (p11 84-85). It is not caused by this change and is listed in notes beside J7-06.

responses.objection: I1-4: the impact missed TYP-17's copy of the declaration and the p17a code rows.
responses.how: p04 459 is edited, and p17a 71 (E2080: a derive whose requirement a field does not meet, `@derive(Error)` included, citing DRV-1 and ERR-3) and p17a 59 (E2040: an implementation that does not meet its parents, citing IFC-3 and ERR-3) are edited. All three are listed under rules changed.

tests.name: k20_open_class_one_thread_subclass_refused
tests.program:
import std.thread

class Level:
    name: String = String("forest")

open class Script:
    entity: int

    fn init(entity: int):
        this.entity = entity

class Enemy(Script):
    level: shares Level

    fn init(entity: int, owns level: shares Level):
        this.level = level
        super.init(entity)

fn main():
    level = shares Level()
    s: Script = Enemy(1, shares level)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns s: s.entity)
    println(h.join())
tests.expected: E7015 at line 22 (`h = thread.spawn(...)`), gist: "`s` is a `Script`, and a `Script` may be an `Enemy` (line 12), whose `level` (line 13) is a `shares Level`, an owner that stays on one thread; give the thread a copy of what it uses: write `entity = s.entity` above line 22 and `h = thread.spawn(owns fn() copy of entity: entity)` in place of line 22"

tests.name: k20_open_class_plain_subclasses_runs
tests.program:
import std.thread

open class Script:
    entity: int

    fn init(entity: int):
        this.entity = entity

    virtual fn score() -> int:
        return this.entity

class Door(Script):
    angle: int = 90

    override fn score() -> int:
        return this.entity + this.angle

fn main():
    s: Script = Door(1)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns s: s.score())
    println(h.join())
tests.expected: stdout: 91

tests.name: k20_interface_parents_generic_extend
tests.program:
import std.thread

interface Command: needs (Send, ThreadShared):
    fn run() -> int

[T]
struct Echo:
    payload: T

extend[T] Echo[T] implements Command:
    fn run() -> int:
        return 1

fn main():
    c: owns dyn Command = owns Echo(payload=5)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns c: c.run())
    println(h.join())
tests.expected: E2040 at line 10 (`extend[T] Echo[T] implements Command:`), gist: "`Command` needs `Send` and `ThreadShared`, and `Echo[T]` holds a `T`, which may be a value that stays on one thread; write `extend[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)] Echo[T] implements Command:` in place of line 10"

to_verify: Today's compiler on the J6-16 program. The spec says it is refused at the spawn line (E7015). Check whether it is refused, or compiles because `R: Send` is not checked yet (std/src/thread.em line 27 still reads `pub fn spawn(owns f: fn() -> R)`).

After std/src/core.em line 80 becomes `pub interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):` (lines 92-99 unchanged): `dyn Error` is inferred Send and ThreadShared, so AnyError (Box[dyn Error], u128, Array[String]) is both, and the J6-16 program compiles and prints the length.

Every std error type still implements Error: io.Error (io.em 17, 45), ParseError (string.em 25), CppError (ffi.em 149), FmtError, SerError, ReloadError, CapacityError, NulError, RangeError, Message and Missing (core.em 222, 228), and the FFI-16 status error types the compiler makes. No std open class implements Error.

Regression scan over tests/, examples/ and the spec's examples: list every error type now refused (holding shares, shares mut, a weakref to a one-thread value, sharedref mut, Cell, a plain fn(), an owns dyn I whose I lacks the markers, or a raw pointer), and every hand-over, scoped `ref`, channel or thread_shared holder of an open-class value now refused because a derived class holds a one-thread part. Expected: none in std.

std ECS (std/src/ecs.em 101-213): a `World` whose components are plain structs is still Send and ThreadShared, and one storing a component that holds a `shares` field is E7015 where it is handed over or given by `ref` to scoped tasks, naming the component's field.

The class rule on separate packages: a library's `pub open class` with a derived class in the program. The program's build counts the derived class. A derived class of a library's Error class is refused at its own line. A library line that sends a base value is reported in the program's build, at the line that passes the value, naming the derived class.
Every std implementation of an interface with parents meets them for every type it covers (search `implements Ord`, `implements IndexMut`, `implements Error`): no generic one needs a new bound.

`@derive(Copy)` on `[T] pub struct Range` and the other range types still gives `Copy` per instance, and `@derive(Error)` on a generic enum writes `extend[T: needs (Debug, Send, ThreadShared)]` in `ember inspect --expand`.
The sixteen tests above give exactly the stated results, including the E2080, E2040 and E7015 messages. Each message's offered line must compile.

A type that is Send only by `unsafe extend X implements Send` (a raw pointer) and implements Error is E2040 at its implementation, with a message that does not offer a vouch for ThreadShared (pending J7-06).
Verdict 114's hand-over check reaches objects owned inside an AnyError's box (through the error's table) when an AnyError is returned from a thread or sent on a channel.

To measure: AnyError's size and the failure-path time of a `?` into it, against today's build; a `@cached` call on an error class with the once-flag against a plain flag, on x86-64 and ARM64; and the time of the hand-over check for an AnyError in a program where an error type owns an object of a class with weakref links.
out.notes:
This revision keeps direction D and rewrites the change as a whole. Objection S1-1 showed that D is sound only if the markers of what an error holds are sound, and for an object of an open class they were not: THR-8's list and the p04 row counted the declared class's fields, while THR-8's own definition says \"nothing reachable from it\". So the change now also fixes the class wording (THR-8, THR-9, p04 577-578) at that cause. It states once in IFC-3 that an implementation meets its interface's parents for every type it covers (generic instances, derived classes), with the refusal's place and its message's line given as properties. That replaces ERR-3's closed list of fixes. DRV-1 now says derives on generic types are per instance, as STR-5, ODR-027 and std's Range already read it. TYP-17's copy of the declaration and the p17a rows are edited. Decision 3 (open classes) is new. The nearest tension is with verdict 61, which turned down a whole-program search through bodies. Option (i) reads the declarations of derived classes, as the language already does for an open class's virtual calls (EFF-24, verdict 122). It is listed for the owner with option (ii), Swift's rule, which would stop std's ECS World from ever going to another thread or being read by tasks.

Existing gaps found on the way, not caused by this change, listed for later:
(1) Whether a `thread_shared fn()` is ThreadShared. THR-9 names no function type, and a `fn() owns n: n += 1` changes its own state when called. It shows today in verdict 165's rule for a thread_shared Bus holding an unguarded `Array[thread_shared fn()]`, which THR-1's own E7015 message offers (p11 84-85). Until it is decided, the message for an error holding a function gives a copy line. Present it beside J7-06.
(2) A ThreadShared vouch for types holding raw pointers (P04, J7-06). Until it is settled, an error type holding a raw pointer cannot be an Error.
(3) Verdict 114's hand-over check through any `owns dyn I` whose interface needs Send. THR-2's words ('every object the handed object owns') cover it, but the table mechanism is not stated.
(4) std/src/thread.em still uses the old spawn signature (implementation, not spec).

Precedents: Swift's `Error` refines `Sendable` (SE-0302), and a non-final Swift class cannot be Sendable. Rust's anyhow::Error requires `Send + Sync + 'static`, and a Rust impl must meet its supertraits for every type it covers.

All work was read-only. The repository's start-up reading (AUTOPILOT, HANDOFF) was skipped, as the team rules direct.

checked: IV.8 / ERR-3 / TYP-17 after the change (p04 676, p13 87-88, p04 458-459): Error needs Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared. Every std error type implementing Error (io.Error, ParseError string.em 25, CppError ffi.em 138-150 with two Strings, the core.em messages) holds only ints and Strings, so no std type crosses as a one-thread value.

AnyError's layout (std/src/core.em 92-99: Box[dyn Error], u128, Array[String]). It is Send and ThreadShared only through THR-8's dyn clause (p11 51) and the new THR-9 clause. Both read the interface, never its implementers, so the soundness of every AnyError route rests wholly on every implementation of Error meeting the parents in the final program. That is where S2-1 breaks.

S1-1's one-package program after the change: DocError(GameError) is E2040 at its own line by the new IFC-3 sentence (p05 411-413 after). No DocError object exists, and nothing one-thread is reachable from the AnyError. Resolved.

One-package class rule (THR-8 p11 47-48 after, THR-9 p11 63-64 after, p04 577-578 after): Script with Enemy holding `shares Level` is E7015 at the send. Door(Script) with `angle: int` runs (prints 91). An error struct holding a plain open-class field whose derived class in the same package holds a one-thread part is E2040 at the struct's `implements Error` line (base IFC-3). It is far from the derived class but safe.

Cross-package and reload versions of the class rule. The check of a dependency's implementation, made in the dependency's build, is not made again when a dependant (MOD-9 p05 38-46) or a reload (HR-14 p20 135, HR-44 p20 54-72) adds or changes a derived class of an open class that the error holds. S2-1.

A generic derived class of an Error class: the new IFC-3 wording 'each instance of a generic one included ... where the derived class is declared, which its own package checks' does not say whether an unbounded `[T] class Wrapped(GameError)` is refused (for every T) or checked per instance. Read per instance, a dependant's instance is checked by no package. Folded into S2-1, with tests.

Generic implementations (IFC-3 after, decision 2 (i)): PoolFull[T], Echo[T], Tagged[T] are refused unbounded and give the bounded line. DRV-1 after: a derive on a generic type is per instance, with the bound written in the generated extend. A `?` of a non-Send instance is refused at the `?`. No hole.

THR-8 p11 49 (`ref T` is Send when T is ThreadShared) with THR-9's new dyn clause: `ref r` of a Result[int] reaching scoped tasks. A `thread_shared` holder of results under an RwLock (verdict 165, THR-1 p11 75-87). Methods that change an error through `ref` are E3023, because effects through dyn count every implementation (p04 728-730, EFF-2 p10 41-42). No hole.
CLS-12 (p05 376-380) after the change. S1-3's program is decided by the words and the cost is now stated. But the stated duty ('a class that implements Error') misses classes an error holds. S2-2.

THR-2 / verdict 114 hand-over check through the error's box (p11 116-124), and RC-5 point 1 (p08 196-203: 'a place ... of `owns dyn I` whose value's state owns one', 'a hand-over ... which may move it'). Both are decided by the words as properties. The run-time cost is stated by the designer. No hole.

THR-20 (p11 285-300, 'A drop runs where the last owner ends') with EFF-24 counting the drops of an ended `owns dyn` value (p10 95-97). A worker ending an AnyError counts the drops of every Error implementation. Safe, possibly a far refusal. The cross-package counting of a dependant's implementations at a library's dyn drop exists today too (see notes).

Errors holding `thread_shared T` (Send when T is Send and ThreadShared, p11 50; biased counts RC-4 p08 155-170): safe. Errors holding a raw pointer with `unsafe extend X implements Send`: refused, since ThreadShared cannot be vouched (TYP-43 p04 583-596). Errors holding views: the region rules of TYP-15 (p04 311-316) follow the value through the box, and a `thread.spawn` function holds no view of its maker's places (THR-17). No new hole.

Today's guarantees kept: no shares owner, weakref to a one-thread value, sharedref mut link (verdict 164) or Cell can be inside an Error. Verdict 23 and verdict 165 are kept. No guarantee of today's text is removed, apart from the routes in S2-1.

previous.why: The new IFC-3 sentence (p05 411-413 after) covers 'each class derived from a class it covers', refused 'where the derived class is declared, which its own package checks, whichever package declares the base'. ERR-3 after (p13 87-88) says the same. Walk of S1-1's program: line 17 passes (GameError holds `code: int`). Line 20, `class DocError(GameError):`, is E2040 naming `doc`, in DocError's own package, so it also holds when GameError is a library's. No DocError object exists, and line 38 hands over nothing one-thread. A different route of the same family remains: an error that holds a field of an open class, which a later package or a reload extends. That route is not a class derived from an error class, so this sentence does not reach it. It is raised as S2-1.

CLS-12 (p05 376-380), 'On an object several threads reach, the kept result is filled once under a once-flag', decides S1-3's program: LoadError implements Error, AnyError is ThreadShared, and two scoped tasks reach the object. It prints 68. The impact now states the duty and its cost (an acquire load per call, one compare-and-swap at the first fill). The duty as stated covers only 'a class that implements Error', and misses classes whose objects an error holds. That is a smaller impact gap, raised as S2-2.

#   language = "0.9.15"

# file game/src/main.em (line numbers below count from its first line)
import std.thread
from gamekit import Script, LoadError

class Level:
    name: String = String("forest")

class Enemy(Script):
    level: shares Level

    fn init(entity: int, owns level: shares Level):
        this.level = level
        super.init(entity)

fn make_enemy(entity: int, owns level: shares Level) -> Result[int, LoadError]:
    return Err(LoadError(script=Enemy(entity, owns level)))   # an Enemy, upcast to Script

fn load(entity: int, owns level: shares Level) -> Result[int]:
    return Ok(make_enemy(entity, owns level)?)                # LoadError -> AnyError

fn main():
    level = shares Level()
    r = load(1, shares level)                                  # r's error holds a second owner of the Level
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns r: r.is_err())             # r goes to another thread, which ends it
    for i in 0..100000:
        other = shares level                                   # +1, then -1 at the end of the round: plain adds
        println(i, other.name.len())
    println(h.join())
objections.walk:
In C++ terms: an engine library's exception type holds a `Base*`. The game's `Derived` holds a non-atomic refcounted pointer. A type-erased `std::exception_ptr` carries it to another thread.
(1) gamekit/src/lib.em line 20, `extend LoadError implements Error:`, in gamekit's build. p04 676 after reads `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):`. IFC-3 after (p05 411-413) reads "An implementation meets its interface's parents for every type it covers". LoadError's one component is `script: Script` (line 10). THR-8 after (p11 47-48) reads "an object of an `open` or `abstract` class may be an object of any class the program derives from it, a library's included". gamekit derives nothing from Script, so in its build Script's components are `entity: int`, and LoadError is Send and ThreadShared (THR-9 after, p11 63-64). Display is line 12 and Debug is line 16. Line 20 passes, and gamekit is done. MOD-9 (p05 38-46): "What a dependant may rely on is what the package's `pub` items write and what the compiler works out from their code ... recorded in the package's interface file".
(2) game/src/main.em line 7, `class Enemy(Script):`, with `level: shares Level` on line 8. CLS-4 (p05 335) lets an open class be subclassed. The new IFC-3 sentence checks a derived class only when it is "derived from a class it covers". ERR-3 after (p13 87-88) says the same: "refused where it implements `Error` or where it is derived from a class that does". The Error implementation covers LoadError, not Script, and Script implements nothing. So nothing checks line 7, and it compiles.
(3) Line 15. TYP-5 rule 8 (p04 86) gives "a class object to a base class (upcast)" at a field initialiser, a coercion site (p04 71). The LoadError now holds an Enemy, and the Enemy holds a second owner of main's Level.
(4) Line 18. ERR-2 (p13 51-52) "returns `Err(F.from(err))`". ERR-8 (p13 95) says AnyError "implements `From[E]` for every `E: needs Error`". LoadError meets that bound through gamekit's line 20 (IFC-3: "So a bound brings its parents"). The edited E2040 row (p17a 59 after) places the parent refusal "at the generic implementation or at the derived class". Line 18 is neither, and so is every other line of game.
(5) Line 23. THR-10 (p11 176) says "`R` MUST be `Send`". R is Result[int, AnyError]. AnyError's `Box[dyn Error]` is Send by THR-8's dyn clause (p11 51), "`dyn I` when `I` requires it", which reads the interface and never the implementers. So line 23 compiles. The changed THR-8 does make LoadError itself not Send in game's build, because Script now counts Enemy's fields. But no line of game checks LoadError's markers. They were checked once, at gamekit's line 20, in gamekit's build, which game's build only relies on (MOD-9).
(6) The worker ends `r`. The box ends the LoadError, which ends the Enemy (CLS-6, p05 353), which ends `level`. RC-4 (p08 155-156) says the counts of a value that is not thread_shared "are changed with plain adds and subtracts, and never cross threads". That -1 on the worker races with main's +1/-1 on lines 25-26. A lost update either leaks the Level, or brings its count to 0 while `other.name` is read: a use after free, then a double free at the last end.
Today the same program is E7015 at line 23. Error needs only Debug and Display (p04 676, p13 88), so by p11 51 `dyn Error` is not Send, and neither is r.
Read the other way, game's build would check gamekit's line 20 again and refuse it with E2040. Then the refusal falls on a dependency's line, which the game's author cannot change, and the text places it nowhere (the 'either ... or' of IFC-3 after). The program is let through or refused depending on which reading is taken.
Route 2, hot reload. Take the same two packages, with game reloadable and Enemy at first holding only `angle: int`. A reload adds `target: Option[weakref Level] = None` to Enemy. HR-14 (p20 135) reads "field added with a default | initialised to that default". HR-44 (p20 54-72) compares only functions' facts (what each may change, read and end), not a type's markers. "Code the reload rebuilds is checked again when it compiles", and gamekit's line 20 is not rebuilt. After the reload, a new Enemy whose `target` links a one-thread Level crosses inside an AnyError. The worker ending it ends the link: a plain weak-count change from two threads (THR-2, p11 99-101).
Route 3, a generic derived class. IFC-3 after reads "each instance of a generic one included ... where the derived class is declared, which its own package checks". gamekit writes `[T]` above `pub class Wrapped(GameError):` with `pub item: T`. Read per instance, as DRV-1 after reads a derive, gamekit sees no instance and passes. game makes `Wrapped[shares Level]` but does not declare Wrapped, so no package checks that instance. Read for every T, as decision 2 (i) reads a generic implementation, gamekit's line is E2040 and the route closes. The text does not say which.
An existing gap, not caused by the change: gamekit's own `pub fn run_later(owns s: Script)` that calls thread.spawn is checked in gamekit's build. game passing it an Enemy races today as well. The change's to_verify says this is "reported in the program's build, at the line that passes the value", but no edited word says so. The suggestion below closes it too.
objections.impact: A use after free and a double free of a one-thread shared value, through the default error type. Nothing is written beyond `thread.spawn`, in the ordinary engine/game split: an engine library with an open `Script` (or `Component`, `Node`, `Widget`) and an error type that keeps the failing object, and a game whose derived class holds a `shares` owner, a `weakref` target or a `Cell`. The ThreadShared half breaks the same way: a derived class's `Cell` read by two scoped tasks through `ref r`, or under a thread_shared RwLock of results. Hot reload reaches the same race by adding a field to a derived class. Every soundness argument for AnyError rests on 'every implementation of Error meets Send and ThreadShared in the final program', and across a package's edge or a reload nothing in the changed text makes that true.
objections.suggestion: Fix it where the derived class is written, as a property. The change already uses that place for a class derived from an error class. The markers a package worked out for one of its open classes, and relied on, are facts of that package's interface (MOD-9, EFF-4), recorded with the class. 'Relied on' means an implementation whose interface needs them, a bound met with them, or a send, scoped `ref` or thread_shared value checked with them. A class derived from that class in a later package, or added or changed by a reload, keeps every such fact. One whose fields break a fact is E2040 at its own line, in its own package or in the reload's plan (E9030 for a reload), naming the line that relied on it and giving a line that compiles (a copy of what it uses). Here that is E2040 at game's line 7, naming gamekit's line 20 and `level`. Within one package the change's rules stay as written. The same property settles route 3: a generic derived class meets the parents for every argument of its parameters, as decision 2 (i) reads a generic implementation, with the bounded line given. It also settles the existing gap of a library's own send of a base value. It is one rule for every interface with marker parents, not a case of Error.

objections.walk:
In C++ terms: a lazily filled `mutable std::string` inside a member object of an exception, read through `what()` from two threads.
CLS-12 (p05 376-380) reads: "On an object several threads reach, the kept result is filled once under a once-flag". Info's fields are a String, so LoadError is Send and ThreadShared (THR-8 p11 47-48 after, THR-9 p11 63-64 after), and line 22 passes. AnyError is ThreadShared by the new THR-9 dyn clause, so `ref r` reaches two scoped tasks (p11 49). Both run LoadError.fmt through the error's table, and both call `this.info.message()` on one Info object. The first call fills the kept String, and later calls return a `ref String` view into it (p05 377-378).
The words of CLS-12 decide it: the Info object is reached by several threads, so the once-flag applies. But the response to S1-3 and the cost section state the duty as "a `@cached` method of a class that implements Error". Info does not implement Error. Its objects are only held by an error. A compiler or a measurement built to the stated scope fills Info.message with a plain flag. Then two tasks store into one place, and one frees the String whose `ref` view the other is reading.
Today `ref r` of a Result[int] to scoped tasks is E7015 (AnyError is not ThreadShared), so this run-time duty is new.
objections.impact: The program must print 68. With a plain flag it has a data race and a read after free. The text is right, so this does not block. But the cost report (and its 'to measure' list) undercounts the once-flag duty: it covers every class whose objects an error may hold, not only error classes.
objections.suggestion: State the duty in the impact as a property of reachability, not of the Error interface. It covers every class whose objects are reachable from an implementer of an interface that requires ThreadShared: its fields, what its `owns` parts hold, and through `owns dyn I` again. Every Error type and everything it holds are included. Such an object is 'an object several threads reach' for CLS-12, and its `@cached` methods are filled under the once-flag. List it under the costs, and measure a `@cached` call on a class held by an error, with the once-flag against a plain flag, on x86-64 and ARM64.

outs.notes:
I am the safety reviewer for round 2 of K20-anyerror-send. All work was read-only, done with Read and Bash cat/sed/grep/ls. Following the team rules, I skipped the repository's start-up reading (AUTOPILOT, HANDOFF).

Both of my round-1 objections are resolved. S1-1's DocError is now E2040 at its own line by the new IFC-3 sentence. S1-3 is decided by CLS-12, and its cost is now stated.

New block S (S2-1): direction D still has a hole across a package's edge and across a hot reload. AnyError is Send and ThreadShared only through the dyn clauses (p11 51 and the new THR-9). Those clauses read the interface, never its implementers, so they are sound only if every implementation of Error meets the parents in the final program. Take an error type in a dependency that holds a field of an open class (gamekit's `LoadError` holding a `Script`). Its implementation is checked once, in the dependency's build (MOD-9). A class that the dependant derives later (game's `Enemy` holding `shares Level`), or a field a reload adds to it (HR-14; HR-44 compares only function facts), is checked by nothing. The new IFC-3 checks only classes 'derived from a class it covers', and Script is not covered. Then the AnyError carries a one-thread owner to another thread, and a plain count races: a use after free or a double free. Today the same program is E7015 at the spawn, so the hole is caused by the change. A generic derived class read per instance (`[T] class Wrapped(GameError)` in a library, instantiated downstream) is a third route. The text does not say whether such a class is checked for every T, as decision 2 (i) reads a generic implementation, or per instance.

Suggested fix, as a property: the markers a package relied on for its open class are facts of its interface, and a derived class in a later package or a reload keeps them. One that breaks them is E2040 at its own line, naming the line that relied on them. A generic derived class meets the parents for every argument of its parameters.

Weighed, block none (S2-2): the once-flag duty in the cost section covers 'a class that implements Error'. CLS-12's words cover every class whose objects an error holds, which is wider.

Existing gaps, not caused by the change, listed for later: (1) A library's own send of a base-class value (`pub fn run_later(owns s: Script)` with thread.spawn) is checked in the library's build. A dependant's derived class with a one-thread part then crosses, today and after the change. The change's to_verify says the program's build reports it, but no edited word says so. S2-1's property closes it. (2) EFF-2/EFF-4 say a call or drop through a dyn counts 'every implementation the program has'. They do not state how a library's lines that end an `owns dyn I` on another thread count a dependant's implementations, for example a drop that changes a main-thread `static mut` (THR-20). This exists today for locally made AnyErrors and for any `owns dyn Job`.

All present at those lines as quoted.

The question's own program (J6-16) is decided by the changed words: p04 676 (after) with p11 51 ('`dyn I` when `I` requires it') makes AnyError Send, which meets THR-10's R: Send (p11 175-176). Not U.

Rules citing or cited by the changed rules: ERR-1, ERR-7, ERR-8 (p13 93-101), ERR-10, ERR-11, ERR-12 (p13 109-112, ODR-050), TYP-5 rule 8 (p04 84-86), TYP-17, TYP-36 (p04 687-700), TYP-43 (p04 581-598), EFF-4 (p10 52-64), EFF-24 (p10 90-105), EFF-25, CLS-12 (p05 376-384), HR-44 (p20-annex-b 54-66), E7015 row (p17a 217). # package engine (a library): engine/src/lib.em
from std.fmt import Formatter, FmtError

pub open class Script:
    pub entity: int

    pub fn init(entity: int):
        this.entity = entity

pub struct ScriptError:
    pub script: Script

extend ScriptError implements Display:
    fn fmt(ref mut f: Formatter) -> Result[void, FmtError]:
        return f.write_str("the script failed")

extend ScriptError implements Debug:
    fn fmt_debug(ref mut f: Formatter) -> Result[void, FmtError]:
        return f.write_str("ScriptError")

extend ScriptError implements Error:
    pass

pub fn fail(owns s: Script) -> Result[int, ScriptError]:
    return Err(ScriptError(script=s))

# package game (uses engine): game/src/main.em
import std.thread
from std.sync import Sender, channel
from engine import Script, fail

class Level:
    name: String = String("forest")

class Enemy(Script):
    level: shares Level

    fn init(entity: int, owns level: shares Level):
        this.level = level
        super.init(entity)

fn tick(owns s: Script) -> Result[int]:
    return Ok(fail(owns s)?)                         # ScriptError -> AnyError

fn work(tx: Sender[Result[int]]):
    level = shares Level()
    tx.send(owns tick(owns Enemy(1, shares level))).expect("receiver is gone")
    n = 0
    for _ in 0..1000000:
        extra = shares level                         # plain add and sub on this thread
        n += extra.name.len()
    println(n)

fn main():
    tx, rx = channel[Result[int]](capacity=1)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns tx: work(tx))
    for r in rx:
        match r:
            Ok(n) => println(n)
            Err(e) => println(e)                     # the Enemy ends here: a plain sub on the main thread
    h.join()

The new class rule closes this inside one package, but not across a package edge, and the AnyError route is new. (1) engine's build. THR-8 (p11 47-48, after) counts in Script's components 'any class the program derives from it, a library's included'. engine's build sees no derived class, so `Script` (`entity: int`) is Send and ThreadShared, and so is `ScriptError`. IFC-3 (p05 411-413, after): 'An implementation meets its interface's parents for every type it covers'. engine line 21 covers `ScriptError`, which meets them in engine's build, so it is accepted. EFF-4 (p10 52-56) records engine's worked-out facts in its interface file, and 'a fact for which a word exists counts only as written': `extend ScriptError implements Error` is written. (2) game's build. `class Enemy(Script):`: IFC-3's derived-class words reach only 'each class derived from a class it covers'. The implementation covers `ScriptError`, a struct, not `Script`, and `Script` implements no interface with marker parents, so nothing is checked here. `fail(owns s)?`: ERR-8 (p13 95) needs `ScriptError: needs Error`, which engine's written implementation meets. IFC-3 places a refusal only 'at the generic implementation' (engine line 21 is neither generic nor in game) 'or where the derived class is declared' (Enemy is not derived from a covered class), so no line of game is refused. `channel[Result[int]]` and the spawn's `owns tx`: a Sender is Send when its element is. `Result[int, AnyError]` is Send because AnyError holds `owns dyn Error`, and THR-8 p11 51 makes '`dyn I` [Send] when `I` requires it', which Error now does (p04 676, after). AnyError's Send rests on the requirement, never on what the box holds. So the program compiles. The worker's loop changes `level`'s plain count while main ends `e`, and with it the Enemy's `level` owner, which is a plain sub on another thread: a race on the count, then a double free or a leak. (3) Today: Error does not require Send, so `Sender[Result[int]]` is not Send, and the spawn's `owns tx` is E7015 (p11 51, THR-10 p11 175-176). The same program does not go wrong today, so the change causes it. The concrete-error version (`channel[Result[int, ScriptError]]`) is refused after the change, because game's build infers ScriptError's Send from its fields with Enemy counted. Only the erased route lets the program through, because it trusts a requirement checked in a package that could not see Enemy. (4) Same cause, existing gaps: to_verify item 6 says a library line that sends a base value 'is reported in the program's build, at the line that passes the value', but no edited rule says so. HR-44 (p20-annex-b 54-61) compares only functions' worked-out facts, so a reload that adds such a derived class is not compared either.
objections.impact: Decision D is sound only if every error's markers hold in the build that uses it. For an error type in one package that holds an object of an open class (a field, an element, an `owns` part), the markers were judged without the classes another package derives later, and every AnyError, channel of results, scoped `ref` and thread_shared holder of results then carries a one-thread owner across threads. Library error types holding a base-class object are ordinary: a game engine's ScriptError holding the failing Script, a UI toolkit's error holding the Widget. The impact report says the class rule closes the open-class hole, but across a package edge it does not, and it gives the library-line placement only in to_verify.
objections.suggestion: A property, one rule (it fits after IFC-3's new words, or in THR-8 beside the class clause). Every fact a package works out that rests on an open or abstract class's markers is part of its interface (EFF-4), and a class derived from that class in another package, or an instance of a generic derived class made there, must keep it. The fact is either an implementation whose interface's parents include `Send` or `ThreadShared` and whose type may hold the class's objects, or a function that hands, shares or gives to tasks a parameter that may hold them. A derived class that breaks an implementation's fact is refused at its own declaration (as IFC-3 places a derived error class). A derived class that breaks a function's fact is refused at the call that passes a value that may be one of its objects (EFF-4's chain). The message names the relying line in the other package and gives a line that compiles: a copy of what the derived class uses (`level_name: String` in place of `level: shares Level`). A reload that adds such a class is compared the same way (HR-44). Inside one package, decision 3's option (i) stays as written. Add the cross-package rows to programs_changed and move to_verify item 6 into the rule text.

tests.name: k20r2_library_error_holding_open_class_derived_in_program
tests.program:
# package engine (a library): engine/src/lib.em
from std.fmt import Formatter, FmtError

pub open class Script:
    pub entity: int

    pub fn init(entity: int):
        this.entity = entity

pub struct ScriptError:
    pub script: Script

extend ScriptError implements Display:
    fn fmt(ref mut f: Formatter) -> Result[void, FmtError]:
        return f.write_str("the script failed")

extend ScriptError implements Debug:
    fn fmt_debug(ref mut f: Formatter) -> Result[void, FmtError]:
        return f.write_str("ScriptError")

extend ScriptError implements Error:
    pass

pub fn fail(owns s: Script) -> Result[int, ScriptError]:
    return Err(ScriptError(script=s))

# package game (uses engine): game/src/main.em
import std.thread
from std.sync import Sender, channel
from engine import Script, fail

class Level:
    name: String = String("forest")

class Enemy(Script):
    level: shares Level

    fn init(entity: int, owns level: shares Level):
        this.level = level
        super.init(entity)

fn tick(owns s: Script) -> Result[int]:
    return Ok(fail(owns s)?)

fn work(tx: Sender[Result[int]]):
    level = shares Level()
    tx.send(owns tick(owns Enemy(1, shares level))).expect("receiver is gone")
    n = 0
    for _ in 0..1000000:
        extra = shares level
        n += extra.name.len()
    println(n)

fn main():
    tx, rx = channel[Result[int]](capacity=1)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns tx: work(tx))
    for r in rx:
        match r:
            Ok(n) => println(n)
            Err(e) => println(e)
    h.join()
tests.expected: E2040 at game/src/main.em line 9 (`class Enemy(Script):`), gist: "`Enemy` is a `Script`, and engine's `ScriptError` (engine/src/lib.em line 21) is an error that holds a `Script`, and any thread may have and read an error, but `level` (line 10) is a `shares Level`, an owner that stays on one thread; hold a copy of what the enemy uses: write `level_name: String` in place of line 10" (with the suggested fix; under the changed words as written it compiles and races)

outs.notes:
I ran the round-2 review in one pass, read-only. All nine round-1 engineering and integration objections are resolved by the rewrite. Every edit's before words are at the stated part-file lines. The question's program is decided, so there is no U, and I found no X.

New: one block S. Decision D's soundness rests on each error type's markers. For an error type in a library that holds an object of an open class, those markers are judged in the library's build, which cannot see the classes a program derives later. IFC-3's new placement ('at the generic implementation or where the derived class is declared, which its own package checks') reaches only classes derived from a class the implementation covers, and EFF-4 counts the library's implementation as written. So a program's `class Enemy(Script)` holding a `shares` owner passes, and AnyError, Send by requirement, carries it across threads. Today this is refused, because AnyError is not Send. The concrete-error version is refused after the change, so only the erased route leaks.

The suggested fix is one property: an open class's relied-on markers are part of its package's interface. A derived class elsewhere that breaks one is refused at its declaration when an implementation relies on the marker, or at the passing call when a function does, and HR-44 compares reloads the same way. It keeps option (i) unchanged inside one package. It also turns to_verify item 6, the library-line placement, into rule text.

Two low points, not blocking. Decision 3's owner_short does not show that (i) has the same far-break shape for which C was turned down in decision 1. And TYP-43's prose (p04 583, 'which its words say') should name the derived classes' words.

Existing gaps, not caused by the change: the plain library-line route, where a library `pub fn` sends a base-class parameter (it goes wrong today too), and HR-44 not comparing class markers on reload.

rulings.objection: S2-1 (safety, block S): a library's error struct holds an object of its own open class `Script`. In the library's build the error is judged Send and ThreadShared. A game in another package derives `Enemy(Script)` holding `shares Level`, and that owner reaches another thread inside an AnyError.
rulings.evidence: Walked through the changed text. (1) gamekit's build. THR-8 after (p11 47-48) counts "any class the program derives from it, a library's included". gamekit derives nothing from Script, so LoadError (`script: Script`, `entity: int`) is Send and ThreadShared, and `extend LoadError implements Error:` meets IFC-3 after ("An implementation meets its interface's parents for every type it covers"). (2) game's build. IFC-3 after places the refusal only "either at the generic implementation ... or where the derived class is declared", and the derived-class check reaches only "each class derived from a class it covers". The Error implementation covers LoadError, a struct. It does not cover Script, and Script implements nothing, so `class Enemy(Script):` is checked against nothing. ERR-3 after says the same: "or where it is derived from a class that does". (3) MOD-9 (p05 38-46) says what crosses a package's edge: the written words, plus the facts it lists ("what each function may change, read and end ... the locks it may take; the function values it stores and the callbacks it hands to C"). No edited word records that gamekit relied on Script's markers. No edited word makes game's build check gamekit's implementation again either. (4) The `?` into AnyError needs `E: needs Error` (ERR-8, p13 95), and gamekit's written implementation meets it. AnyError's `Box[dyn Error]` is Send by p11 51 ("`dyn I` when `I` requires it"), which reads the interface and never what the box holds. So the spawn compiles. The worker ends the Enemy's `shares` owner while main changes the same count with plain adds (RC-4 / THR-2 p11 100-101): a race on a non-atomic count, then a use after free or a double free. Today the same program is E7015 at the spawn: p04 676 and p13 88 give Error only Debug and Display, so by p11 51 `dyn Error` is not Send. So the change causes it. The other reading (game's build checks gamekit's line 20 again) is refused at a dependency's line that the text places nowhere. One of the two readings lets a race through, so this is S. The reload route (HR-44 compares only functions' facts) and the generic-derived-class route come from the same missing rule. I did not walk them separately, and the first route settles the ruling.

rulings.objection: E2-1 (engineering, block S): the same cross-package hole by the channel route. engine's `ScriptError` holds `script: Script`, game derives `Enemy(Script)` holding `shares Level`, and a `Sender[Result[int]]` is spawned.
rulings.evidence: Same cause as S2-1, a second program. In engine's build, THR-8 after (p11 47-48) sees no derived class, so ScriptError meets IFC-3 after at its `implements Error`. EFF-4 (p10 52-56) says "a fact for which a word exists counts only as written", and the implementation is written. In game's build, IFC-3 after's two refusal places ("at the generic implementation ... or where the derived class is declared" for a class "derived from a class it covers") miss `class Enemy(Script):` and `fail(owns s)?`. `Sender[Result[int]]` is Send because AnyError's `owns dyn Error` is Send by requirement (p11 51, with p04 676 after). So the spawn's `owns tx` compiles, and main ending `e` takes a plain -1 from `level`'s count while the worker's loop changes it: a race, then a double free or a leak. Today it is E7015 at the spawn, because Error does not require Send. So the change causes it. The objection also points out something true: the concrete route `channel[Result[int, ScriptError]]` is refused after the change, because game's build infers ScriptError's Send with Enemy counted. Only the erased route trusts a requirement that was checked where Enemy could not be seen. One repair closes both S2-1 and E2-1. to_verify item 6 ("reported in the program's build, at the line that passes the value") is in no edited rule.

rulings.objection: S2-2 (safety, block none): a `@cached` method on `Info`, a class that an error holds but that does not implement Error, is filled from two scoped tasks through `ref r`. The impact limits the once-flag duty to classes that implement Error.
rulings.evidence: The text decides the program correctly. CLS-12 (p05 379-380) reads "On an object several threads reach, the kept result is filled once under a once-flag". After the change the Info object is reached by two tasks: LoadError is ThreadShared by THR-8 after and THR-9 after, AnyError is ThreadShared by the new THR-9 dyn clause, and a `ref T` is Send when T is ThreadShared (p11 49). So the program prints 68 under the words. But the response to S1-3 and the cost section scope the duty as "a `@cached` method of a class that implements Error". Info does not implement Error, so the impact report understates the run-time duty and its to-measure list. The report is wrong. The rules are not.

rulings.objection: E2-2 (engineering, block none): decision 3's option (i) has the far-break property that decision 1 used to turn down option C (an added derived class anywhere breaks a hand-off of the base class elsewhere), and the owner_short does not say so.
rulings.evidence: Under THR-8 after (p11 47-48), adding `class Enemy(Script)` with `level: shares Level` in any module or package makes every hand-over, scoped `ref` or thread_shared holder of a `Script` E7015, naming a class the sending line never mentions. Decision 3's long outcome admits it ("A library's line may depend on a class the program derives"). Decision 1's parameter 5 turns C down for "an edit anywhere break a spawn far away". Decision 3's owner_short step table and option (i) ("nothing written") leave the property out. So the owner would weigh C and (i) on different terms. Program outcomes do not change.

rulings.objection: E2-3 (engineering, block none): TYP-43's prose says the markers are inferred from what a type holds, "which its words say", which after the change is no longer true of an open or abstract class.
rulings.evidence: p04 583: "`Send` and `ThreadShared` are inferred from what a type holds, which its words say." Script's own words (`entity: int`) say Send, while the edited row (p04 577 after) and THR-8 after count Enemy's `level`. TYP-43 also says "the table answers them" (p04 582-583), so the table wins and the program's outcome is the same: no contradiction (not X). But the prose now gives the wrong reason for every open class. It needs one clause.

tradeoffs.objection: S2-2: the once-flag duty for `@cached` methods reachable from an error
tradeoffs.why: Keeping CLS-12's once-flag on every object several threads may reach is the safe and cheapest way that compiles these programs. It is one acquire load per call (a plain `mov` on x86-64, an `ldar` on ARM64) and one compare-and-swap on the first fill, and today it is already the duty for any ThreadShared class given by `ref` to scoped tasks. So the trade-off is justified by goal B. What is not justified is the report's scope. The duty covers every class whose objects are reachable from an error (its fields, its `owns` parts, through `owns dyn I` again), not only classes that implement Error. The cost section and its to-measure list should say that, and add a measurement of a `@cached` call on a class an error holds.

tradeoffs.objection: E2-2: decision 3 option (i): a derived class added anywhere can break a base-class hand-off far away
tradeoffs.why: (i) is narrower than C. It reads one hierarchy's declarations (the words of types, as TYP-43 infers markers), not every `?` line's body. Its message names the derived class and its field. It is the same reach the language already accepts for virtual calls (EFF-2 p10 41-42: "every implementation and override the program has"; verdict 122, "a library's included") and the far edit that verdict 86 accepted when the message names the chain. So it fits the common goal better than (ii) or (iii), which refuse ordinary hierarchies or std's ECS World. But verdict 61 turned down a whole-program search, and the owner_short hides that (i) has this property. The owner must see it, with (i) and C weighed on the same term.

tradeoffs.objection: E2-3: TYP-43's prose reason for the markers
tradeoffs.why: One clause ("and for an open or abstract class, the words of every class derived from it") makes the prose say what the table and THR-8 after decide. Outcomes, cost and verdicts stay the same, so only wording is at stake.

out.summary: Not yet. The change answers J6-16 (direction D: every error is safe to hand to and read from any thread, so `Result[int]` comes back from a worker with nothing written). But it is blocked by one safety hole, reported twice (S2-1 and E2-1). Take a library error struct that holds an object of the library's own open class (an engine's `LoadError` holding the failing `Script`). It is judged thread-safe in the library's build, which cannot see the game's classes. A game in another package then derives `Enemy(Script)` holding a one-thread shared owner. The changed IFC-3 checks a derived class only when it derives from a class that implements Error, and Script implements nothing, so no line of the game is checked. AnyError is Send from Error's requirement alone (p11 51), so the owner crosses threads inside an AnyError and its plain count races (use after free or double free). Today the same program is refused at the spawn, so the change causes it. The repair is one property, not a case. Every thread fact a package worked out from one of its open classes and relied on becomes a fact of that package's interface (MOD-9, EFF-4). A class derived later, in another package or by a reload, must keep it, and is refused at its own line, with the message naming the line that relied on it and giving a copy line. The same property closes the generic-derived-class route, and to_verify item 6 (a library's own send of a base value) should move into rule text. Three objections do not block. S2-2: CLS-12 decides it, but the cost report scopes the once-flag too narrowly. E2-2: decision 3's short text hides that option (i) has the far-break property C was turned down for. E2-3: TYP-43's prose needs one clause. All three are real, and two must go to the owner.

owner_short.one_line: Making every error type safe for any thread (as Swift's errors are) lets the catch-all error (like C++'s `std::exception_ptr`) come back from a worker thread. But as written, an engine library's error that holds a `Base*` can still carry a game's `Derived` object, holding a non-atomic refcount, to another thread.
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | engine library | declares an error that keeps the failing `Script` object; checked alone it is thread-safe | allowed
2 | game (another package) | declares `Enemy`, a kind of `Script`, holding a one-thread shared owner | allowed: nothing checks it against the engine's error
3 | game | puts an `Enemy` into that error, then the error into the catch-all, and hands it to a thread | allowed, though today it is refused
4 | both threads | change the same one-thread count at once | race: freed memory read or freed twice
owner_short.today: A worker returning `Result[int]` is refused at `thread.spawn` without a word of explanation, so the race above cannot happen.
options: Repair and keep D: a class derived later, in another package or by a reload, must keep the thread-safety the library relied on, and is refused at its own line with the fix
D as written: unsafe across libraries, so not acceptable
A: check each error where `?` puts it into the catch-all (the game's own build sees the Enemy, so it is safe), but generic error code and wrappers must write thread words
B: keep today: the catch-all stays on its thread, and workers name their own error type
owner_short.recommendation: Repair and keep D. Ordinary worker code still compiles with nothing written, and the one-thread object is refused at the line of the game's class that holds it.

rulings.objection: E2-2 (engineering, block none): decision 3's option (i) has the far-break property that decision 1 used to turn down option C (an added derived class anywhere breaks a hand-off of the base class elsewhere), and the owner_short does not say so.

Script's own words (`entity: int`) say Send, while the edited row (p04 577 after) and THR-8 after count Enemy's `level`. tradeoffs.objection: S2-2: the once-flag duty for `@cached` methods reachable from an error
tradeoffs.why: Keeping CLS-12's once-flag on every object several threads may reach is the safe and cheapest way that compiles these programs. It is one acquire load per call (a plain `mov` on x86-64, an `ldar` on ARM64) and one compare-and-swap on the first fill, and today it is already the duty for any ThreadShared class given by `ref` to scoped tasks. So the trade-off is justified by goal B. What is not justified is the report's scope. The duty covers every class whose objects are reachable from an error (its fields, its `owns` parts, through `owns dyn I` again), not only classes that implement Error. The cost section and its to-measure list should say that, and add a measurement of a `@cached` call on a class an error holds.

tradeoffs.objection: E2-2: decision 3 option (i): a derived class added anywhere can break a base-class hand-off far away
tradeoffs.why: (i) is narrower than C. It reads one hierarchy's declarations (the words of types, as TYP-43 infers markers), not every `?` line's body. Its message names the derived class and its field. It is the same reach the language already accepts for virtual calls (EFF-2 p10 41-42: "every implementation and override the program has"; verdict 122, "a library's included") and the far edit that verdict 86 accepted when the message names the chain. So it fits the common goal better than (ii) or (iii), which refuse ordinary hierarchies or std's ECS World. But verdict 61 turned down a whole-program search, and the owner_short hides that (i) has this property. The owner must see it, with (i) and C weighed on the same term.

tradeoffs.objection: E2-3: TYP-43's prose reason for the markers
tradeoffs.why: One clause ("and for an open or abstract class, the words of every class derived from it") makes the prose say what the table and THR-8 after decide. Outcomes, cost and verdicts stay the same, so only wording is at stake.

arbiter.summary: Not yet. The change answers J6-16 (direction D: every error is safe to hand to and read from any thread, so `Result[int]` comes back from a worker with nothing written). But it is blocked by one safety hole, reported twice (S2-1 and E2-1). Take a library error struct that holds an object of the library's own open class (an engine's `LoadError` holding the failing `Script`). It is judged thread-safe in the library's build, which cannot see the game's classes. A game in another package then derives `Enemy(Script)` holding a one-thread shared owner. The changed IFC-3 checks a derived class only when it derives from a class that implements Error, and Script implements nothing, so no line of the game is checked. AnyError is Send from Error's requirement alone (p11 51), so the owner crosses threads inside an AnyError and its plain count races (use after free or double free). Today the same program is refused at the spawn, so the change causes it. The repair is one property, not a case. Every thread fact a package worked out from one of its open classes and relied on becomes a fact of that package's interface (MOD-9, EFF-4). A class derived later, in another package or by a reload, must keep it, and is refused at its own line, with the message naming the line that relied on it and giving a copy line. The same property closes the generic-derived-class route, and to_verify item 6 (a library's own send of a base value) should move into rule text. Three objections do not block. S2-2: CLS-12 decides it, but the cost report scopes the once-flag too narrowly. E2-2: decision 3's short text hides that option (i) has the far-break property C was turned down for. E2-3: TYP-43's prose needs one clause. All three are real, and two must go to the owner.

owner_short.one_line: Making every error type safe for any thread (as Swift's errors are) lets the catch-all error (like C++'s `std::exception_ptr`) come back from a worker thread. But as written, an engine library's error that holds a `Base*` can still carry a game's `Derived` object, holding a non-atomic refcount, to another thread.
owner_short.step_table:
step | who | what happens | result
1 | engine library | declares an error that keeps the failing `Script` object; checked alone it is thread-safe | allowed
2 | game (another package) | declares `Enemy`, a kind of `Script`, holding a one-thread shared owner | allowed: nothing checks it against the engine's error
3 | game | puts an `Enemy` into that error, then the error into the catch-all, and hands it to a thread | allowed, though today it is refused
4 | both threads | change the same one-thread count at once | race: freed memory read or freed twice
owner_short.today: A worker returning `Result[int]` is refused at `thread.spawn` without a word of explanation, so the race above cannot happen.
options: Repair and keep D: a class derived later, in another package or by a reload, must keep the thread-safety the library relied on, and is refused at its own line with the fix
D as written: unsafe across libraries, so not acceptable
A: check each error where `?` puts it into the catch-all (the game's own build sees the Enemy, so it is safe), but generic error code and wrappers must write thread words
B: keep today: the catch-all stays on its thread, and workers name their own error type
owner_short.recommendation: Repair and keep D. Ordinary worker code still compiles with nothing written, and the one-thread object is refused at the line of the game's class that holds it.

blockers.objection: S2-1 (safety, block S): a library's error struct holds an object of its own open class `Script`. In the library's build the error is judged Send and ThreadShared. A game in another package derives `Enemy(Script)` holding `shares Level`, and that owner reaches another thread inside an AnyError.
blockers.evidence: Walked through the changed text. (1) gamekit's build. THR-8 after (p11 47-48) counts "any class the program derives from it, a library's included". gamekit derives nothing from Script, so LoadError (`script: Script`, `entity: int`) is Send and ThreadShared, and `extend LoadError implements Error:` meets IFC-3 after ("An implementation meets its interface's parents for every type it covers"). (2) game's build. IFC-3 after places the refusal only "either at the generic implementation ... or where the derived class is declared", and the derived-class check reaches only "each class derived from a class it covers". The Error implementation covers LoadError, a struct. It does not cover Script, and Script implements nothing, so `class Enemy(Script):` is checked against nothing. ERR-3 after says the same: "or where it is derived from a class that does". (3) MOD-9 (p05 38-46) says what crosses a package's edge: the written words, plus the facts it lists ("what each function may change, read and end ... the locks it may take; the function values it stores and the callbacks it hands to C"). No edited word records that gamekit relied on Script's markers. No edited word makes game's build check gamekit's implementation again either. (4) The `?` into AnyError needs `E: needs Error` (ERR-8, p13 95), and gamekit's written implementation meets it. AnyError's `Box[dyn Error]` is Send by p11 51 ("`dyn I` when `I` requires it"), which reads the interface and never what the box holds. So the spawn compiles. The worker ends the Enemy's `shares` owner while main changes the same count with plain adds (RC-4 / THR-2 p11 100-101): a race on a non-atomic count, then a use after free or a double free. Today the same program is E7015 at the spawn: p04 676 and p13 88 give Error only Debug and Display, so by p11 51 `dyn Error` is not Send. So the change causes it. The other reading (game's build checks gamekit's line 20 again) is refused at a dependency's line that the text places nowhere. One of the two readings lets a race through, so this is S. The reload route (HR-44 compares only functions' facts) and the generic-derived-class route come from the same missing rule. I did not walk them separately, and the first route settles the ruling.

blockers.objection: E2-1 (engineering, block S): the same cross-package hole by the channel route. engine's `ScriptError` holds `script: Script`, game derives `Enemy(Script)` holding `shares Level`, and a `Sender[Result[int]]` is spawned.
blockers.evidence: Same cause as S2-1, a second program. In engine's build, THR-8 after (p11 47-48) sees no derived class, so ScriptError meets IFC-3 after at its `implements Error`. EFF-4 (p10 52-56) says "a fact for which a word exists counts only as written", and the implementation is written. In game's build, IFC-3 after's two refusal places ("at the generic implementation ... or where the derived class is declared" for a class "derived from a class it covers") miss `class Enemy(Script):` and `fail(owns s)?`. `Sender[Result[int]]` is Send because AnyError's `owns dyn Error` is Send by requirement (p11 51, with p04 676 after). So the spawn's `owns tx` compiles, and main ending `e` takes a plain -1 from `level`'s count while the worker's loop changes it: a race, then a double free or a leak. Today it is E7015 at the spawn, because Error does not require Send. So the change causes it. The objection also points out something true: the concrete route `channel[Result[int, ScriptError]]` is refused after the change, because game's build infers ScriptError's Send with Enemy counted. Only the erased route trusts a requirement that was checked where Enemy could not be seen. One repair closes both S2-1 and E2-1. to_verify item 6 ("reported in the program's build, at the line that passes the value") is in no edited rule.

final.intent: A thing one thread made and another let go of (a pooled connection, a GPU texture, a packet buffer) is ended soon by its drop, at a point where running that drop breaks no rule, and is never left undone because its making thread sleeps in the job pool.

cause.where: RC-4 point 3 (tasks/spec-0.9.9/parts/p08-classes.md 169-172), with RC-4 point 4 (p08 173-178), THR-20's headline 'A `drop` runs where the last owner ends' (p11-concurrency.md 296-301) and DRP-8 (p07-ownership.md 865-873).
cause.why_there: A check point is where a queued value is ended, so it is where its drop runs (RC-4 point 2, p08 166-168; WK-3, p08 365-367). DRP-8 makes every end a call of the drop 'for every rule that needs them'. Point 3 places those ends by position only. So they land inside a lock the drop takes, inside a walk or view of what it changes, inside a scope whose tasks touch it, or inside a no-waiting function (J7-01). It also ties the last end to the thread's end, which a pool worker reaches only with the process (THR-16) and a host thread never shows (FFI-31a) (J7-02). The debate showed the same cause three more ways. (1) A value whose maker can never run its drop safely must not be queued at all, and that is judged by where its making line runs, not by where it is written (point 4). (2) A by-type view rule is untrue for what the queue ends only for a view that holds a count or reads through an owner. A `weakref` view of an object that is not `thread_shared` does neither. (3) A thread's last point must come before its join is let go. Then THR-20's count (the making thread may run the drop) stays true and THR-19 judges the join. The reporting rules are right as written: each one sees only what point 3 and THR-20 hand it.
cause.reported_at: BRW-18, EFF-24, FFI-22, HR-3a, JOB-2, RC-3, RC-4, THR-16, THR-19, THR-20, WK-3
